PREFACE 


BEFORE anything else is said it is proper that the thanks of all who have been concerned 
in the preparation of this book should be offered to the earl of Winchilsea and Notting- 
ham, the owner by inheritance of the original manuscript. They thank him in the 
first instance for permission to print an edition of the documents included in this 
notable collection. They also desire to acknowledge his forbearance in allowing the 
original manuscript to remain for long periods in London in order that the editorial 
work might be carried through. 

The Book of Seals was recalled to the memory of the present generation of scholars 
when the thirteenth Lord Winchilsea, the grandfather of the present owner of the book, 
showed it to Canon C. W. Foster at Haverholme Priory in Lincolnshire in 1921. With 
a generosity characteristic of his line Lord Winchilsea allowed the Canon to borrow 
the book, and it joined the cartularies of Lincoln Cathedral in the safe which was the 
most noticeable piece of furniture in the hall of Timberland Vicarage. Canon Foster 
at once showed the book to my husband and to me and told other scholars interested 
in charters and family history. There was not enough Lincolnshire material in the 
book to justify its publication as a volume of the Lincolnshire Record Society. Canon 
Foster therefore consulted Mr. G. N. Clark about the possibility of printing the early 
charters in the English Historical Review of which he was at that time editor. Mr. Clark 
was sympathetic, but Canon Foster did not carry the proposal any farther. Lord 
Winchilsea left Haverholme Priory in 1926. After his death in 1927 his son, the four- 
teenth earl, deposited his collection of manuscripts, including the Book of Seals, in 
the custody of the Northamptonshire Record Society for the use of students. 

At a meeting of the Council of the Society held on 26 November 1936 it was agreed 
that an edition of the Book of Seals should be published by the Society and that Mr. 
L. C. Loyd should be asked to undertake the work. Mr. Loyd was a foundation mem- 
ber of the Society, was closely connected with Northamptonshire, and had recently 
retired from the Treasury Solicitor’s Office. His unique knowledge of feudal genealogy 
both in England and Normandy enabled him to carry through the laborious work of 
identifying the names and families of those who issued the charters and of determining 
the origin of their connexion with the lands involved. This task was the more difficult 
in that the charters range in time over the whole medieval period and in place through 
every English county. 

In the years before 1939 Mr. Loyd had identified surviving originals of the charters 
entered in the Book of Seals, had well begun the work of identifying the people and 
places mentioned in the charters, and had begun to collect notes from Dodsworth’s 
manuscripts for the Introduction. The outbreak of war sent him back to his desk in 
the Treasury Solicitor’s Office, but he continued to spend his spare time on the Book 
of Seals. He put his transcripts in envelopes each containing fifty charters, and as he 


completed work on the contents of an envelope he sent it for safety to his brother’s 
5172 b 


Vii PREFACE 


house at Lockinge. Failing health after six years of war, spent almost without a break 
in London, made Mr. Loyd unwilling to face the task of revising the work, writing 
the Introduction, making the indexes, and seeing the book through the press. I there- 
fore suggested that if my husband and I came into the work, with which we had both 
been in close touch through these years, Mr. Loyd might be able to turn his mind 
to the remaining problems of the charters. In the event the work has fallen to me, 
for my husband became Vice-Chancellor of his University in 1946 and was obliged 
temporarily to abandon historical work. Mr. Loyd had almost completed his annota- 
tions before his last illness and his death in August 1947. Those who know his work 
in the Complete Peerage will recognize the master touch in such notes as, for example, 
those to Nos. 35 or 107. 

The problem of paying for the printing of such a volume was far graver in 1947 
than it had been ten years before and was now beyond the unaided resources of the 
Northamptonshire Record Society. At the suggestion of the President of St. John’s 
College, Mr. A. L. Poole, the Delegates of the Clarendon Press have made the present 
publication possible, and it is now issued as a joint tribute to my husband from his 
individual friends and from the Society which he helped to found. The Secretary of 
the Clarendon Press and all the members of the staff involved in its production have 
spared no pains to make this book in its own way as beautiful as the Book of Seals 
itself. I am very grateful to every one of them. To the readers of the Clarendon Press 
my especial gratitude is due, for they have saved me from many inconsistencies and 
errors. 

My part in this book has been to revise Mr. Loyd’s copy for press, to write notes on 
the charters not annotated by him, to make the indexes, and to write the Introduction. 
Mr. Loyd, conscious of the size and probable cost of the volume, had planned to 
print in full only such charters as could be dated before about 1220; even that number 
seemed formidable. The rest he abstracted in full. Some of the documents of a later 
date than that set by Mr. Loyd have seemed to me of such interest that I have printed 
them in full. To make room for this I have somewhat cut down Mr. Loyd’s abstracts, 
but I hope that nothing of any importance has been omitted. 

Mr. Loyd would have wished to add his thanks to mine for the generous help we 
have both received from many scholars while this work has been in progress. Without 
the enterprise and public spirit of the Northamptonshire Record Society and its 
Honorary Editor and Secretary, Mr. Loyd would never have begun the work. Miss 
Dorothea Paton, lecturer in Old French in the University of Reading, has read for us 
the documents in that language. On all points of law I have turned remorselessly to 
Professor T. F. T. Plucknett for help which he has unstintingly given. One long note 
he has been good enough to allow me to print under his name. I am grateful to 
Mr. C. E. Wright of the British Museum not only for telling me about Sir Frederick 
Madden’s Notebook and thus filling a gap in the history of the Book of Seals, but also 
for the generous way he has allowed me to draw upon his profound knowledge of the 
antiquaries of the seventeenth century. 


PREFACE ix 


This work could never have been carried to completion without the help of Mr. 
Charles Clay. In 1936 Mr. H. S. Kingsford agreed to write the heraldic description of 
the seals, a task for which Mr. Loyd felt himself to be unqualified. Before he had 
dealt with half the seals Mr. Kingsford died. When the plan of the present volume was 
under discussion in the summer of 1948 Mr. Clay most generously offered to take 
charge of this part of the work. He checked the descriptions already written and wrote 
the large number still remaining to be done. His profound knowledge of the feudal 
world, and particularly his knowledge of the north, was frequently drawn on by 
Mr. Loyd as he was working on the genealogical aspect of the charters. It has been as 
freely at my service. Hehasread the first proofs of the book and immediately responded 
to any appeal for help. I must, however, recognize that responsibility for any errors 
in the final proofs is mine. 

This book is dedicated to my husband, who from the day he first saw the Book of 
Seals at Timberland Vicarage has constantly urged that it should be made available in 
print. It is his birthday present from his friends, and from the Society which he 
helped to found. They will not reproach me for appealing, as I have worked, to him 
de cuius stillicidiis nos quoque modicum id quod habemus per traducem accepimus. 


D. M. S.

INTRODUCTION 
I 


SIR CHRISTOPHER HATTON’s Book of Seals! consists to-day of 128 vellum folios, each 
approximately 17; 133in. Charters are entered on both sides of folios 1 to 118, with 
the exception of the dorse of folios 1, 5, 10, 17, 24, 39, 59, 83, 89,94, 95, 98, 107, 108, 
113, 115, 116, 117, 118. Of the 529 charters in the book 240 are facsimiles of the 
original deed done with painful care. Some of the charters facsimiled in the book 
survive in the British Museum. These have been printed from the originals, and variant 
readings are given in footnotes. The absence of such variant readings where the charter 
is in facsimile and their rarity in other cases is a striking testimony to the accuracy of 
the draftsman. The photographs in the present volume well illustrate the technical 
perfection of the work, but no photograph can give the full beauty of the charters as 
they are portrayed in the Book of Seals itself. The photograph shows a hardness of 
outline, a clear-cut squareness which reveals the basic drawing of the charter upon 
the page. In the book itself this harshness is less apparent because most of the charters 
are carefully tinted to give the impression of old parchment. The tinting makes them 
stand out from the vellum page as would an actual charter laid on it. The colour 
of the cords, where cords were used to attach the seals, and the colour of the seals 
themselves are shown. At the head of each page the name and titles of the owner of 
the deeds shown below are boldly written in scarlet letters, so that the open book 
conveys a richness and variety of colour delightful to the eye. 

The artist, for the man who made the book deserves this title, was careful to repro- 
duce the exact size and shape of the document. The indentation of chirographs, the 
turn-ups at the bottom of charters, the width of seal strips, the ribands below or above 
them, the plaiting or knots in seal cords are all faithfully drawn. Even if he did not 
reproduce the whole deed in facsimile he was careful to give an exact representation 
of enough of the writing to show the hand. He never supplied words which were 
already decayed when the charter came into his hands. For the earlier charters 
which he did not facsimile he developed a plain script form of writing, not unlike a 
simple twelfth-century hand. For later deeds he used a smaller script. So completely 
was he the master of his pen that he succeeds in eliminating his own personality from 
his writing, so that it is very difficult for those who use his work to judge whether one 
or more men shared in it. The twelfth-century charters inevitably draw the attention 
of the modern student, and it was on them that the greatest care was lavished by the 
transcriber, but it would be difficult to find elsewhere a more representative collec- 
tion of late medieval deeds, including appointments of seneschals and attorneys,

enfeoffments to uses, wills, and even a letter from the lord to his tenants, free and 
serf, informing them that he has parted with the manor (372). 

Folios 56-9 Folios 56-9 in a sense stand apart from the rest of the book. On them are entered 

of Piilipol’s Nos. 252-79, the concluding charters of the large collection of John Philipot 
Somerset Herald. These pages present an unfinished appearance, for the outline of 
the charters is not drawn in, and although the seals are sketched and coloured no 
indication is given of the way in which they are attached to the documents. The 
charters are much abbreviated and are written in a flowing italic hand like that of a 
competent seventeenth-century clerk. It has been suggested that Philipot wrote these 
pages, for the hand bears a strong likeness to that of the Catalogue of Constables of 
Dover Castle signed by Philipot himself.’ It is not beyond the bounds of possibility 
that Philipot made himself responsible for the preparation of certain folios containing 
charters which, if he had not himself prepared the text, would have been omitted from 
the book. Even so, it is hazardous to argue from a form of handwriting so stylized 
and so commonplace as that in which the charters on these folios are written. 

Precision in The Plate of seals included in the present edition shows well the pains with which 

icki the seals were tricked.” The seal of Roger de Quincy, earl of Winchester and constable 

of Scotland, is a particularly fine piece of work, even showing the lugs which had 
held the seal and counterseal together. All the seals shown on the plate are either 
perfect or in reasonably good condition, so that a seal-tricker might delight in portray- 
ing them. But it is worth remarking that he showed as much care in drawing broken 
seals and fragments. Occasionally, probably when the seal was rubbed, the tricker 
was led by his enthusiasm to introduce detail which the original can never have borne. | 
He portrayed Michael Belet, who held the manor of Sheen by a butler serjeanty, sit- 
ting on a wine cask in Jacobean doublet and hose (147). The original document still 
survives in the British Museum and a figure seated on a wine cask can be dimly seen 
on the seal. In regard to the clothes alone did the artist allow his imagination to direct 
his pencil. There was little danger that in an age acutely conscious of arms, heraldic 
devices would be inaccurately shown. A passage from the autobiography of Sir 
Simonds D’Ewes? supports belief in the accuracy of the tricker. 

ae Diab asks’ Sir Simonds tells how going home from the Tally Office at Westminster where he 

No. 407 had spent Saturday morning copying Domesday Book, he called on Mr. William 

Neve, York Herald, who lent him an original deed of Richard Basset. Later, Mr. Neve 
gave the deed to Sir Simonds, who accounted it ‘the most precious monument’ in his 
library, and it was reproduced in the Book of Seals under his name (407). With the 
rest of his library it passed into the Harleian Collection and so into the British Museum. 


‘The seal’, says Sir Simonds, ‘hangs at the upper end, or beginning of the deed, in a strong label of thick 
white leather; the manner of it being so exotic and rare, as I never yet saw any other seal so affixed, but 
ever placed at the bottom of the deed. The seal itself is orbiculate and round, and of a great bigness and 
circumference,—the colour of it a bright auburn. The circumscription of it at first was, doubtless, SIGILLVM 
RICARDI BASSET, though the letters following, CARDI BAS, were only remaining when I received the same 


‘ Archaeologia Cantiana, 1947, Ix, 51 and 134. 3 The Autobiography and Correspondence of Sir Simonds

INTRODUCTION XVii 


deed from Mr Neve. ... And I am the rather persuaded that this seal was used by the said Richard Basset 
after he was the chief Justice of England, and as long as he continued in that place; because I have seen 
another deed of his with an ordinary round seal with a horseman upon it. . .. Upon the great orbiculate 
seal is seen a man armed in a coat of mail, the beaver of his headpiece open, holding on his left arm a 
great torqueted shield, covering his body, with a cross on it, and five orbs or globes on the cross... . In 
the right hand of the said armed man was a sword, with which he had riven open the upper jaw of a 
griffin, and cut it almost through; which griffin is very lively portrayed on the seal, (though some part of 
it be broken since off) holding a naked child in his mouth, which by that means, it seems, was delivered 
from being devoured by that monster.’ 


At some length Sir Simonds develops the theme that the figure represents the Justiciar 
himself, the shield bearing his coat armour, and is ‘a hieroglyphical allusion to his 
place of office’. The drawing of this seal in the Book of Seals is reproduced on Plate III. 
Both document and seal seem as unique to-day as they did to their fortunate récipient 
in the seventeenth century. His careful description of the seal, which is now almost 
obliterated by mending, is a welcome confirmation of the tricker’s skill and honesty. 

On the last ten folios in the Book of Seals, folios 119-28, an attempt was made 
to present a comprehensive view of the seals of English and Welsh boroughs and 
corporate institutions. The seals are shown under their county headings in alphabetical 
order of counties; first the English and then the Welsh shires. Each seal is depicted 
hanging from a scroll on which a description of the owner of the seal is written. From 
these descriptions it is clear that the seals are drawn from impressions attached to 
documents available to the draftsman. A list of the seals on each folio, with the descrip- 
tions written on the scrolls, is printed at the end of this Introduction. From this 
list it can be seen that the original plan in regard to the seals was never completed. 
Blank circles depend from some scrolls which bear descriptions evidently taken from 
deeds. From other scrolls nothing depends at all. It would seem from this that 
interest rather than material failed, and in all probability the plan proved too am- 
bitious for completion. Nevertheless the book may well owe its title to these folios 
of seals with which it ends. 

That the title Book of Seals was used in the seventeenth century to describe this 
book is certain, for it recurs again and again in Roger Dodsworth’s own handwriting 
in three of his manuscript volumes in the Bodleian Library, vols. 68, 90, and 100. 
Many charters which are to-day in the Book of Seals are entered in Dodsworth’s 
volumes under the heading ‘In Sir Christopher Hatton’s Booke of Seales’, although 
they are rarely transcribed in the order in which they appear in the Book of Seals 
itself. Moreover, interspersed with them and under the same heading are charters 
which are not in the Book of Seals at all. In vol. 68 there are entered on folios 1-7 
under the heading ‘In Sir Christopher Hatton’s Booke of Seales’ and in the following 
order Nos. 434, 38, 303, followed by an agreement not in the Book of Seals, then Nos. 
298, 43, 42, 280, 286, 285, 297, 307, 40, and another charter not in the Book of Seals. 
The last two charters had both been printed by Augustine Vincent in his correction of 
the errors of his fellow herald, Ralf Brooke. Dodsworth has put a reference to Vin-

Hattoniana’. On folio 158 are entered notes from another collection, but the dorse of 
the folio is again headed as from the book of Seals and contains No. 514, a charter 
of the empress Maud for Bordesley Abbey. On folio 159 Count Waleran’s charter, 
which the empress confirmed, is transcribed, but it is not in the Book of Seals. 

Of the charters transcribed in vol. 100 a similar, but even more complicated, story 
must be told. Folios 71-6 contain, under the heading ‘In Sir Christopher Hatton’s 
Booke of Seales’, first a charter not in the book, followed by Nos. 406, 409, 418, 411, 
412, 58, 422, 430, 416, which is the inspeximus of John Earl Warenne for Thetford 
priory. It runs over on to folio 77 and is immediately followed by a long run of charters 
which have a number of separate headings interspersed among them stating that some 
of these transcripts were taken from the Book of Seals and that some were from the 
muniments of the Constables, Viscounts of Dunbar. The charters themselves are 
derived from two separate families, each bearing the name Constable. One is the 
family of Constable of Flamborough and Holme on Spalding Moor, represented in 
1640 by Sir William Constable, some of whose charters (Nos. 515-25) are in the Book 
of Seals. This family was an offshoot of the Constables of Chester, being descended 
from an illegitimate son of the second William the Constable who died before 1139.° 
The other family is that of Constable of Halsham, of which the representative in 1640 
was Henry Constable who had been created Viscount Dunbar in 1620. He died in 1645 
of wounds received at the siege of Scarborough castle and was succeeded by his son

INTRODUCTION xix 


John, who married, in September 1635,’ Mary, daughter of Thomas Lord Brudenell 
of Deene, a near neighbour of Sir Christopher Hatton’s at Kirby Hall. That there 
should in later centuries be some confusion between the muniments of two prominent 
East Yorkshire families each named Constable is not surprising. 

The Book of Seals does not profess to contain any of the muniments of Henry 
Constable, Viscount Dunbar, but two of its charters, Nos. 520 and 521, attributed to 
Sir William Constable of Flamborough, are in reality charters of Robert ancestor of 
the Constables of Halsham, which had passed into the possession of Bridlington priory 
and thence, presumably, to the hands of the Constables of Flamborough. Dodsworth 
was clearly well aware of the pitfalls in regard to the Constables’ Evidences and took 
care, by the headings he inserted, to indicate the source of his material. Below the 
earl of Warenne’s charter on folio 77y. is the heading ‘In cartis Johannis vicecomitis 
Dunbar 1648’, and the same heading, but dated 17 September 1649, occurs on folio 78. 
It is hardly necessary to say that the charters under these headings are not in the Book 
of Seals. On folio 79 the Book of Seals heading precedes a charter of Erenburch of 
Burton, wife of Ulbert the Constable of Halsham, for Swine priory. It, too, is not in 
the Book of Seals. Erenburch’s husband was the father of Robert the Constable, grantor 
of Nos. 520 and 521 in the Book of Seals. Maud the prioress and the convent of 
Swine exchanged the land given by Erenburch with Bridlington priory, which probably 
explains how Erenburch’s charter had come into the possession of the Constables of 
Flamborough by the seventeenth century.” Erenburch’s charter is followed by another 
heading ‘In Sir Christopher Hatton’s Booke of Seales transcript’ ex original’ cartis 
penes dominum Henricum Constable militem vicecom’ Dunbarr’. On folio 85 is 
another heading ‘Ex cartis in custodia Henrici Constable militis vicecomitis Dunbarr 
15 June 1641’. The charters under these two headings appear to be Constable of 
Halsham deeds and they are not in the Book of Seals. These headings and a less 
precise description ‘From the Constables’ Evidences’ along the tops of each page 
cover the charters to the end of folio 91v. None of them is in the Book of Seals. But 
on folio 92 comes again ‘In Sir Christopher Hatton’s Booke of Seales ex cartis Willelmi 
domini Constable nuper de Flamborough et Holme in Spaldingmore in com’ Ebor’ 
militis et baronetti’, and then, following it, occur the charters numbered 515-19 and 
522 and 523 in the Book of Seals. The general page heading ‘From the Constables’ 
Evidences’ is continued on the dorse of each folio up to and including 95y. on which 
this series comes to an end. 

It is impossible to escape the conclusion that a far larger selection of charters lay 
before Dodsworth when he made his extracts from the Book of Seals than is contained 
in it to-day. Two alternative inferences offer themselves. Either the Book of Seals 
was originally much larger than it is now, or its compilation was abandoned before all 
the charters deposited for inclusion in it could be dealt with by the draftsman. The 
latter alternative seems the more likely, for in at least three notable cases a charter 
which appears in Dodsworth’s transcripts but is omitted from the Book of Seals has

so close a connexion witha document in the Book of Seals that if entered there at all 
it is inconceivable that it should not have been entered on the same folio. If Earl 
Waleran’s charter for Bordesley abbey had been entered in the Book of Seals it would 
surely have been associated with the charter of the empress Maud which confirms 
it (514). Again, the quitclaim to Aubrey de Vere, earl of Oxford, of the marriage 
portion of the countess Rohesia by the countess herself and Geoffrey earl of Essex 
would surely have been put on the same folio with Henry II’s charter to Earl Aubrey 
granting him the third penny of Oxfordshire that he might be earl thereof (40). 
The third example is even more significant. No. 298 is a charter of Gilbert de Gant 
for Geoffrey de Armenteres reducing for Geoffrey the knight service owed by his 
father from 10 knights to 8 as a marriage portion for Gilbert’s daughter Juliana. In 
Dodsworth’s transcripts this charter is preceded by a tripartite agreement between 
Gilbert de Gant, Henry de Armenteres, and Geoffrey de Armenteres, Henry’s son, 
setting out in full the complicated arrangements which this marriage necessitated. 
The agreement is printed later in this Introduction. Here it is only necessary to point 
out the intimate connexion between the two documents. 

The outside limits of date given in the Book of Seals itself are November 1640 and 
November 1641, but as not all the collections are dated the work may have begun 
earlier and gone on later than these two dates suggest. In any case the collection of 
documents for the book must have been going on during the summer and autumn of 
1640. A rich harvest of documents could be reaped in September 1640 in Sir Christo- 
pher Hatton’s library. That so assiduous a gleaner as Dodsworth should fail to take 
advantage of the collection in a single library of records drawn from the length and 
breadth of England was unthinkable. He probably hastened to the spoils before the 
work was well begun. He was certainly working in the Hatton Library on 15 September 
1640, for he headed his transcript of an inspeximus of Henry III for Coventry ‘In carta 
originali sub sigillo in custodia Christoferi Hatton militis balnei de Kirkeby in comi- 
tatu Norhanton 15 September 1640’.? The charter is not in the Book of Seals. Dods- 
worth cannot have stayed long at Kirby Hall on this occasion, for he was at work 
on the Belvoir cartulary on 18 September and he was still at Belvoir on 20 September, 
going from there on into Lincolnshire. Dodsworth’s itinerary, worked out by Sir 
Edmund Craster and Mr. Denholm-Young from notes in his manuscript collections, 
gives no hint of any other visit to Kirby Hall while the Book of Seals was in the making, 
but it is possible that he was at Kirby earlier in September, riding over from Belvoir, 
where he had been on 6 and on 12 September.*? By no means all the transcripts from 
the Book of Seals in Dodsworth’s manuscripts are in his own handwriting, but the 
Book of Seals heading seems as a rule to have béen written by Dodsworth himself. 
Brief visits to Kirby would have sufficed to instruct a copyist and to look over his 
work.

a more accurate but longer description giving both the owner of the charter and its 
temporary place of custody, for he has given us the perfect title for the present book. 
At this point it becomes necessary to consider three fundamental questions: what 
was the original plan of the Book of Seals, when was it conceived, and how nearly 
was it carried to completion? The originator of the plan, Sir Christopher Hatton, was 
a Northamptonshire gentleman of position whose seat was at Kirby Hall. He was a 
first cousin twice removed of Queen Elizabeth’s lord chancellor of the same name, 
for his great-grandfather was a younger brother of the chancellor’s father. Sir Christo- 
pher Hatton was an outstanding member of the group of antiquaries who up to the 
opening years of the Civil War were actively engaged in the collection and transcription 
of medieval records. Some of them worked in this field throughout the miseries of 
the times, but others were forced by their position to turn their attention to politics. 
Sir Christopher Hatton supported the king, was created Baron Hatton of Kirby in 
July 1643, and took his oath as Comptroller of the Household on 29 December of the 
same year. He remained with the king until Charles I left Oxford to join the Scottish 
army in April 1646. Foreseeing the coming surrender, Sir Christopher sent his son, 
afterwards the first Viscount Hatton, away from Oxford on 23 April 1646. Lord 
Hatton and the marquis of Dorchester were the only two members of the Council 
who refused to join in the demand, made on 15 May 1646, that overtures for the sur- 
render of Oxford should be made to Sir Thomas Fairfax, the Parliamentarian com- 
mander. For Lord Hatton to remain in England was impossible and on 24 November 
1646 he went from London to Dover and reached Calais three days later. In September 
1656, after considerable difficulty, he obtained leave from the Commonwealth govern- 
ment to reside in England on account of his financial difficulties. He died in 1670. 
These details are recorded in the diary of the most eminent of Sir Christopher’s 
literary associates, William Dugdale of Blyth Hall in Shustoke, Warwickshire,’ whose 
part in the compilation and subsequent preservation of the Book of Seals was by no 
means the least among his innumerable services to English history. Born in 1605, 
Dugdale was a man of standing in the antiquarian circles of 1640. He was respected 
for his energy and enthusiasm, and he was already showing that ability to plan research 
with a view to ultimate publication, which distinguishes him from many contemporaries

or deservinge, in affoardinge me my dyet gratis with him, both the last termes, soe long 
as he was in London.’ Sir Christopher and Sir Thomas Shirley ‘with many others of 
that kinde, lovers of Antiquitye’ sent their greetings to Sir Symon by Dugdale in the 
same letter.’

the task laid upon Mr. Dugdale. 

There survives among Dugdale’s manuscripts at the Bodleian Library a note-book? 
which contains just what might be expected to result from an undertaking ‘to collect 
and copy all armoriall seales, with a breviate of ye deedes, and ye true dimensions of ye

appendentium exemplaria per me Willelmum Dugdale Norroy Regis Armorum’. The 
Patent granting Dugdale the office of Norroy did not pass until 1660, long after the 
majority of the entries were made in this note-book, although Dugdale occasionally 
added to its contents in the fifties and sixties of the century. One charter is even dated 
as late as 1678. Almost every entry is carefully dated in red ink and the owner of the 
document is named. Dugdale’s fastidious scholarship is nowhere better shown than 
in the neat and exact entries in this book. The earliest were made in 1636, but by far 
the greatest number in 1637 and 1638. The book is a slim vellum-covered paper 
volume, 103 x8} in. It contains 144 pages, some of which are blank. The num- 
bering is consecutive from front to back of the folios. At the end are indexes of 
persons and places also made by Dugdale. The pages are crowded closely with notes 
of charters and deeds with precise drawings of the seals, transcripts, and drawings alike

obviously the work of one hand. With few exceptions, the red ink references and dates 
are written close beneath the breviate of the deed, and when a charter has passed to 
another owner since Dugdale saw it he notes and dates the change. Most of the charters 
recorded in this book were in Warwickshire country houses or houses to which Dug- 
dale could get access in neighbouring shires. The collections of Sir Christopher Hatton 
on 3 November 1639 are represented by nine documents apparently derived from the 
archives of the see of Coventry and Lichfield, and on 9 April 1642 Dugdale entered a 
charter of Thomas of Arden then in Sir Christopher’s hands. In the fifties he tran- 
scribed one or two documents from the Cottonian Library. But Dugdale, like all 
students of English charters after him, could not resist the beauty of a twelfth-century 
document. His breviates tend to become not only full transcripts, but facsimiles of the 
whole document.’ From every point of view this book can be regarded as a forework 
of the Book of Seals. One who for his own delight could make this book would rejoice 
at the opportunity of compiling for a rich man a collection on more lavish and in- 
clusive lines. 

The only direct reference to the making of the Book of Seals in Dugdale’s published 
correspondence occurs in the postscript of a letter from him to Sir Symon Archer in 
which he says 

Dugdale to ‘Sir Chr. Hatton is upon a collection of rare charters and deedes, I meane the copyinge of them in the 
Sir Symon letter, observinge the shape of the deede. He hath allready made a good progresse therin, which I know you 
Archer wilt not only approve but admire. I pray you bring wth you some of your choycest, I meane such as are 
most historicall or observable, eyther antient or other, especially that of Wm the Conq. and of Siward de 
Arden (though the Seale be gone;) your Bull for the Chappell is a good one; and what other you think fitt. 
It will be noe little honour to you amongst sucha collection to be mencioned. My Lo. Marshall is exceedingly 
delighted therwith.”? 
This letter was written in March 1641 from Blyth Hall. Dugdale was about to go to 
London ‘to lodge at my chamber in the Office of Armes’ and in his letter arranged to 
meet Sir Symon Archer at Banbury that he might have his ‘ good companye to London’. 
None of the charters referred to by Dugdale are in the Book of Seals, nor is Sir Symon 
Archer’s collection represented there. 

When he came to write his autobiography Dugdale said nothing of this collection 
of deeds, but in an often-quoted passage he described the making of what must be 
regarded as a companion volume to the Book of Seals.

Like the Book of Seals this volume, known to its owners as ‘the Dugdale Book’, is 
now in the possession of the Earl of Winchilsea and Nottingham. 

In 1658 Dugdale published his History of St Paul’s Cathedral, which he prefaced 
by a dedicatory letter to ‘the Right Honourable Christopher Lord Hatton Comptroller 
of the Household to the late king Charles and one of his Majesties most honourable 
Privy Council’. He dated his letter from Blyth Hall on 7 July 1657 and in it he 
reminded 

“your Lo? that soone after the beginning of our late Long Parliament (of which you were then a member) 
So great was your foresight of what we have since by wofull experience seen and felt, and specially in the 
Church, (through the Presbyterian contagion, which then began violently to breake out) that you often and 
earnestly incited me to a speedy view of what Monuments I could, especially in the principall Churches of 
this Realme; to the end, that by Inke and paper, the Shadows of them, with their Inscriptions might be 
preserved for posteritie, forasmuch the things themselves were so neer unto ruine. 

“But how little I then credited this sad Prediction, your Lordship well knows: yet so much was I ever 
inclined to the regard of such things that . . . (through the noble favour of your Lordship in affording me 
assistance by another hand and support to us both, in our travaile, whilst we laboured therein) I neglected 
no pains to take notice of those which were then here, and in many other Cathedralls.’ 

Could the Book of Seals have been brought to completion similar sentiments might 
well have been expressed about the dangers to the charters portrayed upon its pages. 

Dugdale’s letters show that his search for monuments was in progress in the summer 
of 1640, a year earlier than the date given in his autobiography. In August 1640 he 
wrote to Sir Symon Archer from Packington, Warwickshire: 

“Beinge the last night returned home from my Cheshire journey, and willinge to take all advantage of 
S‘ Christopher Hatton’s servant who hath bin with me to trick the Armes, Pictures in Windowes, and Monu- 
ments of the familye, for which I have bin employed; I thought it good to take him to Warwick, where soe 
many rare and speciall peeces of that nature are, as noe parte of our countrye nor much of this Kingdome, 
can paralell. And therfore have resolved to be there wth him to morrow by nyne of the clock, and to stay 
Fryday, soe that he may from thence goe home into Northamptonshire on Saturday. This beinge my 
determinacion, I have herewth adventured the boldnesse to lett you understand the same, soe that if you 
would please to give meetinge there (in case yo" occasions may p’mitt) we might visitt Mr Throckmorton at 
Haseley, or Mr Beufoe, beinge not farr distant, and soe make some further discoverye of those Antiquityes 
wch they themselves I suppose are ignorant of.”2 

No doubt Dugdale was mainly concerned with his projected History of Warwick- 
shire in thus planning to collect evidences at Haseley. His success is reflected in 
the Book of Seals, where nine charters are entered under the heading ‘ Ex cartis Clemen- 
tis Throckmorton de Haseley in comitatu Warr’ armigeri anno 1640’ (506-14). Before 
Dugdale went on the Cheshire journey he had written in July to Sir Symon urging him 
to ‘borrow Mr Broomes Deedes till my returne out of Cheshire’, concluding his letter 
‘Loose not yo’ opportunitye with Mr Broome, for the deedes are very rare ones which

At the end of this Introduction is set out a page-by-page description of the book, 
giving the headlines and the numbers of the charters on each page. The men who 
planned the book were working for the benefit of posterity. They regarded the head- 
lines as offering proof to future generations of the provenance of the deeds shown 
below them. The pencil note above No. 37 on folio 10 shows the importance that was 
attached to these headings. There was some uncertainty as to the owner of the charter, 
which must, presumably, have reached the collection by the agency of ‘Mr Allen the 
paynter’, doubtless the arms painter referred to by Dugdale in his letter to Sir Simonds 
D’Ewes 27 February 1640.° Along the top of the folio is written in pencil “Enquire of 
Mr Allen the paynter in whose hand to vouch this deede’. The hand is very like Dug- 
dale’s. Such pencil notes of direction for the draftsman are often almost illegible; 
on some pages they only survive as a faint shadow on the parchment, sometimes they 
have vanished altogether, but occasionally the note is clear and, as in this case, its 
writing suggests the hand of Dugdale. 

How long the charters stayed in Sir Christopher Hatton’s library is another matter 
of doubt and speculation, but some of them seem to have been there still in 1651.

had been in Warwickshire since the summer of 1649 and Dodsworth was anxious to 
have him in London to help with the Monasticon. In May 1651 Dodsworth wrote 
again saying: “I cannot possibly get the passe, for all my Cosen and I can do.... 
My Lady Hatton is in Towne... . She hath allowed my Lo. Brud. to looke and make 
use of the bookes. I wish you would give any directions for finding the Bull of Dudley, 
and I would put him upon itt.’ The Bull of Dudley is without doubt No. 59 of the 
Book of Seals. It is unlikely that Dodsworth secured another look at the original in 
1651, for the reference to it in the Monasticon is dated 1640, which must mean that 
the transcript was made when the document was being used for the Book of Seals.

INTRODUCTION XXVIlI 


The heading in the Book of Seals above the Dudley Bull is ‘Ex cartis Willelmi Ward 
de castro de Dudley armigeri Marc’ 1640’. The Monasticon inaccurately gives the 
owner’s name as ‘Edward Ward’. William Ward was a London goldsmith who on 
1628 had taken over the estates of the impoverished Edward Sutton or Dudley, 
together with his grand-daughter and heiress, Frances, who was married to William 
Ward’s son, Humble Ward. Frances was raised to the rank of a daughter of a baron 
in 1635, and when her grandfather, Edward Sutton, died in 1643 her husband was 
created Baron Dudley. Humble Ward died in 1670 and Frances in 1697, when their 
son Edward inherited the title and lands.’ 

Dodsworth himself contributed charters to the collection for the Book of Seals, 
for Nos. 460 to 489 are headed ‘Penes Rogerum Dodsworth de comitatu Eboracensi 
generosum September 1641’. But it is very doubtful if these charters were permanently 
in his possession. Five of them are printed in the Monasticon; of these No. 470 is 
marked as ‘ex autographo penes Sam. Roper’. The reference given for Nos. 468, 473, 
and 474 is ‘ex cod. MS in Scacc. penes Remem. Regis’. No. 484 is described as ‘ex 
autographo in bibl. Hattoniana’. It was in 1635 ‘at the lodgings of Mr Samuell Roper 
in Lincolnes Inne’ that Dugdale and Dodsworth first met and ‘readily engaged them- 
selves to prosecute the gayning what Transcripts they could’ for the furtherance of 
the work of monastic foundations begun by Mr. Dodsworth, ‘but still, with this 
reservation, that Mr Dugdale would not neglect his Collections touching the An- 
tiquities of Warwickshire’.? All three men were avid collectors of manuscripts in an 
age of collectors, some of whom were none too scrupulous in their pursuit of a desired 
document. Nos. 468, 470, 473, 474 are all charters of Mottisfont priory in Hampshire 
founded by William Briwerre, one of the leading ministers of King John. Whether the 
Monasticon account of that priory was the work of Dodsworth or Dugdale cannot now 
be decided, nor the date when it was written, nor from what book in the Exchequer 
the charters were taken. It is certain that Hampshire charters can only have come into 
Dodsworth’s possession by gift, loan, or purchase. He may well have parted with them 
to secure others or deposited them permanently in Sir Christopher Hatton’s library. 
That he should have given No. 470 to Samuel Roper was natural, for it is a confirma- 
tion by Pain of Chaworth, in whom as a Derbyshire man Samuel Roper would have 
been interested. 

That one of Dodsworth’s deeds is quoted in the Monasticon as from an original in 
the Hattonian Library suggests that he had not removed it after he deposited it for the 
Book of Seals. Five other deeds in the Book of Seals are quoted in the Monasticon 
as from an original in the Hattonian Library,* and one ‘ex rotulo pervetusto’ there.* 
Reference to an original in the Hattonian Library is given in the case of a number of 
charters in the Monasticon which are not in the Book of Seals.® One of these charters, 
that of Waleran count of Meulan for Bordesley abbey, has been quoted already as

entered in volume 90 of Dodsworth’s MSS. under the heading ‘Sir Christopher Hat- 
ton’s Book of Seals’. It would therefore seem certain that Dugdale and Dodsworth 
used for the Monasticon charters originally deposited in the Hattonian Library for 
the Book of Seals giving the library as the reference.’ When individual charters were 
examined for the purpose of the Monasticon cannot be known with certainty, but it is 
at least arguable that it was later than the months during which the charters were 
being used for the Book of Seals, since that title is never given by the Monasticon as a 
reference. It may be that by the time they were used for the Monasticon the project 
of the Book of Seals had been long laid aside and forgotten. It may even be that the 
rightful owner of the charters too had in many cases been forgotten. 

The production of these folios of charters must have been a slow and delicate business. 
That the original plan was to give precise facsimiles of all the deeds which could be 
collected is made clear by Dugdale’s letter to Sir Symon Archer. Before long the 
implications of this stupendous task were recognized and a compromise was adopted. 
Partial facsimiles of deeds not regarded as of the first importance were given and docu- 
ments from the later Middle Ages, which did not seem far away in 1640, were treated 
with less precision. Some pages, notably those containing the end of the Philipot 
collection, show signs of hurried work and are obviously unfinished. Some pages, 
always the backs of folios, are blank. The pages of seals at the end of the book were 
never completed. The title ‘Book of Seals’ preserved by Dodsworth must have been 
the name used by those who were actually working on the book in the autumn of 
1640. Had they been able to complete their plan, including the provision of bold 
scarlet headlines attesting the ownership of the deeds beneath them, a scholar who 
wished to refer to these documents might justifiably have cited them under the title 
of the book rather than by the names of the individual owners. Dodsworth, anticipat- 
ing the completion of the work, adopted this method of reference. When the plan was 
abandoned the title, too, was dropped. 

There is no need to seek elaborate explanations for the abandonment of the work. 
The storm foreseen by Sir Christopher Hatton broke in 1642. In his autobiography 
Dugdale records that on 19 March 1642 the king, prince, and duke of York betook 
themselves for safety to the city of York, while the queen went to her relatives in 
France.” On 1 June Dugdale was summoned, by virtue of his office as Rouge-Croix 
Pursuivant of Arms, ‘forthwith to repare thither’ to the king. About the middle of 
July he received further command to ‘attend the right Ho" Spenser Earle of North’ton, 
then L* Lieut of the County of Warwick’.? The castles of Banbury, over the Oxford- 
shire border, and Warwick being held for the Parliament, the earl obtained the royal 
warrant dated 4 August 1642 directed to Dugdale and commanding him to summon 
the two castles to surrender. ‘In his Coat of Armes, w® Trumpets sounding before 
him’ Dugdale rode up to Banbury castle and read the summons.’ Banbury was accord-

castle, Sir Edward Peto of Chesterton, who had provided one of his charters for the 
Book of Seals (529). Dugdale remained in attendance upon the king until after the 
battle of Edge Hill and the march on London. Then Oxford being made the king’s 
chief garrison, Dugdale settled there and was admitted Master of Arts on 1 November 
1642. By the king’s command Dugdale stayed at Oxford until it was surrendered to 
the rebels about 26 June 1646, his own estate in the country being sequestered all that 
time. Although in 1644 he went to Worcester to seek materials for his work,’ there 
is no evidence that he visited Kirby Hall again before the surrender of Oxford. 

The fate of the unfinished Book of Seals can be dimly discerned from an entry which 
Dugdale made in his diary under the year 1663, over twenty years after work on the 
book had been abandoned. ‘Of those sheets in parchm‘ belonging to my L. Hatton, 
wherein divers antient Deeds are transcribed, there are in number 68.2 Even without 
removing the present binding from the Book of Seals—a process unlikely to yield any 
conclusive result—it is possible to establish a reasonable relationship between the 68 
sheets of parchment in Dugdale’s hands in 1663 and the 128 folios of the Book of 
Seals. Of these 128 folios, 118 contain copies of charters and 10 contain drawings of 
seals. There is reason to believe that the charters were entered on large sheets of parch- 
ment which could be folded into two down the middle for the purpose of making up 
into a book. The employment of such double sheets for some at least of the charters, 
notably Nos. 59, 416, and 420, was made necessary by their size. It seems highly 
probable that the 118 folios of charters now in the Book of Seals consisted in 1663 
of 59 of these large double sheets of parchment and that the remaining 10 folios of 
the Book of Seals, containing the drawings of the seals, made up the number of sheets 
in Dugdale’s hands in 1663 to 68. Seals take less space than charters and would 
naturally be depicted on the more easily manageable single sheets, or folios, of parch- 
ment. To make the numbers correspond precisely with Dugdale’s 68 it is only neces- 
sary to assume that one of the pieces of parchment containing drawings of seals was 
a large double sheet, into which the rest of the pieces on which seals were drawn could 
be slipped. If this argument can be accepted, nothing has been lost of the work done 
in 1640 and 1641. 

It is unlikely that Dugdale carried the Book of Seals away from Kirby before the 
troubles broke out in 1642. The first entry in Dugdale’s diary after his account of the 
surrender of Oxford implies that the writer was at Kirby Hall. Under the date 9 
September, nearly twelve weeks after his last entry, Dugdale notes: ‘Mr Gunning came 
to Kirby as Tutor to Mr Ch. Hatton and Mr Compton.”* It was not until 24 November 
that Lord Hatton went from London to Dover on his way to exile.” The months 
between June and November, when Dugdale made no entries in his diary, offered time 
for the packing up of deeds, books, and manuscripts at Kirby in preparation for 
departure. In the ten years of Lord Hatton’s exile Dugdale visited Kirby on several 
occasions. He evidently acted in some sort as an agent for Lord Hatton during these

parchment sheets which are now the Book of Seals. In 1663, as has been noted, they 
were in his charge at Blyth Hall. At some time, by Dugdale or his executors, they were 
sent back to Kirby Hall, where they remained unbound until the nineteenth century. 

There is no evidence that the Book of Seals was used again until George Baker of 
Northampton was writing his history of Northamptonshire.” Baker was born in 1781, 
less than a hundred years after Dugdale’s death, and he lived on into the reign of 
Queen Victoria, dying in 1851. Lord Winchilsea, the tenth earl, lent the Book of 
Seals to Baker, who cited in his history thirteen of the charters. The book was still 
unbound and Baker refers to it as ‘the Hatton portfolio of deeds’. Baker’s pencil notes 
of village names still remain on some of the folios. Only in the case of No. 54 does the 
reference number given by Baker agree with the present numbering of the charters in 
the Book of Seals. As the footnote below shows,’ Baker’s reference number some- 
times approximates to the present number of the charter. The divergence is due 
to the renumbering of the charters consequent on the rearrangement of the folios 
when the book was bound. Baker also cited No. 271 as in the possession of G. W. 
Finch Hatton, Esq., of Kirby. He is probably referring to the Book of Seals rather 
than the original deed.

INTRODUCTION XXX1 


When Baker was writing in the first half of the nineteenth century Kirby Hall had 
entered on its last phase as an inhabited house. The son of Sir Christopher of the 
Book of Seals lived until 1706, making Kirby his home and beautifying its garden. 
His son the second Viscount and third Baron Hatton lived mainly in London. He 
died unmarried in 1760, and his brother and successor died, also unmarried, two years 
later, when the title became extinct and the property passed to his half-sister. In 1764 
Edward Finch Hatton, son of the half-sister of the last two Viscounts Hatton of Kirby, 
inherited the estate. In 1769 he also inherited Eastwell Park in Kent and he died in 
1771. His son George rebuilt Eastwell but also lived partly at Kirby, for his son 
George William was born there in 1791. He is the G. W. Finch Hatton, Esq. to whom 
Baker refers. He succeeded to the earldoms of Winchilsea and Nottingham in 1826, 
being the tenth earl of Winchilsea. There seems to be no one day when the decision to 
abandon Kirby was taken. Concrete information about the last years of Kirby Hall 
as an inhabited house is difficult to find. Lady Gunning, whose father, the Rev. W. R. 
Finch Hatton, was born in 1827, remembers hearing from him that he used, as a boy, 
to visit his cousins at Kirby. She thinks that the house ceased to be inhabited between 
1837 and 1847, after which date it quickly fell into ruin. The Office of Works accepted 
the guardianship of Kirby Hall in 1929.1 

It was probably through the interest in the book shown by Baker that the binding of 
it was undertaken. I must again record my indebtedness to Mr. C. E. Wright, who 
wrote to me on 30 July 1949 saying that ‘on Friday afternoon’ in the course of 
examining a number of uncatalogued manuscripts at the Society of Antiquaries he had 
discovered ‘a small note-book in the handwriting of Sir Frederick Madden who was 
Keeper of Manuscripts at the British Museum from 1837 to 1866’. On the first leaf 
of the note-book is written: 


“Notes from a vellum MS containing faesimile-copies of Ancient Charters, with drawings of the Seals 
made for Christopher, Lord Hatton in the xviith century now in the possession of Lord Winchelsea. 
(November) 1831. 

‘It was lent by Lord W. to Geo. Baker Esq. of Northampton, in whose hands I saw it [signed] F.M.’ 

“In June 1858 this MS. was placed in my hands by the next Lord Winchelsea for the purpose of being 
bound, and I rearranged the sheets.’ 


The eleventh earl, at whose directions the volume was bound, succeeded to the title in 
January 1858. Sir Frederick Madden took notes from the early pages of the manu- 
script, but after he had proceeded as far as folio 54 he adds: ‘I didn’t proceed further 
with these Notes F.M.’ On a folded sheet of blue paper, dated 1858, Madden listed 
the charters in the order in which he found them. He brought together, as far as 
possible, the charters from the same collections, bringing, for example, three groups 
of Dodsworth’s charters into one. He then corrected his original numbering in 
pencil on this blue paper. Madden says that he added fresh numbers in red ink 
in the manuscript itself, but there is now no sign of any red ink numbering on

to the Book of Seals can be traced between 1862 and 1921, when the thirteenth Earl of

Canon Foster. The fourteenth earl of Winchilsea deposited the Book of Seals with the 
Northamptonshire Record Society in 1930.

INTRODUCTION XXXili 


A third heading might perhaps be made for two famous seventeenth-century libraries 
represented in the book, the Arundel Library and the Cottonian Library. Three hun- 
dred and thirty-eight charters in the Book of Seals were provided by three collectors 
who probably welcomed the opportunity of perpetuating the memory of their personal 
success in accumulating deeds. Sir Henry St. George, John Philipot, and Sir William le 
Neve, who produced respectively 105, 108, and 125 charters for registration under their 
names in the Book of Seals, were all Heralds. The numerous pedigrees of doubtful 
authenticity produced by some of the Heralds in the Elizabethan age has tended to 
obscure the good work done by their successors in the seventeenth century, particularly 
in the rescue of evidence from destruction. That men of such distinction as Augustine 
Vincent, William Camden, and William Dugdale were Heralds has seemed to be in- 
cidental, rather than to contribute to their reputations. No one hada better opportunity 
than a Herald to make a great collection of ancient charters. When Heralds made 
their visitations and gentlemen produced evidences of their ‘gentility’ the whole 
country-side was aware of the presence of men concerned with relics of the past. The 
Book of Seals indicates the way in which three Heralds at least used their opportunities. 

Sir Henry St. George was the son of Sir Richard Saint George, Clarenceux King of 
Arms, and the father of three Kings of Arms: Sir Thomas St. George, who succeeded 
Dugdale as Garter; Sir Henry, who in turn became Garter; and Richard, who became 
Ulster King of Arms. References to Sir Henry in Dugdale’s correspondence show 
him as one of the little group associated closely with Sir Christopher Hatton in the 
years before the Civil War. Dugdale sent Sir Henry’s greetings to Sir Symon Archer 
together with those of Sir Christopher Hatton, Sir Henry Spelman, ‘and the rest’ in 
1637. When the Book of Seals was made Sir Henry was Clarenceux. In April 1644 he 
became Garter, but enjoyed that office only until November when he died. John 
Philipot, Somerset Herald, was fortunate in that his wife was the niece of Robert 
Glover, Somerset Herald from 1571 until his death in 1588.1 It was on collections 
made by Glover that Philipot founded his Catalogue of Chancellors.2 Philipot was 
made Somerset Herald in 1624. His death in November 1645 occurred too soon for 
the king to carry out his intention of appointing him Norroy King of Arms. Although 
he is no more than barely mentioned in Dugdale’s correspondence, the presence of 


his collection in the Book of Seals shows that he was a member of the same group of 


‘lovers of Antiquity’, to use a contemporary phrase. Sir William le Neve was made 
Norroy King of Arms in 1633 and Clarenceux in 1635. A newsletter of his to Sir 
Christopher Hatton written from London on 24 September 1640 quotes letters of Sir 
Henry St. George who was with the king at York, and Sir William concludes by send- 
ing his ‘kinde love to Mr Dugdale’.? All three men were royalists and, like Dugdale, 
suffered for their loyalty, but Sir William le Neve fared the worst. He was badly 
Shaken by his experiences when he vainly summoned the rebel army at Edge

If no other charters had been portrayed in the Book of Seals, the collections of these 
three men would have made a notable book. As a group they contain at least one 
document from every English county except Cheshire and Durham. Wales, Scotland, 
and Ireland are also represented. In addition to deeds relating to the transfer of land 
and other property each of these collections contains documents of more general 
political, constitutional, or economic significance. Sir Henry St. George possessed 
a most interesting document which throws light on the financial instability of Edward I 
before ever he became king (64). A joint bond made before the bailiff and mayor of 
Sandwich by Robert Walerand, one of the king’s chief ministers and a former warden 
of the Cinque Ports, Stephen of Pencester, a future holder of that position, and Robert 
Burnel, the future chancellor, acknowledging a debt of £225 for wine, shows in associa- 
tion two of the four men in whose charge the lord Edward left his affairs when he went 
on crusade in 1270 (94). The charter which Robert Arsic made in his court at Cogges 
shows a lord laying out a village and inviting settlers to take land there (114). The 
charming agreement made before the bishop of Lincoln, the archdeacon of Leicester, 
and the whole chapter between Peter the forester of Rutland and the parson of Allexton 
setting out the conditions on which Peter may have an oratory in his own house shows 
how effectively in the twelfth century the bishop could protect the parish priest from 
encroachment on his tithes and offerings (163). All these documents belonged to Sir 
Henry St. George. 

John Philipot and Sir William le Neve were perhaps even more fortunate than Sir 
Henry in the documents of general interest which they secured. Philipot possessed 
letters patent of Elizabeth de Burgh, lady of Clare, of 25 September 1333 setting out 
her rights as patron of Anglesey priory during a vacancy (242), a document which is 
paralleled by Sir William le Neve’s ratification by the prior and convent of Castle Acre 
priory, Norfolk, of an agreement made between Roger of Huntingfield, the patron, and 
the priory of Mendham, Suffolk, at a much earlier date (325). Philipot preserved the 
military indenture made between Edward III and Edmund Mortimer, earl of March, 
in February 1372, by which the earl agreed to serve in person with the king in war 
for a year accompanied by 19 knights, 60 esquires, and 120 archers (227). Sir William 
had also a military indenture, again an earlier document than Philipot’s. It was made 
in June 1297 between Roger Bigot, earl of Norfolk, and John of Seagrave and sets out 
the service that John shall do to the earl (320). A copy of this document was found 
by Mr. Denholm-Young among Dugdale’s transcripts and has been printed by him. 
Le Neve possessed the charter which recorded the restoration by Henry II of the office 
of Marshal and the lands which went with it to John son of John the Marshal (280). 
Philipot had acquired the agreement between Rannulf earl of Chester and William 
de Fougéres touching the marriage portion of the earl’s wife, a document which in- 
corporates also an agreement between William de Fougéres and the countess of 
Chester’s brother, Geoffrey de Fougeéres (236). The importance of the people who 


INTRODUCTION XXXV 


made this deed brings it almost to the rank of a document of international diplomacy. 
More important still, Philipot rescued from oblivion the feudal treaty made in King 
Stephen’s reign between the earl of Gloucester and the earl of Hereford. In Geoffrey de 
Mandeville Round published a text of this document derived from Dugdale’s transcript 
of Philipot’s original. Since he had not seen the document itself or the facsimile in the 
Book of Seals, Round felt no assurance that Dugdale’s text was complete. The fac- 
simile made in 1640 in the Book of Seals which shows the seal strip at the bottom of 
the deed resolves this doubt (212). 

These three great collections are in a real sense complementary to each other. Twenty- 
three religious foundations are represented among Sir Henry’s deeds, twenty-five 
among Philipot’s, and twenty-one among Sir William’s. No religious house appears 
in each group except Bruern abbey, of which Philipot and le Neve had each one deed, 
while Sir Henry St. George had three. Sir Henry had as many as five deeds, all 
interesting early documents, from Southwark priory. Neither Philipot nor le Neve 
had any from that house. From Bordesley abbey Sir Henry had four charters and 
Philipot two, of which No. 197 refers to a previous charter by the grantor, which was 
No. 143 of Sir Henry’s collection. Philipot had a single specimen from the muniments 
of Anglesey priory, Stoneleigh abbey, and Langley priory, while Sir George had three 
Stoneleigh abbey deeds and one each from the other two houses. Of the eighteen 
religious houses from which Sir George had charters, but Philipot had none, only two 
—Boxley abbey and Canons Ashby priory—appear on Sir William le Neve’s list. 
It is roughly true to say that the strength of Sir George’s collection lies in the midlands; 
of Philipot’s in the south and west; and of le Neve’s in East Anglia. Four early deeds 
of Quarr abbey in the Isle of Wight and single deeds from Maiden Bradley, Monkton 
Farleigh, Plympton, Clifford, and Monmouth priories, and from the abbeys of Dore, 
Evesham, and Pershore help to give a distinctive local character to Philipot’s collection. 
Le Neve possessed a charter from the Maiden Bradley muniments and three from those 
of Dore abbey, but his collection, alone of the three under discussion, gives the im- 
pression that it was formed by a man with a strong interest in the history of a particular 
part of the country. He was a Norfolk man and collected East Anglian charters. 
Twelve deeds from Sibton abbey, five from Thetford priory, three from Mendham, 
one from Normansburgh, and one each from Carrow and the hospital of St. Mary 
Magdalene by Norwich testify to his success. It becomes more evident when to the 
deeds which he had derived from East Anglian religious foundations are added the 
twenty-one charters issued by and to laymen and concerned with land in Norfolk or 
Suffolk. 

The documents which these men preserved are all, or almost all, collectors’ pieces. 
Even Nos. 252-79 of Philipot’s collection which are entered in a very cursory manner 
in the Book of Seals have among them several documents which Baker was interested 
to cite (270, 271). Among them too is a charter by which a certain Roger Pantulf 
made a modest provision for his mistress and her children (269). No. 265 is also worth

Sir William le Neve’s choice of individual items for his collection appears to have 
been guided not only by his interest in his native East Anglia, but also by a general 
interest in the development of feudal society. Many of his later deeds evidently came 
in as a little collection of the Duke of Norfolk’s documents, but individually they 
illustrate important aspects of English medieval life. The collection contains appoint- 
ments of attorneys to deliver seisin (388, 389); the delivery to an heir of a manor held 
in wardship (401); the grant for life by a magnate of an annuity to ‘his well-beloved 
esquire’ (387); letters from the steward of the royal household permitting a magnate 
to hold his hundred courts and leets notwithstanding the presence of the king and 
within the verge of the court (366); the appointment by Cecily duchess of York, the 
king’s mother, of a feodary for her knights’ fees in Buckinghamshire, Bedfordshire, 
Northamptonshire, and Oxfordshire (390). But the most interesting of all these later 
deeds is the indenture made between John de Mowbray, lord of the Isle of Axholme 
and of the honors of Bramber and Gower, of the one part and his Welsh tenants of 
Susboys” of the other, by which he pardoned all his tenants’ trespasses by way of

Two of le Neve’s charters have been reproduced among the illustrations to this book. 
One of them (302) is a grant by Bernard de Baliol of the manor of Faxton, Northampton- 
shire, in exchange for the land which Gerold’s father and Gerold himself should have 
held of the donor overseas by doing the service of four knights, a pleasing illustration 
of one of the ways in which the new aristocracy in England brought tenants into the 
country from their overseas possessions. The other (301) is a charter made by an 
honorial baron in the court of his lord. The grantor was also a tenant of the king by 
despenser serjeanty as the legend on his seal testifies. In addition to the interest of the 
matter of the deed, the seal attached to it shows a gentleman of modest estate depicting 
on his seal a seated figure holding a sword in its right hand, presumably in imitation 
of the king in glory. The pig rampant to the dexter somewhat reduces the majesty of 
the picture. No. 298 must also be mentioned as one of the early charters belonging to 
le Neve which reflect the inner workings of great estates. It is a charter of Gilbert de 
Gant giving to Geoffrey de Armenteres in marriage with Gilbert’s daughter the service 
of two knights by reducing the service owed from the fee which Geoffrey’s father held 
of Gilbert de Gant from ten knights to eight. Gilbert also quitclaimed to Geoffrey the 
relief due from him for entering upon the inheritance of his father Henry. Taken alone 
this charter is important as an example of a recurring situation, the marriage of one 
of the daughters of the chief lord to one of his principal tenants. Its full significance 
and its date can only be seen when it is read in association with the tripartite agreement 
of which a copy is preserved in Dodsworth’s transcripts from the material collected 
for the Book of Seals."

Dodsworth sketched the counterseal and noted that the seal bore an eagle ‘with one 
head displaid’, the same seal which was borne by No. 298. Only the first few lines of 
this agreement were transcribed by Dodsworth himself, but he checked it and corrected 
slips. One or two words copied inaccurately or indistinctly he wrote in the margin. 

The identity of the witnesses to both the agreement and the charter shows that they 
were made at the same time. It is possible that the marriage agreement may mark the 
conclusion of a dispute about the tenure of Stow between Gilbert de Gant and Henry 
de Armenteres, who seems to be getting the better of the bargain, provided that he was 
on good terms with his son. Henry’s own knight service is reduced; he gets the con- | 
siderable sum of 60 marks; his lord will bear the expense of knighting his son ; although 
Stow is to be given by charter to Juliana in dower, Henry is to receive its issues for life. 
Moreover Gilbert de Gant will aid Henry to suppress Geoffrey should Geoffrey try to 
oust his father prematurely from possession of the profits of Stow. Since the first 
instalment of the 60 marks was to be paid at Martinmas 11 John the agreement was 
probably made during the autumn of 1209. The ceremony of knighting Geoffrey, 
unless by common counsel it seemed best to postpone it, would have taken place in the 
summer of 1210. The marriage could have been celebrated soon afterwards, but Juliana 
must have been still young at that date. Gilbert de Gant was under age when his father 
died in 1191 and did not come of age until 12Q1. The phrase ‘common counsel’ 
probably means the general opinion of the chief tenants of the honor rather than the 
judgement of an honorial council. Whatever the precise meaning of these words, the 
agreement, as definitely as the charter of William de Anesye, No. 301, takes the modern 
reader into the workings of an honorial court. 

Sir William le Neve’s charters are followed in the Book of Seals by those of a notable 
seventeenth-century character. Sir Simonds D’Ewes was a country gentleman with a 
‘sweet and pleasant seat’ at Stowlangtoft in Suffolk’ purchased by his father. From 
his maternal grandfather Sir Simonds inherited an estate in Somerset, and he married 
a Suffolk heiress, descended as he was proud to claim, from “a prime and ancient 


1 Stowe Nine Churches. . Sic. 3 Autobiography, ii. 52. 


INTRODUCTION 


family of that county’.! University-bred and trained to the law, his abilities would have 
won him a distinguished practical career. But his interests were overpoweringly drawn 
to the past and he was happiest transcribing rolls and records and preparing for the 
true history of England which he never wrote. He sat in the Long Parliament and kept 
full diaries of its proceedings from a profound conviction that history was daily being 
made and should be recorded. The merits of these diaries, their copiousness and 
accuracy, have given to Sir Simonds D’Ewes a most distinguished place among the 
authorities for English history in the seventeenth century. On the other hand, too much 
of a Puritan in temperament to stomach Laud, too good an historian to be happy in 
rebellion against the king, Sir Simonds was driven to take refuge in his ivory tower of 
antiquity. He collected books and coins as well as charters. The Book of Seals shows 
how carefully he selected the objects which he prized. His naive account of the way he 
obtained the Basset deed from Mr. le Neve shows how single-minded urgency can 
prevail over a weaker will. Sir Simonds wanted the deed, Mr. le Neve let him have it2 
Not a single one of the deeds depicted under Sir Simonds’s name in the Book of Seals 
can have been his inherited muniments. His acquisition of the Fineshade charter and 
the Chester-Fougéres agreement after the deaths respectively of Sir Henry St. George 
and John Philipot shows that he was still buying choice pieces long after the Book of 
Seals had been laid aside. Dodsworth heartily disliked him. ‘The knight att West- 
minster”? or ‘our freind of Westminster”! is his ironical, and ‘the beast’® his more 
usual, way of referring to Sir Simonds in letters to Dugdale. Sir Simonds lacked the 
dignity of Dugdale and the innocent disinterestedness of Dodsworth, but he would 
Tejoice to realize that the greater part of his collections are now safe in the British 
Museum, where in the words of his will ‘all lovers of learning of known virtue and 
integrity’® may have access to them. Sir Simonds’s collections were bought in 1706 
through the agency of Humphrey Wanley for the library of Sir Robert Harley. By 
that time four of the charters shown in facsimile in the Book of Seals had been lost. 
‘Two had passed into the Cottonian Library, but the other twelve are now among the 
Harleian charters. 

Every one of Sir Simonds’s charters entered in the Book of Seals is shown there in 
full facsimile. Sir Simonds possessed the deed, now lost, by which the sureties of the 
last Ferrers earl of Derby handed over the lands of the earldom to Edmund the king’s 
son (411). Historically, this document is so important that the facsimile has been 
reproduced as one of the illustrations to this book.” Sir Simonds had also collected

xl BOOK OF SEALS 


three documents concerned with the establishment of the see of Ely in the reign of 
Henry I. One of them is the solemn charter of the king, founding the new bishopric 
(419). There seems no adequate reason for doubting its authenticity. The other two 
documents are similar to each other in wording. One professes to be the charter 
whereby Hervey, the first bishop, separated the lands of the bishopric from those 
which he assigned for the maintenance of the cathedral priory (420). By the other 
charter the second bishop, Nigel, professes to do the same (415). These charters sur- 
vive and can be examined in the British Museum. It is certain that neither of them can 
have been written as early as the first half of the twelfth century. But Nigel’s charter 
bears an endorsement which appears to be in a twelfth-century hand and it is probable 
that they were cast into their present form before that century was over. The shape of 
these documents is highly unusual, for two seal strips protrude from the left-hand side 
of each of them. In the early years of the twelfth century before custom had established 
the fashion in which seals were attached to charters, a strip might well be cut for the 
seal on the left-hand side of the parchment which was being prepared for use. It is — 
worth noting that the charter by which Henry I gave the bishopric of Ely to Bishop 
Hervey has just such a strip protruding from its left side. This document is now 
among the Cottonian charters in the British Museum. It was entered in facsimile 
among the charters from the Cottonian library in the Book of Seals (430). Again 
there is no adequate reason to doubt its authenticity. It is possible that its form in- 
fluenced that of the two documents which the monks prepared to pass as the deeds of 
the two first bishops. | 

Sir Simonds’s charters are immediately followed in the Book of Seals by seventeen 
items from the Cottonian Library. Sir Robert Cotton, its founder, had incurred the 
king’s distrust by his association with the leaders of the opposition and in 1629 an 
occasion had been seized to deny him access to his library. Sir Simonds D’Ewes records 
how he went several times to see Sir Robert during 1630 to comfort him and Sir 
Robert told him that ‘they had broken his heart that had locked up his library from 
him’. He died in 1631. In addition to the political suspicion that Sir Robert had 
incurred, it was undoubtedly felt that he had usurped for himself a treasury of records 
that of right should belong to the Crown. Sir Robert’s son, Sir Thomas Cotton, 
recovered control of the library before 1640. Since some of the charters possessed in 
1640 by St. George, Philipot, and D’Ewes, all of whom died between 1644 and 1650, 
are now in the Cottonian collection it is clear that Sir Thomas was adding manuscripts 
to his library in the middle years of the century. He was as generous as his father in 
allowing scholars to use his books and manuscripts. He even lent Sir Simonds D’Ewes 
his father’s coins.

The bilingual letter of Odo bishop of Bayeux and earl of Kent addressed to Arch- 
bishop Lanfranc, Hamo the sheriff, and all the men of Kent, has suffered considerable 
damage since the Book of Seals was made (431). Odo’s seal, showing him bothasa knight 
and a bishop, no longer survives. This document is one of those chosen to illustrate this 
book. Henry I’s charter granting the bishopric of Ely to Hervey the bishop still 
survives (430), but the fine ratification by Henry II of the agreement made between 
the sons of Savaric fitz Cana must have perished in the fire which destroyed the Cot- 
tonian Library in 1731 (434). A charter of John as count of Mortain was included 
among the Cottonian exhibits (435), as was the charter of Stephen as count of Boulogne 
and Mortain to Savigny abbey which resulted in the foundation of Furness abbey (423). 
Two charters of Queen Maud, wife of King Stephen (424, 426), are included, two of 
Harald king of Man and the Isles (428, 432), and one each of Louis IX king of France 
(427), Malcolm king of Scotland (436), and Richard king of the Romans (437). No. 
433 is a letter of Nigel de Mowbray, but it is addressed to Henry bishop of Winchester, 
King Stephen’s brother (433). The remaining three charters from this collection in the 
Book of Seals are a charter each of Simon de Senlis III, earl of Northampton (439), 
his wife, the countess Alice (425), and Simon de Senlis, the earl’s brother (438). Seven 
of these important documents have been lost since the Book of Seals was made. 

That no more than two deeds from the Arundel Library are contained in the Book 
of Seals may be accounted for by the heavy preoccupations of Thomas Howard, the 
second earl of Arundel of his line. He became steward of the household on 12 April 
1640 and on 29 August was appointed Captain-General south of the Trent. In March 
and April 1641 he presided as lord high steward at the trial of the earl of Strafford. 
At the end of June the earl petitioned the king for the restoration of his grandfather’s 
title of Duke of Norfolk, but could get no satisfaction. In August 1641 the earl resigned 
his post as steward of the household and before the end of the year he had left the 
country to reside abroad. He was out of sympathy with the court, but was not drawn 
to the opposition. During the war he aided the royalist cause financially. He died 
at Padua in 1646 as he was preparing to return to England. From Oxford in 1644 the 
king had issued a patent granting him the title of earl of Norfolk. Neither of the two 
documents from the Arundel library shown in the Book of Seals has been traced. It is 
possible that the earl’s departure from England prevented their return to his library. 
One of them is the only document coming from the Anglo-Saxon period which the 
Book of Seals contains (440). The other is. the appointment of a seneschal for his 
demesne of Oswestry in the March of Wales by William earl of Arundel in 1439 within 
six months of his succession to the title (441). 

A document belonging to the earl of Arundel’s fifth son, born in 1614, is also entered 
in the Book of Seals in full facsimile under the heading ‘ex autographo penes Willel- 
mum Howard militem balnei’. He was made a Knight of the Bath at the coronation 
of Charles I and married in 1637 Mary, sister of Henry last baron Stafford, who died 

unmarried at about that time. Created Baron Stafford on 12 September 1640, he was
