It is a charter which came to his wife as her brother’s heir. By it Nicholas son of 
Robert of Stafford and Robert his eldest son and heir confirm to Kenilworth priory 
the church of Stone and the lands sold to Geoffrey of Glympton for the use of the 
church (130). This charter can be dated 1130-2. It is sealed in an unusual manner. 
Two strips project downwards from the left-hand side of the charter, each bearing an 
equestrian seal. By the time that the Book of Seals was made these seals must have 
been almost indecipherable, for the draftsman has given the figures on horseback a 
curiously contemporary appearance, apparently dressing one of them as a woman. 
The charter itself has disappeared, but it was printed in the Monasticon ‘ex rotulo 
pervetusto in Bibl. Hattoniana’. Stafford and his wife returned to Antwerp when the 
Civil War broke out, and it is probable that this charter remained unclaimed in the 
library of Sir Christopher Hatton. Thirty-six years later, as an unpopular peer of 
the Roman Catholic faith, Lord Stafford fell a victim to the excitement caused by the 
invention of the Popish Plot and was beheaded on Tower Hill on 29 December 1680. 

‘From the charter chest (armario) of the very noble lord, George earl of Rutland 
at Belvoir’ nine charters are entered in the Book of Seals. No date is added to this 
heading and there is no other evidence to indicate when the charters were carried from 
Belvoir to Kirby Hall. Nevertheless it is permissible to wonder whether Dodsworth, 
who was working on the manuscripts at Belvoir on 6 and on 12 September, was at Kirby 
on 15 September, and back again at Belvoir on 18 September 1640,” may not have 
carried with him to Kirby a small packet of the earl of Rutland’s charters for inclusion 
in the Book of Seals. On his way from Belvoir to Kirby he looked in on the earl of 
Westmoreland’s library at Apethorpe to take a few extracts from the Red Book of 
Thorney.” The Belvoir charters in the Book of Seals are well distributed over the 
centuries. A charter of Stephen (442) and one of William d’Aubigny III (443) represent 
the twelfth century. A charter of Hawise countess of Aumale of 1212-14 (444) and a 
charter of her son William de Forz, count of Aumale, of about 1214 (445) represent the 
thirteenth century. The other five belong two to the fourteenth (446, 449) and three 
to the fifteenth centuries (447, 448, 450). It is possible that ‘ye gentleman with the 
broadbrim’d hat’,’ as Dugdale once described Dodsworth, thought he would take a 
representative handful of documents to please his friends at Kirby. They do not seem 
to have been returned to Belvoir, for none of them are to be found in the report made 
of the documents of the duke of Rutland for the Historical Manuscripts Commission. 
The death of George earl of Rutland in March 1641 and the succession of his second 
cousin to the title and estates may help to explain why the documents entered in the 
Book of Seals were not returned to Belvoir. The new earl was a supporter of the 
Parliament.*

Eighteen charters in the Book of Seals were derived from the charter chest of the 
most noble lady Katherine duchess of Buckingham, and the heading above them is 
dated July 1641. The widow of George Villiers, created duke of Buckingham in 1623 
and assassinated on 23 August 1628, this lady had married in 1635 as his first wife the 
marquis of Antrim. Dugdale notes in his diary under 10 January 1645 ‘The E. of 
Antrim and Dutches of Buck. came to Oxford’! The duchess died in 1649.” The heir 
to the dukedom of Buckingham was born in February 1628, so that, although he took 
his M.A. at Cambridge in 1642, he was still a minor when the Book of Seals was made.? 
His mother retained the title derived from her first marriage, and the deeds entered 
under her name in the Book of Seals must in great part have been derived from her first 
husband’s family. He was the fourth son of Sir George Villiers of Brooksby, Leicester- 
shire.* Most of the duchess’s documents are concerned with Leicestershire properties 
and had been part of the title-deeds of Garendon abbey. A few of them were derived 
from Belvoir and were probably brought thence by Katherine, who was the daughter 
and ultimately the only surviving child of the sixth earl of Rutland. From her father 
she inherited the barony of Ros.® The letters patent of William de Ros of Helmsley 
granting to Belvoir priory the right to purchase the churches of Uffington, Lincoln- 
shire, and Norton by Twycross, Leicestershire (16), and the confirmation charter of 
Newstead priory, ‘the new place at the bridge of Uffington’ (11), were in no sense title- 
deeds belonging to the barony of Ros. They may, however, have been regarded as of 
especial interest to the holder of that title. 

Henry fifth earl of Huntingdon provided eleven documents for the Book of Seals. 
He was descended from that Sir William Hastings of Kirby Muxloe in Leicestershire 
and Burton Hastings in Warwickshire, who took an active part in the Wars of the 
Roses and became chamberlain to Edward IV. He was raised to the rank of a baron 
with the title of Lord Hastings early in Edward’s reign.” The muniments of the Hast- 
ings family were reported on by the Historical Manuscripts Commission before they 
were sold to the Huntington Library in America. The report, of which the first volume 
was issued in 1928, shows that the family possessed a very extensive collection of 
records ranging from the twelfth down to the seventeenth century. The fifth earl must 
therefore have made a careful selection for the Book of Seals. He seems to have chosen 
such records as he considered would best illuminate the family history, in particular 
such as would show its connexion with people of greater consequence. The makers of 
the Book of Seals were particularly interested in documents issued by great men, and 
the muniments of the Hastings family could provide a representative collection of 
deeds issued by members of the nobility in the later Middle Ages. Letters of George 
duke of Clarence and of John Lord Lovel are entered in the Book, each appointing 
Lord Hastings as his steward for certain of his lands, and each describing Hastings as 
‘kinsman’ of the grantor (28, 32). The letter by which Anne duchess of Buckingham

Edward IV (33) and the letters patent of Queen Elizabeth Woodville appointing her

Northamptonshire lands (22) were two documents which could not be omitted from 
the earl’s contribution to the book. Two documents were included to illustrate the 
family connexion with Kirby Muxloe (29, 30), but perhaps the most interesting item 
in the earl’s contribution is the charter by which Walter Rumseye gave to Walter de 
Hungerford his rights as patron of the priory of Maiden Bradley, Wilts. (31) This 
document had come into the family with the wife of the second Lord Hastings, 
daughter of Sir Thomas Hungerford and heiress in her own right of the baronies of 
Botreaux, Hungerford, and Moleyns. Five of the earl’s charters shown in the Book of 
Seals appear to have been lost since 1640 as they were not among the records reported 
on in 1928. The fifth earl died in 1643. Neither he nor his successor appear to have 
been sufficiently moved by contemporary passions to take an active part in the Civil 
War. . ; 

Three extremely interesting twelfth-century charters were provided for the Book of 
Seals by a man described in the Dictionary of National Biography as ‘a soldier of 
fortune’. Sir Simon Harcourt was the son of Sir Robert Harcourt of Ellenhall, Staf- 
fordshire, and Stanton Harcourt, Oxfordshire, who had lost large sums of money in 
his attempts to promote a settlement of Englishmen in South America. Sir Simon was

unsuccessful efforts in colonization forced his son to attempt to make a career for 
himself, and a great part of his life was spent in military adventures abroad. He was 
knighted at Whitehall in 1627 and he was in England in 1636 to look after his private 
affairs. His father had died in 1631 after selling Ellenhall and his Berkshire estate at 
Wytham. The expedition against the Scots in 1639 gave Sir Simon employment in 
England, and it was probably at this time that he handed his three charters to Sir 
Christopher Hatton for inclusion in the Book of Seals. Sir Simon commanded a 
regiment of foot in the army against the Scots and in 1641, when the Irish revolt broke 
out, he was appointed governor of Dublin with the rank of Colonel. He died of wounds 
in March 1642. It is improbable that such a man troubled to retrieve his charters from 
Kirby Hall in the months of life left him after they had been entered in the Book of 
Seals (42-4). No trace of them has been found. 

Of all the charters shown in the Book of Seals perhaps the most important is No. 
39, the charter of Henry I conferring upon Aubrey de Vere in fee and inheritance the 
office of Master Chamberlain of England. It is entered under the heading ‘from the 
charters of Robert Bertie earl of Lindsey Great Chamberlain of England’. Robert 


INTRODUCTION xlv 


Bertie was the son of Peregrine Bertie, Lord Willoughby d’Eresby, by Mary daughter 
of John de Vere, earl of Oxford. On the death, without issue in 1625, of his cousin 
Henry de Vere, earl of Oxford, Lord Willoughby d’Eresby claimed the title of earl of 
Oxford and the office of Lord Great Chamberlain against Robert de Vere. According 
to Sir Simonds D’Ewes this claim was ‘to all men’s wonder and the great distaste of 
most’. The title of earl of Oxford and the place of Lord Great Chamberlain, Sir 
Simonds points out, ‘had, with little interruption, been joined, near upon 500 years last 
past, together in that great and noble surname of Vere. Whereas the family of Bertie 
was certainly very mean and ordinary in the male line.’ Sir Simonds claimed that he and 
Sir Robert Cotton ‘both joined our best skill and searches together to assert and up- 
hold the said Robert de Vere’s just and undoubted title to the same earldom; which 
in the issue . . . was settled upon him; though he most unfortunately lost the place of 
Lord Great Chamberlain of England, which the Lord Willoughby obtaining, was 
afterwards created Earl of Lindsey’. The ashes of this suit were still hot in 1640, and 
those who made the Book of Seals were careful to facsimile not only the charter but 
also the endorsements on it. It has been chosen as one of the illustrations of this book. 
Although judgement went against Lord Willoughby d’Eresby in regard to the earldom 
of Oxford, he seems to have retained possession of the charter of Henry II confirming 
the earldom to Aubrey de Vere (40). The third charter provided by the earl of Lindsey 
for the Book of Seals was one of the title-deeds of his father’s family (41). The earl of 
Lindsey was very much a Lincolnshire man. From 1629 until his death he was Lord 
Lieutenant of his county. Many Lincolnshire gentlemen turned out for the king in the 
Civil War because of their respect for the earl of Lindsey. He died of a wound received 
in the battle of Edge Hill. 

One of those Lincolnshire gentlemen who was commissioned by the earl to raise 
forces for the king in his own parts was also a contributor to the Book of Seals. 
Gervase Holles of Grimsby, who refers affectionately to the earl as ‘our old generall’,? 
came of a younger branch of the family of Holles of Haughton, Nottinghamshire, the 
head of which was made earl of Clare by James I in 1624. Gervase Holles was the son 
of Frescheville Holles, so named after the family of his mother, a daughter of Peter 
Frescheville of Staveley, Derbyshire. The mother of Gervase Holles was Elizabeth 
daughter and heiress of John Kingston of Grimsby, where Gervase was born. In his 
history of the Holles family Gervase tells a lively tale of his grandfather’s runaway 
marriage with Frances Frescheville? and draws an attractive picture of his hot-tempered 
but generous and lovable father, Frescheville Holles, who died in 1630. Gervase 
Holles was himself a collector of charters and in the years before the Civil War he was 
visiting Lincolnshire churches and taking notes of the monuments and arms in them. 
He visited Mansfield, Haughton, and Tuxford in Nottinghamshire and Staveley in 
Derbyshire as well, because of his family connexions with those parts. In 1640 he was 
living at Newark and he was still living there in 1642 when his son Frescheville was

The most notable work of Gervase Holles is his account of his own family and of all 
the families allied to it. The writing of this story solaced his exile, and in the writing 
he was helped, he says, by ‘my worthy good freind M* W™ Dugdale who was pleased 
to take the paynes to make search for me (w™ favour I likewise ow him for severall 
other things in this treatise)’.? Two of the three documents provided by Gervase Holles 
for the Book of Seals came from families whose connexion with his own he traces in 
this book. One was the appointment by John de Beaumont, Viscount Beaumont, of 
William Tyrwhit, knight, to be his steward (55). The sister of Gervase Holles’s Fresche- 
ville grandmother had married William Tyrwhit of Kettleby, Lincolnshire.’ The other 
is a grant by William Longsword son and heir of the earl and countess of Salisbury of 
land in Wanborough and Aldbourne in Wiltshire to Philip Lucy (56), presumably a 
thirteenth-century member of the family of Lucy of Charlecote. The connexion of 
Gervase Holles with the Lucy family was remote. His great-grandmother Anne wife 
of Sir William Holles was the daughter of Mary daughter of Sir William Lucy of 
Charlecote.* 

It seems very probable that it was through the agency of Gervase Holles that the 
first two charters entered in the Book of Seals reached Kirby. The absence of the 
scarlet headline on the first folio of the book meant that it was not until the note-book 
of Sir Frederick Madden was found by Mr. Cyril Wright that the ownership of those 
two charters could be certainly known. The pencil note that they were ‘Frescheville’ 
deeds was much more easy to read in 1858 than it is nearly a hundred years later. It 
is still faintly visible when the reader knows what to look for. When Gervase Holles’s 
grandfather ran off with Frances Frescheville she and her sister were co-heiresses of 
Peter Frescheville of Staveley. But in his old age he married again and had a son and 
heir, Sir Peter Frescheville, ‘an honest and worthy gentleman of good erudition, and 
a great lover of learning and learned men’.® His son and heir was John Frescheville, 
born at Staveley in 1606. He supported the king until after the battle of Marston 
Moor ‘when he delivered up his house unsummoned’. After being in London for a 
time he returned to the royal allegiance. He was made governor of Welbeck, but gave 
it up without action, when he was surprised by a band of rebels.®° The charter of

Thomas de Chaworth, No. 1 in the Book of Seals, had passed before the Monasticon 
was printed into the possession of Sam. Roper like another Chaworth deed entered in 
the Book of Seals under Dodsworth’s name. It is possible that, like Dodsworth’s deeds, 
the Frescheville charters were left at Kirby and by some means the two Chaworth 
documents came into the possession of a collector of Derbyshire evidences. 

That the Book of Seals should contain a charter from the muniment room of Thomas 
Wentworth earl of Strafford is remarkable, for while the book was being made Straf- 
ford was on trial. He was executed on 12 May 1641 before work on the book was laid 
aside. The heading ‘From the charters of Thomas earl of Strafford lord lieutenant of 
Ireland’ is given no definite date. It is written in the usual bold scarlet letters and 
below it in what appears to be Dugdale’s hand the same heading is written in pencil 
for the guidance of the draftsman. The charter (170) is of no particular note, and it is 
unlikely that the earl himself can have been interested at this time to provide it for the 
Book of Seals. But those who were doing the work were notably royalist in sympathy 
and may well have been anxious to have an example of the earl of Strafford’s docu- 
ments. The most likely agent to be able to procure a charter of Lord Strafford’s was 
Gervase Holles, for the earl had married in 1625 a cousin of his, Arabella, one of the 
sisters of the second earl of Clare. Her death in childbirth in 1630 caused a breach 
between Strafford and his father-in-law. Gervase Holles records that his own father 
could never well agree with the second earl of Clare, but ‘had a most tender affection’ 
for the Lady Arabella, viscountess Wentworth and ‘frequently receaved letters full 
of kindenes and affection’ from her.1 

The Book of Seals contains a group of charters from the muniments of another 
royalist of the north who was also a kinsman of the earl of Strafford. Sir William Savile 
of Thornhill, baronet, was a son of Sir George Savile who in 1607 married a sister of 
Thomas Wentworth, afterwards earl of Strafford. Sir William succeeded his father in 
1626, was a member of the Council of the North, and served in the expedition against 
the Scots in 1639. When war broke out he took up arms for the king. In April 1643 
he became governor of Sheffield and a little later of York also. He died at York in 
1644. It is possible that his documents were obtained for the Book of Seals while the 
Great Council met at York in September 1640. Sir Henry St. George was in York, 
and others must have been there whose documents are in the Book of Seals. The work 
on Sir William’s charters is dated July 1641. It is unlikely that the first charter entered 
under his name was ever his property. It is a letter from the citizens of York to Arch- 
bishop Geoffrey about the advowson of the church of All Saints in the Marsh. When 
Drake printed it in his Eboracum in 1739 this document was ‘amongst the records of 
the city on Ouse-bridge’. Sir William may well have removed it from the archives 
of the city for registration in the Book of Seals. Drake’s reference shows that he took 
care to return it. Since 1739 this letter has strayed from York, but fortunately it is now 
safe in the British Museum. Two of the other charters entered under Sir William’s 
name had come into the possession of Colonel Gascoigne of Parlington Hall, Leeds,

The single charter of Lord Fauconberg entered in the Book of Seals (37) was not pro- 
cured direct from its owner for inclusion in the book. The pencil note below the scarlet 
headline on this page has been discussed earlier in this Introduction." It indicates that 
the charter had been acquired through the agency of John Allen the painter, from whom 
inquiry must be made as to its owner before the headline can be inserted. Thomas 
Belasyse of Newburgh, Yorkshire, was created Baron Fauconberg of Yarm in 1627 
and in 1643 was rewarded for his loyalty to Charles I with the title of Viscount Faucon- 
berg of Henknowle. After the battle of Marston Moor in 1644 he fled abroad and 
there became a Roman Catholic. He died in 1653.” That the charter entered under his 
name was one of his title-deeds there can be no doubt, for it deals with the place from 
which his family name was derived. 

Lord Fauconberg’s charter is followed in the Book of Seals by a single specimen of 
another royalist’s documents (38). Sir Hamo Lestrange was the second son of Sir 
Hamo Lestrange of Hunstanton and brother of Sir Nicholas, the first baronet. As a 
younger son he probably had few ancient charters of his own. He was an historian 
and a theologian. Although he was involved with his father and brother in an attempt 
to deliver King’s Lynn to the royalist forces he came to terms with the government in 
1651. His work on the liturgies of the Church of England was published in 1659 and 
dedicated to Christopher, Lord Hatton. 

It was probably from his ‘Cheshire journey’ taken in 1640 with Sir Christopher 
Hatton’s servant to collect drawings of monuments that Dugdale brought back for 
inclusion in the Book of Seals the two charters ‘of Sir Thomas Aston of Aston in the 
county of Chester, knight’. The date when they were registered in the book is given 
as December 1640. Dugdale was particularly interested in those parts, because of the 
suggestion of the Elizabethan ‘pedigree makers’ that the Hatton family was derived 
from Hatton by Chester—‘I doubt’, says Dugdale, ‘this is a fiction.’* Dugdale cor- 
responded with Mr. William Vernon of Shakerley in Lancashire and was in touch 
with Mr. Peter Leicester, later Sir Peter, of Tabley. He was in correspondence with 
Mr. Vernon about the Hatton pedigree in 1647. ‘Such was the ambition that those 
mercenary fellows had to obteyne y° favour of y° late lord Chancelour y‘ they brought 
to him divers old deedes of yt name, which had no relation to Cheshire Hatton.’* The 
two deeds of Sir Thomas Aston in the Book of Seals are both from the fourteenth 
century and of more interest to the genealogist than the historian (45, 53). Sir Thomas 
was a royalist and came of a family long settled in Cheshire. He represented his county 
in the Short parliament of 1640 and wrote ‘A Remonstrance against Presbytery... with 
a short survey of the Presbyterian discipline, showing the inconveniences of it, and the 
inconstancy thereof with the constitution of this state. ..’. When the war broke out

Sir Thomas supported the king and was captured at Middlewich in March 1643. He

Through the help of his friends in Warwickshire, notably of Sir Symon Archer, The war- 
Dugdale was already in 1636 acquiring access to muniments in country houses for his "ickshire 
work on the history of that county.” The Book of Seals is therefore the richer by 
Dugdale’s acquisition of a number of choice specimens from Warwickshire collections. 

The ‘rare’ charters of Robert Brome have already been mentioned in this Introduction? 
Dugdale chose for inclusion only such Warwickshire charters as he considered worthy 
of a full facsimile, and from several of the Warwickshire houses he included one 
charter only in the Book of Seals. Richard Yardley’s charter touching the Beauchamp 
chantry in the chapel of Guy’s Cliff, No. 490, is quoted also in the history of Warwick- 
shire. It is possible that Richard Yardley had no other muniments. One charter, 
belonging to Anthony Stoughton and coming from the muniments of the hospital of 
St. John the Baptist in Warwick, is entered in the Book (491). The seal has been in- 
cluded in the Plate of seals. In his History of Warwickshire Dugdale states that the 
hospital passed to Anthony Stoughton, ‘a servant to the Queen’, grandfather of ‘the 
present possessor thereof’.* The decayed state of this charter suggests that the rest of 
the muniments of the hospital may have been consumed by rats or mice. The last 
charter in the Book of Seals (529) came from a Warwickshire gentleman who had many 
other charters but served the Parliament in the civil war, Sir Edward Peto of Chesterton. 
No. 528, which provides important evidence about the history of scutage and military 
service, was owned by a gentleman named Stanton, whose Christian name Dugdale 
never learned. It has already been noticed that he quoted the charter in his History of | 
Warwickshire as it is entered in the Book of Seals ‘penes . . . Stanton’. 

There can be no question that the eight charters entered in the Book of Seals in 1641. Robert Arden 
under the name of Robert Arden of Park Hall are his hereditary family deeds. Park %?4”* #4! 
Hall had been the seat of the family of the Ardens ‘for neer CCC Years last past’, 
as Dugdale says in his History of Warwickshire.’ In the reign of Elizabeth Edward 
Arden ‘had the hard Hap to come to an untimely Death’, being convicted of high 
treason in 1583, largely through the insistence of the earl of Leicester, whom ‘he had 
irritated in some Particulars’. When he was attainted his lands were given to Edward 
Darcy, but after long litigation the greater part of them were recovered by Edward 
Arden’s son, Robert, ‘a prudent person, and well read in the Laws’. Robert Arden 
lived to a great age, with ‘no small Reputation in his Countrey’. He was succeeded 
by the Robert of the Book of Seals, who before the History of Warwickshire was writ- 
ten, “being much accomplisht with Learning, and other excellent Parts, died in the 
Flower of his Youth, whereby the Inheritance of this antient Family resorted to his 
Sisters ’.”

Michael Throckmorton, secretary of Cardinal Pole, when it fell in to the Crown on the 
attainder of John duke of Northumberland in 1553. Michael Throckmorton, who 
had been in Italy with the cardinal, preferred to live at Mantua and gave Haseley to his 
nephew Clement, third son of Sir George Throckmorton of Coughton. Clement be- 
came a protestant and his son, Job, was, says Dugdale, ‘one of those notable Zelots in 
Q. Eliz. Time’. Job’s son, Sir Clement, was ‘a Gentleman not a little eminent for his 
Learning and Eloquence’.? He was the father of the Clement Throckmorton of 1640. 

Seven Warwickshire charters are entered in the Book of Seals as in the possession of 
William Lord Craven at Combe (499-505). The date of the entry is given as Novem- 
ber 1641. William Craven, earl of Craven, was the son of a man who, born at Apple- 
treewick near Skipton, was sent to London when no more than a boy to be apprenticed 
to a merchant taylor, was elected Lord Mayor in 1610, and died a rich man. His son 
William was born in 1606 and took service with the Prince of Orange before he was 
twenty. Charles I knighted him in 1627 and made him Baron Craven of Hampstead 
Marshall, Berkshire. With Prince Rupert Lord Craven was captured in 1637 during the 
expedition under Charles Lewis, eldest son of the Queen of Bohemia, to try to weaken 
the imperial hold on the Palatinate. Lord Craven ransomed himself in the autumn of 
1639. It was presumably while he was in England at this time that the Combe charters 
were secured for the Book of Seals. Dugdale gives no information about Lord Craven’s 
acquisition of the estate and there is no evidence that he ever lived there. Most of his 
time was spent at the court of Elizabeth of Bohemia, for whom he seems to have felt 
a romantic affection. He repeatedly helped Charles I, and Charles II after him, with 
money and was rewarded with an earldom. 

Five charters are described in the Book of Seals as belonging to Sir Thomas Shirley

describes him as ‘a great Lover of Learning, and especially affected to Antiquities, in 
the study whereof he hath attained to much knowledge, and thereby given no small 
Lustre to this antient and worthy Family’.* He was born about 1590, knighted in 1622, 
and established by his father in the manor of Bottle Bridge, now part of Orton Longue-

It is worth noticing that although Sir Edward Dering was one of the signatories of

Book of Seals was well begun. Although Sir Edward Dering’s charters are not repre-

appear there. |

of these families could be traced . . . to an undistinguished Sussex man living under 
Edward I; for each of them he invented a distinguished pedigree from a far antecedent 
date . . . by deliberately tampering with the evidence of public records’.* Philipot’s 
latest biographer suggests that this bogus pedigree was in all probability taken over 
from an earlier fabrication.2, However that may be, there is no doubt that when 
Philipot accepted the pedigree he must have inspected the deeds. It is at least arguable 
that the Pelham documents in the Book of Seals remained in Philipot’s hands after his 
visitation of 1634 or even from an earlier occasion. He may well have produced them 
for the Book of Seals, informing those who made it as to the name of the true owner 
of the deeds. 
Sir William The other parliamentarian whose deeds are in the Book of Seals is Sir William 
pours, Constable of Holme on Spalding Moor.? He married Dorothy daughter of the first 
Holme on Baron Fairfax and was therefore uncle by marriage of Sir Thomas Fairfax, the Parlia- 
Spalding mentarian general. Fairfax would have saved the king’s life if he could and he refused 
to act as a judge at the trial. He was a lover of learning, the protector of the Bodleian 
Library when Oxford was taken, and the patron of Dodsworth. Constable, on the 
other hand, was assiduous in attendance as a judge at the king’s trial and was one of 
the signatories of his death warrant. Sir William had sold his manor of Holme in 1633 
and his manor of Flamborough in 1636, so that in the Book of Seals he is accurately 
described as ‘formerly’ of Flamborough and Holme. That he had also parted with 
his charters when he sold his land there is no evidence but a high probability. It may 
be significant that Dodsworth himself had in his possession two Constable deeds when 
the Book of Seals was made (488-489). In this company of royalists the Sussex 
sequestrator and the Yorkshire regicide seem strangely out of place.

Ex cartis Edwardi Peto de Chesterton in comitatu Warr’ militis. No. 529. A note of the heading in 
pencil in the top left-hand corner. ‘Ex chartis .. . .’ in pencil in the bottom right-hand corner. 
Blank. On folios 119 to 128 an attempt has been made to present a comprehensive view of the seals 
of English and Welsh boroughs and corporate institutions. The work was never completed. The 
counties are dealt with alphabetically, first the English and then the Welsh counties. Each seal is 
depicted hanging from a scroll on which the description of the owner of the seal is written.

borough of Chipping Wickombe. The common seale of the baliff and burgesses of Buckingham. 
The seale of the baliff of the borough of Aylesbury. Note it hath 2 burgesses of Parliament though 
no incorporacion. Two blank scrolls. .

charters which they have from his antecessores, and grants that the present instrument of itself shall suffice 
for their security. Warranty and sealing clauses. ‘Hiis testibus domino Nicholao Wak’ . domino Johanne 
le Heriz . domino Willelmo de Staynsby dominis Willelmo et Egidio de Meynile Roberto Sautcheuerel

The first donor was despenser of the earl of Chester, of whom he held land in Loughborough; he was the 
ancestor of the well-known baronial house (HKF ii. 58 et seq.). From a number of related instruments 
printed by Nichols from the Garendon cartulary (op. cit. iii, pt. ii. 817-18) it would seem that the Thomas 


KATHERINE DUCHESS OF BUCKINGHAM 3 


of the present instrument was son of Geoffrey the Despenser and identical with the Thomas who occurs 
under Leicestershire in 1176 (PR 22 Hen. II, 185), but it is impossible to date it closely. The other donors 
also occur in the same documents. Holywell Hall lies about 2 miles south-west of Loughborough. Nichols’s 
copy from the cartulary is inaccurate and incomplete.

Anschetil Mallory was dead at Michaelmas 1186 (PR 32 Hen. IT, 126). William de Breteuil was the eldest 
son of the earl and died shortly before his father; Robert his brother succeeded to the earldom and is 
better known as Robert fitzParnell. The family of de Bosco were tenants of the earl’s Norman honor of 
Breteuil from the 11th century, deriving their name from Bois-Arnault near Breteuil, upon which in turn 
they bestowed the distinctive name of Ernald. By marriage with Emma daughter and coheir of Payn of 
Houghton they acquired a moiety of Little Houghton and Brafield-on-the-Green, Northants., and other 
fees held of the honor of Huntingdon (HKF ii. 309). Owing to the fact that for more than 200 years the 
head of the family bore the name of Ernald it is as a rule a practical impossibility to distinguish between 
them.

The original charter, of which secondary evidence is here given, had presumably been lost or destroyed, 
The present instrument must be later than the departure of Earl Robert Blanchesmains at the end of 1189 
on the crusade on which he died (CP, 2nd ed. vii. 532); it is probable that it was later than the death of Earl 
Robert fitzParnell in Oct. 1204, but this presumption is weakened by the fact that he was much absent 
from England, being first on crusade and afterwards occupied by the war in Normandy during which he 
was for a time a prisoner. The only safe limits of date are therefore 1190-1212, the death of the countess 
(ibid. vii. 533). The presence of Herbert prior of Ware is accounted for by the fact that Parnell had 
Ware in dower. He is mentioned in a charter of William bishop of Lincoln between 1203 and 1206 (CDF, 
No. 648, where the name is wrongly given as Hubert, see Jnventaire sommaire de l’Orne, Série H, i. 190). 
It is interesting that the countess records that the original charter was sealed with the earl’s counterseal. 
The loss of the original charter seems to have been a continuing source of anxiety to the monks; as late 
as 1344 they were obtaining a confirmation from Alice de Beaumont (No. 13); see also Nos. 17 and 20.

SEAL on tag: obv. and rev.; yellow; same as to No. 418 (q.v.); no legends. 


Roger de Quincy, earl of Winchester, was the son of Saher the first earl by Margaret sister and coheir of 
Robert fitzParnell, earl of Leicester. Roger married firstly Helen daughter and coheir of Alan lord of 
Galloway, constable of Scotland; secondly Maud daughter of Humphrey de Bohun, earl of Hereford and 
Essex; thirdly Eleanor daughter of William de Ferrers, earl of Derby, and widow of William de Vaux. 
The countess Eleanor is mentioned in this charter, and since her first husband died shortly before 5 Dec. 
1252 (CP, 2nd ed. iv. 199) it cannot be earlier than 1253; Roger himself died 25 Apr. 1264. This charter 
must be earlier than No. 19, although not necessarily much earlier. So that the later limit of date may be 
regarded as 1260. It is possible that in Richard the knight of Thorpe lies the origin of the place-name 
Knight Thorpe between Loughborough and Garendon.

Newbottle is a lost place-name in Water Stratford (EPNS Bucks. 49); the other places named are Shalstone 
and Dodford in Stowe, Bucks. With this charter should be compared one of Hugh de Camville (Oxford 
Charters, No. 54), which deals with Godington, Oxon., about six miles south of the places here in question. 
It is witnessed by Richard de Camville and ‘Alardus’, who may well be identical with the ‘ Oelardus clericus’ 
of this charter. Mr. Salter suggests that Hugh de Camville was probably a younger son of Richard de 
Camville, the elder, by his first wife, and the fact that Hugh’s son Thomas was living in 1227 (Bracton’s 
Note Book, No. 262) affords chronological support for this view. But the Godington charter shows Hugh 
to have had a brother Roger, and there is no evidence that Richard had either a son Hugh or a son Roger. 
On the other hand, a charter of Richard for the abbey of Jumiéges dated 1170 (Vernier, Chartes de Jumiéges, 
Soc. Hist. Norm. ii. 1) mentions his deceased brother Roger, and his foundation charter for Combe 
abbey of 1150, or slightly later, is witnessed by his brother Hugh (Von. v. 584). On this view the grantor 
is Richard de Camville, the elder, who died in 1176 (PR 3 & 4 Ric. I, xxv—xxvi), rather than Richard, his 
son by his second wife. It is not chronologically impossible that his nephew, Thomas de Camville, Hugh’s 
son, should have survived as late as 1227. That the Thomas de Camville of 1227 was the son of the Hugh 
of the Godington charter is evident, for he mentions his mother Christina, the domina Cristina of the 
charter. The charter is copied into the Biddlesden cartulary (Harl. MS. 4714, f. 338) at the end of the 
Westbury section and bears no relation to the other Westbury charters, all of which are of considerably 
later date. This Camville interest in Westbury seems hitherto to have escaped notice. In the 13th century 
the Harangs became the predominant family there (VCH Bucks. iv. 263; cf. No. 9 ante).

Roger de Somery married Nichola, sister and coheir of Hugh d’Aubigny, earl of Arundel, who died 
7 May 1243, which Hugh was son of Mabel, sister and coheir of Ranulf III, earl of Chester (CP, 2nd ed. 
i. 237). The Despenser lands in Loughborough and the neighbourhood (Nos. 3 and 19) were held of the 
honor of Chester, and Roger’s interest must have been derived through his wife and her mother. On the 
Close Roll of 1244 the service of Philip de Corlingstorp of a third of a fee in Thorpe Muntford was assigned 
to Roger and his wife in respect of their share of the Chester and Arundel inheritance (Close Rolls, 1242-7, 
251). The name of Thorpe Muntford has disappeared, but Farrer (HKF ii. 63) suggests that it is now 
represented by Woodthorpe near Loughborough. This seems very likely, for the same third of a fee in 
Thorpe Muntford is mentioned in a list of Arundel fees of 1235-6 which includes the Despenser lands and 
others. in this district (Fees, 517). The agreement must be later than the earl of Arundel’s death in 1243. 
It is probably very little later than that date. No. 19 is witnessed by Serlo son of Richard son of Serlo de 
Torp, who is presumably the son of Richard and the grandson of Serlo, who both witness the present 
charter. It is possible that the Henry son of Serlo and Richard his brother, associated as grantors with 
Thomas Despénser in Henry II’s reign, may be an earlier generation of this family, see No. 3.

This document appears to be slightly later than the other deeds of this period relating to the common 
rights of Garendon Abbey, see Nos. 7 and 12 above. The grantor succeeded Hugh Bigod as justiciar in 
1260, but was displaced in favour of his father-in-law Philip Basset in 1261 until J uly 1263, when he was 
again in office. He was killed at Evesham in 1265. Since he is not called justiciar it may be presumed 
that he was not in office when it was issued.

The inscription on the seal shows the donor to have been son of a Roger le Venur. In the Hastings collec- 
tion are many Kirby Muxloe deeds in which the Le Venur family figure (Hist. MSS. Com. Hastings Rep. 
i). By one dated 20 Apr. 1253 Robert le Venur son of Roger grants to John le Venur for 2 marks of silver 
half a virgate (loc. cit. 12, No. 56). The grantor of that charter was probably the son of a Roger le Venur 
who held half a knight’s fee in Kirby Muxloe of the honor of Peverel in 1235-6 (Fees, 520) and also identi- 
cal with the Robert of the present charter. He occurs again as Robert le Venur, who, with his son Roger, 
was holding land in Hathern of Matthew le Venur in 1255 (Cal. Ing. p.m. i, No. 339). In 1259 there is an 
inquisition on the death of a Robert le Venur who held land in chief in Kirby Muxloe and Hathern 
(ibid., No. 438), but as his heirs were two daughters aged 5 and 3 he was probably the son of Matthew. 
The date of this charter would seem to be about the middle of the 13th century.

Calke was a cell of Repton priory. In 1235-6 and 1242-3 East Leake was held of the honor of Ferrers 
(Fees, 533); at the Dissolution Repton priory possessed a pension on the rectory (Mon. vi. 431). The only 
certain limits of date for this charter are 1162, when the grantor obtained possession of his lands, and 
1190, the year of his death. The mention of his children and the attestation of Roger Pantulf, a younger 
son of William Pantulf who held one fee of the earl in 1166 (RB 337), suggest that it was not very early in 
this period. Though in form a gift, this is in reality a confirmation, the church having been given to the 
priory by Harold of Leake, whose charter is printed in Hist. MSS. Com. Hastings Rep. i. 119.

™ SIGIUU : PRILIPPI . DE . ALBINIACO BM 6794 


The grantor is Philip d’Aubigny, bailiff of the Channel Islands in the reign of Henry III. A charter of his 
for Le Mont-St-Michel has a seal identical with that of the present charter, and among the witnesses to that 
charter are ‘P. de Garclip. B. fratre suo’ (Cartulaire des Isles Normandes, Soc. J ersiaise, pl. vii and p. 25). 
For an account of the family see CP, 2nd ed. iv. 93 et seq. In the 13th century d’Aubignys occur in the 
dioceses of Dol and Rennes in Brittany, bearing the same arms (Morice, Hist. de Bretagne, ‘Preuves’, 
i, cols. 776, 784; pl. vii, figs. 64, 65), and there seems to be no doubt that they came from Aubigné, dép. 
Ille-et-Vilaine. Round has shown this to have been the original home of Aubigny ‘Brito’ of Belvoir (Hist. 
MSS. Com. Rutland Rep. iv. 107). We have here another branch of the family establishing itself in England 
at a later date. Philip had two brothers, Oliver and Marchisius (Round, CDF, No. 408). The manor of 
Enderby was given to Oliver by Parnell countess of Leicester, a gift confirmed by King John, 16 Dec. 1204 
(Rot. Chart. i. 140); Oliver gave land in Enderby to Croxton abbey, which was confirmed by his brother 
Philip (Nichols, iv, pt. i. 157). Oliver must have died without issue and been succeeded by Philip. Philip 
died in the Holy Land in 1235 (M. Paris, Chron. Mai., RS, iii. 373). Oliver de St. George occurs on the 
rolls between 1230 and 1235. He accompanied Philip to the Holy Land, as did Bertram de Garclip (Pat. 
Rolls, 1232-47, 101). Roger de Quincy took the title of earl of Winchester on his mother’s death in 1235-6.

In Pudsey Deeds, Yorks. Arch. Soc. Rec. Ser. 72, Col. Littledale identifies Belasis with Malasis, a district

No seal or tag shown. 


For the grantor see HKF iii. 398. It has sometimes been assumed that a gift pro salute anime implies that 
the person named was alive and a gift pro anima that he was dead. This cannot be regarded as a rule 
which holds good in all cases, and the present charter illustrates the point; see also Facsimiles of Early 
Charters, NRS iv. 67. The first formula is applied both to the grantor and to his father, who died in 1259, 
whereas the second is applied to the bishop of Norwich who was still alive. It is perhaps significant that 
the bishop, Roger Skerning, bore the name of one of the villages with which the charter deals.

This important charter is the root of title to the Master Chamberlainship or, as it is now called, the office 
of Lord Great Chamberlain. The history of the office has been exhaustively treated by Mr. G. H. White in 
CP, 2nd ed. x, Appendix F, 47-90, this charter being discussed at pp. 54-6: he has rendered further com- 
ment superfluous. The date can be fixed within narrow limits. A charter of the king dated at Winchester, 
1133, has a long list of witnesses including Aubrey de Vere, of whom no less than seven witness the present 
charter (Farrer, Itin., No. 697). Two charters are dated at Westbourne in transfretatione, one being dated 
1133 (ibid., Nos. 704, 707); Fareham lies between Winchester and Westbourne. The actual crossing to 
Normandy took place on 2 or 3 Aug. (ibid., No. 714). Thereafter a charter dated at Rouen 1133 is attested 
by five of the witnesses to this charter (ibid., No. 715).

This charter and the circumstances leading up to it have been discussed by Round in Geoffrey de Mandeville, 
179-94, 239-40, 439, but notwithstanding his high authority the view there put forward seems to call for 
further examination. 

Not later than 1139 Aubrey had married Beatrix, who on the death of her grandfather Count Manasses 
in that year became countess of Guisnes. In 1142 the Empress Maud executed a charter creating Aubrey 
earl of Cambridgeshire and giving him the third penny of that county, unless it should be that the king 
of Scotland already had that earldom; if it thus happened that Aubrey failed to obtain this earldom she 
granted that he should be earl of one of four counties, Oxfordshire, Berkshire, Wiltshire, or Dorset, as 
he might choose (Round, op. cit. 180). Later in the same year this grant was confirmed by the future 
Henry II, then a boy of 94, as rectus heres Anglie et Normannie (ibid. 186). In the empress’s charter 
Aubrey is described as comes and rightly, for he was then count of Guisnes in right of his wife. In or 
before 1146 the marriage of Aubrey and Beatrix must have been annulled, for she died, apparently in 
1146, as the wife of Baldwin of Ardres (ibid. 189). Aubrey never in fact became earl of Cambridge, and in 
a charter not later than 1147 he styles himself earl of Oxford (ibid. 194). 

Round’s view (op. cit. 239-40) is that the present charter is a new creation, that Henry did not recognize 
the validity of his mother’s charter of 1142, which would render the present grant of the third penny 
unnecessary, and that the comital style here given to Aubrey is referable to his countship of Guisnes. To 
this there seem to be serious objections. Aubrey’s marriage with the countess had been annulled; more- 
over, she was dead without issue and her cousin Arnold of Ghent was in possession of the comté and 
actually styled count: neither in law nor in fact was Aubrey count of Guisnes. To meet this Round prints 
a charter of Ording, abbot of St. Edmunds, making a grant Alberico comiti Gisnensi (op. cit. 189), Ording 
being the successor of Abbot Anselm who died in 1148. At first sight this seems sound evidence that 
Aubrey continued to. be styled count of Guisnes after the annulment of his marriage and his wife’s death; 
but Ording’s charter has since been again printed by Warner and Ellis (BM Facsimiles, No. 18), who point 
out that in 1138 Anselm was elected to the bishopric of London and Ording made abbot in his stead; 
Anselm’s election was ultimately quashed and he resumed the abbacy, ousting Ording probably in 1141; 
on Anselm’s death in 1148 Ording again became abbot. They attribute this charter to Ording’s first 
abbacy, and if Aubrey was styling himself earl of Oxford in 1147 it is unlikely that the abbot would style 
him count of Guisnes in 1148 or later. The argument that if Henry had recognized his mother’s grant as 
valid the present grant would have been unnecessary seems to be based on a misconception; the only 
third penny granted by the empress was that of Cambridgeshire; there was no express grant of the third 
penny of Oxfordshire and it is difficult to see what warrant the officials concerned would have had for 
paying it to him. Finally, it must not be forgotten that Henry had himself confirmed the empress’s grant. 
Had he wished to escape obligation, his youth at the time of that confirmation might have afforded a good 
pretext. 

It is submitted that the present charter is really based on the assumption of the validity of the empress’s 
charter and recognizes it to have created Aubrey an earl. That grant, however, was incomplete and the 
position exceptional. In modern parlance Aubrey had been given an option over the earldom of Oxford 
and had exercised it, but something more was needed to perfect his title and to put him in possession, and 
the problem was to accomplish this without impugning the earlier grant. It was done by the grant of the 


28 ROBERT BERTIE EARL OF LINDSEY 


third penny of Oxfordshire ut sit inde comes; armed with this he would receive the third penny which, 
operating after the manner of esplees, would be evidence that the earldom had been delivered to him and 
that he had possession of it.

Both Pinchon and his son Hugh were stewards of the bishop of Durham. In 1115 Pinchon the steward 
held of the bishop 2 car. 7 bov. in Fulstow (Lindsey Survey, LRS xix. 248) and 4 car. 6 boy. in Fulletby 
and Oxcombe (ibid. 257); while Hugh son of Pinchon held 4 bov. in Friskney of him (ibid. 253). In the 
Book of Fees and Feudal Aids the descent of these lands can be traced through the family of Bek to Robert 
of Willoughby who obtained the inspeximus of 1411; this similar devolution identifies the Pinchon and 
Hugh of the Survey as father and son. We learn from the continuator of Simeon of Durham (RS i. 156-7) 
that in 1144 Hugh son of Pinchon, the steward of William de Sainte-Barbe, bishop of Durham, betrayed 
his lord and joined William Cumin, who had usurped the see; the full tale of his iniquities is set out. An 
original charter of Bishop William de Sainte-Barbe in the treasury of Durham cathedral confirms Hugh’s. 
gift of Windgate and Smeaton, co. Durham, to Hugh Burrel (Surtees, Hist. of Durham, i. 97). At an 
uncertain date Hugh, described as seneschal of the bishop of Durham, gave land at Wainfleet, Lincs., to 
Bury St. Edmunds (Douglas, Feudal Documents, No. 213). He was still living in 1166, when he was returned 
as holding of the bishop of Durham 7 knights’ fees of the old feoffment in Lincolnshire and one of the 
same in the bishopric (RB 416-17): this is his last occurrence. A series of charters for Kirkstead abbey 
(Stenton, Danelaw Charters, Nos. 172-9) dealing with land in Kirkby on Bain show that it was by the 
marriage of Hugh’s daughter and heiress Agnes to Walter Bek that his lands passed to that family, but 
since the earliest of these is dated 1162, when Hugh was still living, Kirkby must have been Agnes’s mar- 
riage portion. The materials for dating the charter are scanty. Since Ranulf earl of Chester succeeded 
his cousin, Richard, who was drowned in the White Ship on 25 Nov. 1120, it can hardly be earlier than 
1121; the later limit is the king’s last crossing to Normandy at the beginning of Aug. 1133. Robert Bertie, 
earl of Lindsey and Lord Willoughby d’Eresby, in whose possession this charter was in 1640, was the 
representative of the Robert of Willoughby of 1411; it was therefore still in proper custody.

RICARDI DE CAMVIUE 
Richard de Camville, the grantor, was the eldest son of Richard de Camville the elder by his second wife 
Milisent, widow of Robert Marmion (of Tamworth who died 1143-4) and cousin to Henry I’s queen 
Adeliza, who gave her part of the manor of Stanton Harcourt, giving other parts to Reading abbey, the 
Templars, and William de Harfleur (White Kennett, Parochial Antiquities, 2nd ed. i. 154, from a Reading 
cartulary). Richard the father died in 1176 (PR 3 & 4 Ric. I, xxxvi); the date of Milisent’s death is un- 
certain, but the language of a charter of 1170 by which her husband, Richard de Camville, gave tithe in 
Hautot-l’Auvray, Seine-Inf., to the abbey of Jumiéges suggests that she was then dead (Vernier, Chartes 
de Jumiéges, Soc. Hist. Norm. ii. 1). The family took its name from Canville-les-Deux-Eglises, Seine- 
Inf., arr. Yvetot, about 4 miles from Hautot-l’Auvray. The grantor died at Acre on crusade in 1191; his 
eventual heir was his daughter Isabel who married Robert de Harcourt (PR 3 & 4 Ric. I, 251). Assuming 


that the land here granted at some time reverted to the Harcourts this charter was in 1640 in proper custody. 
Continuous entries on the Pipe Rolls from 1177 to 1191, confirmed by an entry in the Eynsham cartulary 


30 SIR SIMON HARCOURT 


(i. 398, Ox. Hist. Soc.), suggest that the manor was throughout that period in the king’s hand, but the 
present charter seems to show that at some time Richard de Camville was in possession and it may be 
that the entries in question relate to other parts of the manor. The actual transaction seems to have been 
in essence a gift by Robert Pipard to his brother Richard, effected by a surrender to the chief lord of the 
fee and a regrant by him, thus avoiding the creation of a mesne tenancy: for a similar case see No. 301.

Hugh earl of Chester was deprived of his earldom in 1174 as a result of his share in the great rebellion 
and was restored to full possession of his lands at the council of Northampton in Jan. 1177; he died 30 June 


SIR SIMON HARCOURT 31 


1181. John of Oxford was consecrated bishop of Norwich 14 Dec. 1175. The king left England in Apr. 
1180 and did not return until the end of July 1181. This gives the limits of date 1177-80, and in view of 
the names of the witnesses it seems certain that the charter passed at the council of Northampton in Jan. 
1177. Eyton noticed this charter from Dodsworth MSS. cxxx, f. 1195 and attributed it to this occasion (Itin. 
210). Nicholas of Stafford seems to have enfeoffed Noel with Ronton and Cooksland probably before 
1100 and Nicholas’s son, Robert of Stafford, seems to have enfeoffed Noel’s son, Robert, with Burgh by 
Gnossal in the reign of Stephen (W. Salt Coll. ii. 219 and 256). Robert son of Noel founded Ronton priory, 
and much information about the family is to be found in General Wrottesley’s abstract of the cartulary in 
W. Salt Coll. iv. William de Harcourt, son and heir of the Robert of No. 44, married Alice daughter and 
coheir of Thomas the grantee. In 1640, therefore, the original of this charter was in proper custody. The 
inquisition on the death of Richard de Harcourt in 1258 (Cal. Ing. p.m. i, No. 41 1) shows him holding the 
manor of Ellenhall, Staffs., of the bishop of Lichfield and Coventry for half a knight’s fee. In the bishop’s 
return of 1166 (RB 263) Robert son of Noel is shown as holding half a knight’s fee of the old enfeoffment. 
Richard Peche was consecrated bishop in 1161, so that his charter, here confirmed, was a regrant, or 
confirmation of Thomas’s inheritance. Laurence occurs as prior of Coventry in 1144 and died 29 Jan. 
1179 (VCH Warw. ii. 58). The charter of Abbot Anselm confirming Hawstead to William son of Albold, 
here confirmed, is printed by Professor Douglas in Feudal Documents, 127. The wife of Robert son of 
Noel was named Alice (W. Salt Coll. iv. 271) and, as Hawstead came to Thomas by inheritance, she would 
seem to have been the eventual heir of William son of Albold.

The early descent of Arden is shown by a suit of the year 1208 (Cur. Reg. Rolls, v. 241). The Domesday 
tenant-in-chief Thurchil of Warwick, or Arden, left by his first wife a son Siward of Arden, living in 1130 
(PR 31 Hen. I, 108), who left two sons, Henry, the present donor, and Hugh (see Nos. 52, 138), who in 
1166 held 5 and 54 fees respectively of the earl of Warwick (RB 325). The suit of 1208 shows that Henry’s 
successor in title was then his son Thomas of Arden (see No. 159); Henry’s son William must therefore 
have died without issue and probably in his father’s lifetime. By a second wife, Leveruna, Thurchil left a 
son Osbert of Arden, living 1130 (PR 31 Hen. I, 105), for whom and his descendants see Cur. Reg. Rolls, 
vii. 102; BM Facsimiles, No. 12; Stenton, English Feudalism, 187, 279. There is an elaborate pedigree of 
the family in Dugdale’s Warwickshire, 1765 ed. 651, which, however, requires correction.

his father Henry in 1209 and died in 1232, being succeeded by his son, another Henry (CP, 2nd ed. x. 523).

ROBERT ARDEN, ESQ. 35 


The grantor is the well-known Gervase Paynel of Dudley, for whom see EYC vi. 48-50: the grantee 
held Rugby, from which he took his name (Dugdale, Warwickshire, 1765 ed. 17). The inquisition taken on 
the death of Roger III de Somery, Gervase’s representative in 1291, shows Mabel, daughter and coheir of 
Rannulf of Rugby, holding Saltley near Birmingham by the service of one-fifth of a knight (Cal. Inq. p.m. 
li, No. 813), which identifies the ‘Saluthleia’ of this charter. The date must be later than the grantor’s 
return of his knights in 1166 (RB 269), since this holding is not included. The latest limit is not easy to 
fix; Mr. Mander has shown (op. cit. 48) that Peter ‘dapifer’ is Peter of Birmingham. Alan occurs as 
Gervase’s steward in 1180 (PR 26 Hen. II, 79), also in 1181 and 1182; he also so occurs in 1193, just before 
Gervase’s death (PR 5 Ric. I, 99), and may be presumed to have held office during the intervening period. 
Peter of Birmingham occurs in 1171 (PR 17 Hen. II, 54), but in 1176 his son William makes a render for 
a forest offence (PR 22 Hen. II, 169); this taken in conjunction with the occurrence of Alan as steward 
in 1180 points to Peter being dead in 1176. John de Somery, who married Hawisa, sister and heiress of 
Gervase, was the first Somery lord of Dudley (Staffs. Coll., 1941, 35).

Ela daughter of William Longespée, earl of Salisbury, married first Thomas earl of Warwick, who died 
26 June 1262 without issue, and secondly Philip Basset, who died 1271. She died 6 Feb. 1297. For Thomas 
of Arden see Dugdale, Warwickshire, 1765 ed. 650-2. Dugdale assumes that Thomas was ruined by fine 
exacted by the Dictum de Kenilworth, since he alienated most of his properties during the years after 1281. 
Curdworth among other lands was given to Hugh de Vienne in 1281, a grant Dugdale assumed to be 
‘no other than a trust; for very soon after did the same Thomas convey the inheritance to Thomas de 
Arden of Hanwell’ (Dugdale, op. cit. 649). The present document must date from Ela’s first widowhood.

John de Wahull was under age at the time of his father’s death in 1269; he died in 1296 leaving a widow, 
Agnes, and a son, Thomas, aged 23 (HKF i. 67). He must have been married between 1269 and 1272. 
Since the land was to be held of the donor and his heirs the gift must have been made before the statute 
of Quia Emptores in 1290. William de St. John of Plumpton died shortly before 1288, leaving as his heir 
his grandson, William, who was under age and died in 1331 (HKF i. 88). Therefore this charter was 
made in the reign of Edward I, probably before 1288. It is cited by Baker, Northamptonshire, i. 725, as 
from ‘Hatton portfolio of deeds no. 54’. According to Dugdale (Warwickshire, 1765 ed. 652) the grantee, 
Thomas de Arden of Hanwell, married Rose daughter of Ralf de Vernon, ‘by whom (I think) he had the 
said lordship of Hanwell’. From Thomas de Arden of Ratley he received Peddimore, Curdworth, and 
other lands in about 1286 (Dugdale, op. cit., see note to No. 51). The pedigree of the family given by 
Dugdale, op. cit. 651, does not agree in all respects with his account of the immediate descendants of 
Thomas of Arden of Hanwell on the following page.

The grantor was the son and heir of the earl and countess of Salisbury, William Longespée and Ela (see 
note to No. 62), but he never became earl. His father died 7 Mar. 1226. His mother having taken the 
veil at Lacock abbey in 1238, he had succeeded to his inheritance; he was slain in Syria 8 Feb. 1250. 
‘Hammes’ is probably Hampreston, Dors., in the hundred of Cogdean; it lies near Canford Magna, which 
was a fee of the earl of Salisbury. See also No. 192.

Charter of William de Percy, son of Henry de Percy, confirming to Thomas de Archis, son of Alan de

Fragment of equestrian seal on tag. 


The places mentioned are all in the West Riding of Yorkshire except Rainton in Topcliffe in the North 
Riding, Stamford in the East Riding, and Somerby near Brigg in Lincolnshire. On the death of William 
de Percy, the last of the first house, his lands were divided between his daughters, Agnes (d. 1205) wife of 
Joscelin of Louvain, and Maud (d. c. 1204 s.p.) wife of William earl of Warwick. Agnes’s son and heir 
Henry de Percy died in his mother’s lifetime, and on the death of the coheiresses the Percy lands were 


BY | 3 


GERVASE HOLLES, ESQ. 39 


divided between Henry’s son and heir, William, the present grantor, and his uncle Richard de Percy, 
Agnes’s younger son, an arrangement which led to prolonged litigation. William de Percy was under age 
at Trinity 1212 and in ward to William Briwerre, who then recovered against Richard de Percy the service 
due from Rainton, lately held by Alan de Arches, who was dead (Cur. Reg. Rolls, vi. 321). But William 
must have been of age by Trinity 1214, when he occurs as plaintiff in an assize of darrein presentment 
respecting the church of Kirkby Overblow (ibid. vii. 224). He was living in 1242-3, when Thomas de Arches 
is returned as holding Somerby of him (Fees, 1013), but was dead by 28 July 1245 (CP, 2nd ed. x. 452). 
These facts give an outside limit of date for the present charter of 1214-45, but on 11 June 1231 William 
de Percy by a final concord recognized the right of Thomas de Arches to 6 carucates in Rainton (Percy 
Chartulary, Surtees Soc. 25), and in Oct. 1234 there is a record of the final settlement of the disputes 
between him and his uncle Richard before the justices at Westminster by which among other things 
Richard recognized William’s right to the manors of Tadcaster and Linton and the tenure of Thomas de 
Arches from William (ibid. 464). This charter must be later than the former of these, and in all probability 
is shortly after the settlement between nephew and uncle. By a final concord made 19 Jan. 1234/5 Thomas 
de Arches gave 21 bovates of land in Rainton to St. Leonard’s hospital, York (Yorks. Fines 1232-46, 
Yorks. Arch. Soc. Rec. Ser. Ixvii. 35). This possibly gives the latest limit of date. For the Percy family 
see CP, 2nd ed.'x.

BS FACSIMILE. 
PRINTED: Mon. v. 84, ‘ex autogr.’ Mentioned: Dugdale, Baronage, i. 613. 


An indulgence granted by Archbishops Basil of Jerusalem (Jerosolomitanus), Adenulf of Consa della 
Campagna (Adenulfus Consanus), and Rannulf of Cagliari in Sardinia (Rannaus Calaritanus), and bishops © 
Adam of Martorano (Maituran’), Nicholas of Nicastro (Neocastrens’), Nicholas Colcedoine, Angelus of 
' Fiesole (Fesulanus), Bernard of Parenzo (Parentinus), Thomas Etesien, Nicholas of Tortiboli (T: ortibulen’), 
Anthony Chenodien’, Bernard of Badajoz in Spain (Pacens’), Benedict of Dragonaria (Dragonensis) 
remitting 40 days of enjoined penance to all who are truly penitent and confessed, so often as they shall 
devoutly say the Lord’s Prayer together with the Angelic Salutation for the soul of Roger de Someri, who 
lies buried in the priory church of Dudley in the diocese of Coventry and Lichfield, and for the souls of all 
the faithful departed. Sealing clause. “Datum Rome anno domini millesimo trecentesimo Pontificatus 
domini Bonfacii Pape octaui anno sexto.? Rome: 22 Feb.-24 Dec. 1300. 


This indulgence for the soul of the third Roger de Somery must have been granted during the jubilee of 
1300, proclaimed by a bull dated 22 Feb. 1300; the last day of the year according to the Roman reckoning 
was 24 Dec. The bishops must have acted pursuant to a papal commission, which is not, however, en- 
rolled in the register. The second Roger de Somery of Dudley died shortly before 26 Aug. 1273 and was 
succeeded by his son, another Roger (Cal. Ing. p.m. Edw. I, i, No. 16). About the first Roger de Somery 
of Dudley there is doubt; see Staffs. Coll., 1941, 29 et seq. The third Roger died shortly before 11 Oct. 1291 
(Cal. Ing. p.m. Edw. I, p. 813). In the Monasticon (v. 84) is printed an indulgence for the soul of Roger de 
Someri in similar terms to this, granted by Roger Longespée, bishop of Coventry and Lichfield, on 18 Feb. 
1290/1, which must refer to the second Roger.

Lucius III was elected 1 Sept. and crowned 6 Sept. 1181; he died 25 Nov. 1185. The year of grace in the 
Datum is therefore impossible, but the year of the pontificate and the indiction agree and give the date 
16 June 1182, which is clearly correct; the pope was at Velletri at that time. The Cluniac priory of St. 
James of Dudley was founded by Gervase Paynel.

Letters of John the abbot and of the convent of the monastery of the Blessed Mary of Halesowen of the 
Premonstratensian order of the diocese of Worcester reciting that, Whereas King Edward IV has granted 
to the abbot and convent his priory of Dodford in the diocese of Worcester so that it may be united to 
the abbey; Therefore the abbot and convent grant and promise that on every 30th December being the 
day of the death of Richard duke of York, the king’s father, they will in perpetuity solemnly celebrate at 
the altar of the conventual church a mass of requiem for the soul of the said duke and the souls of all 
the faithful departed and on the evening of the preceding day will sing solemnly (per notam solemniter 
dicent) Placebo and Dirige in the quire of the church aforesaid; they will repair and maintain the quire of 
the priory of Dodford and will cause a fitting priest twice a week at least there to celebrate masses for the 
souls of the founders and every weekday to say the office of the dead for the souls of Richard the king’s 
father and of Edmund earl of Rutland. Every canon of the monastery at his profession and every 
abbot at his installation or within three days thereof shall take his corporal oath faithfully to observe the 
foregoing. 

‘Et ut hec omnia et singula omni dolo et fraude postposita fideli et perpetua firmitate conseruentur nos 
omnes et singuli promisimus bona fide et in verbo dei pro nobis ecclesia nostra et successoribus nostris. 
Renunciantes expresse in hiis omnibus et singulis omni priuilegio indulto vel indulgendo et omnibus 
impetratis et impetrandis et constitucioni de duabus dietis edite in concilio generali. Item priuilegio fori 
et omni cauillacioni appellacioni dilacioni defensioni excepta et omni iuris et facti remedio et omnibus 
aliis que nobis possint uel successoribus nostris seu ecclesie nostre aliquo modo contra premissa predicta

episcopi Wygorn’ qui pro tempore fuerit ad cuius iurisdictionem dictus prioratus de Doddeford noscitur

Charter of Ela, countess of Salisbury, in her widowhood giving to Nicholas Lungspeie her son the manor 
of Edgware, Middx. (Egesware), and whatever may come to her in the village of Cowlinge, Suff. (Colinges),

to hold to him and the heirs of his body rendering a sparrowhawk at the feast of St. Peter Ad Vincula 
(1 Aug.) for all services except the king’s service. If Nicholas die without an heir of his body the premises

Ela, the daughter and heir of William, earl of Salisbury, married William Longespée, illegitimate son of 
Henry II, who became earl of Salisbury and died in Mar. 1226. In 1238 she became a nun at Lacock abbey 
which she had founded and of which she was abbess from 1239 to 1257; she died in 1261. Her son Nicholas 
was treasurer of Salisbury cathedral in 1284 (Charters &c. of Salisbury Cathedral, RS, 362), was conse- 
crated bishop of Salisbury 16 Mar. 1292, and died 18 May 1297. The date of this charter must be before 
Ela’s entry into religion and its terms suggest that Nicholas had not yet embraced an ecclesiastical career. 
For Cowlinge see Fees, 391.

Hubert de Burgh was created earl of Kent on 19 Feb. 1227 and died 12 May 1243. On 9 Mar. 1235 Henry 
III inspected and confirmed a charter of Hubert giving land in Soham together with a number of tenants 
and their holdings to Philip Basset, son of Alan Basset (Cal. Chart. Rolls, i. 195); among the tenants so 
given is the Aylsy Nad of this charter, which must therefore be a subsequent exchange. This therefore 
supplies the earlier limit of date. Philip Basset lived until 1271 and the later limit is therefore the death 
of Hubert.

The abbot of Peterborough was John de Caux, ‘a kinsman of the queen of England; wherefore he was 
treasurer of King Henry IV and justice itinerant’ (Walter de Whitlesey, Historia Anglicane Scriptores 
Varie, 129). He became treasurer in 1260. Philip Basset was appointed justiciar in 1261 and Walter of 
Merton chancellor in the same year. Henry III obtained absolution of his oath to observe the Provisions 
of Oxford from Pope Alexander in April and May 1261. In Feb. 1262 Pope Urban confirmed Alexander’s 
bulls. The king was attempting to recover his royal authority, lost when the barons revolted in 1258. 
Both parties were appealing to King Louis IX of France, and Henry III left England for Paris 8 July 1262 
(Annales Monastici, iii. 218), returning early in the next year. The queen had clearly been helping her son 
to raise funds to enable him to attend tournaments in France. He was abroad from early in Nov. 1260 to 
the spring of 1261, and again in July of that year. These letters prove his presence in England in early 
June 1262. According to the annals of Dunstable (Annales Monastici, iii. 216) he took a great company 
of knights abroad to tourney in 1260 and was soundly beaten, losing all he took with him. The same 
authority records that in June 1262 he was beaten again and seriously wounded in a tournament abroad 
(op. cit. 218). For the political situation in these years see F. M. Powicke, Henry III and the Lord Edward, 
ii. 411-30. 


Professor T. F. T. Plucknett has very kindly supplied the following note on the law of this document. 

‘The queen and Edward (who admit that they are the principal debtors) raised a loan from the Floren- 
tines, who, however, insisted on five substantial persons joining in the bond. The bond (containing the 
five additional names) was engrossed, but only four sealed; for reasons unknown Walter of Merton refused. 

‘It would be natural for the lenders to call upon the would-be borrowers to find a substitute for Walter. 
The fact that they did not do so seems to show that they had already parted with their money and lost 
their bargaining power. They took instead the deed here printed, which assumes that the remaining four 
are still bound, and asserts that the queen and Edward recognise themselves as principal debtors. The 
merchants seem uncertain of their rights against anyone save the queen and Edward, who then proceed 
to give the very curious indemnity which is the substance of this document. Since they demanded five 
sureties in the first place as security for a loan, it is difficult to see how the merchants could pee from 
this indemnity by the debtors themselves, in effect, guaranteeing their own debt. 

‘The “new constitution” is Justinian’s Novel 99; Accursius in his gloss on Auth. VII. 11 cedere explains 
that the benefit of this law can be renounced.’ 

Professor Plucknett adds that he has ‘traced the second renunciation of jus de principali to Novel 4,alaw 
saying that the creditor cannot sue a surety until after he has sued the principal debtor, which of course 
takes time’.

Both this charter and No. 104 are now in the Harleian collection, sold to the nation in 1753 by the widow 
of the second earl of Oxford and Mortimer (CP, 2nd ed. x. 267-8 n.). It is difficult to see how they can 
have still been in the possession of Thomas Astle when they were used by Watson, op. cit. Both charters 
are concerned with the rights of pasture on Hatfield Moor near Hatfield Chase, Yorks., W.R.; a general 
account of the locality will be found in Hunter’s South Yorkshire, Deanery of Doncaster, i. 150 et seq., and 
in J. Tomlinson’s Level of Hatfield Chase. Lindholme stands in the middle of the moor and is a piece of 
arable land about 60 acres in extent raised above the general level (Hunter, op. cit. i. 196). Thorne lies 
to the north of the moor and the river Thorne to the south. The memory of ‘Hutholmes de Clunes’ or 
“Glunes’ seems to be preserved, shown to the west of Lindholme on Hatfield Moor (map facing p. 83 in 
Tomlinson, op. cit.). Cowbridge-end is mentioned among the boundaries of the Chase in an inquest of 
1607 (Tomlinson, op. cit. 62), but does not now appear upon the map. The grantor was a natural son of 
Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and the second husband of Isabel, the Warenne heiress. The reference to the 
counts of Maine is due to the fact that Count Geoffrey’s mother, Erenburgis, was a daughter of Helias 
de la Fléche, count of Maine. Since Henry II is mentioned as dead the charter cannot be earlier than 1189, 
and the grantor died 7 May 1202. The date is probably late in this period, for William de Livet as steward 
and Thomas of Horbury witness together a charter for Lewes priory c. 1198 (Yorks. Arch. Journ. xxxi. 312).

Stanlawe abbey, founded by the donor’s father, John de Lacy, constable of Chester, was moved to Whalley 
at the end of the 13th century. Alan of Marland’s charter to Roger de Lacy is entered in the Coucher Book 
immediately before the present charter; it is witnessed by Philip of Orby as justice of Chester, an office 
which he acquired before Oct. 1208 (Cartulary of Chester Abbey, Chetham Soc, i, p. v) and possibly before 
13 Nov. 1207 (ibid. ii, p. xxix). The later limit of date is supplied by the donor’s death in 1211. The witnesses 
to this charter should be compared with those to one of Roger for Kirkstall abbey (ZYC iii. 212 n.). Hugh 
of Elland, who here appears as Roger’s overlord for Marland, was himself a Lacy tenant in respect of 
Elland (Yorks., W.R.); presumably Alan of Marland had been Hugh’s tenant before he sold the land to 
Roger. An account of the Elland family will be found in Yorks. Arch. Journ. xxvii. 225-48, with a pedigree.

The charter of Robert, son of Erneis, giving the church of Goxhill to the priory is printed by Farrer (EYC, 
_ tii, No. 1341) and is really a confirmation. Notes on the family will be found in Farrer (loc. cit.) and in 
Registrum Antiquissimum, LRS, ii. 212. In Aug. 1203 Walter de Ver, the grantor, was under age (Cur. 
Reg. Rolls, iii. 64), and was apparently still a minor in 1205 (Farrer, op. cit. iii. 61). Walter was living in 
1212 (Fees, 159), but was dead by Michaelmas 1213 when Sybil his widow was suing for dower (Cur. Reg. 
Rolls, vii. 5). She married as her second husband Nicholas de Chavencurt, a witness to this charter. 
Nicholas and Sybil recovered her dower against the abbot of Thornton Curtis before justices itinerant in 
1218-19. The case was adjourned from Lincoln and judgment in the plaintiffs’ favour was given at 
Nottingham in Mar. 1219 (Rolls of the Justices in Eyre for Lincolnshire, 1218-19, Selden Soc. 53, case 
705). Walter de Ver’s heir, Simon, was then a minor in custody of the bishop of Lincoln.

The complicated dealings with the earldom of Gloucester at this period are treated at length in CP, 2nd 

ed. vy. 689-93. Amaury was the son of Amaury de Montfort, count of Evreux, of the elder line of the 

family of Montfort-l’Amaury (ibid. vii. 716 7.) and Mabel eldest daughter and coheir of William, earl of 
Gloucester. John ceded to Philip II of France Amaury’s comté of Evreux, giving to Amaury in exchange 

the earldom of Gloucester. Early in June 1200 he wrote from Caen to Geoffrey fitzPeter, earl of Essex and 

Justiciar, informing him that he had given to Amaury ‘the third penny of the county of: Gloucester as 

all who were earls of Gloucester have had it and girt him with the sword and made him earl thereof’ 

(Pipe Roll. Soc. xxi, N.S. 89). As from Easter Amaury received the third penny (PR 2 John, 119). By a 

charter dated at Le Goulet in May 1200 John quitclaimed Evreux to Philip (J. J. Vernier, Facsimilés des 

Chartes normandes, Soc. Hist. Norm., No. 16); in which charter Amaury is described as earl of Gloucester, 
but uses his equestrian seal as count of Evreux. He died shortly before 1213. 

By a charter dated at Oxford 29 Mar. 1205 King John confirmed to the abbey this gift of William the 
chamberlain’s among others (Mon. v. 497). The limits of date of the present charter are those of Amaury’s 
tenure of the earldom, but in view of the king’s confirmation it probably belongs to the earlier part of it. 
A number of charters of a William the chamberlain for Margam abbey are printed in Clark, Cartae de 
Glamorgancia, 2nd ed. iii. 890-3; he may be identical with the present donor.

The earlier history of Allexton will be found under No. 146; the present donor was a descendant of the 
John de Bachepuis the donee of No. 146. During the early part of the 13th century and in 1226 the patron 
of the church of Allexton was a John de Bachepuis (Rot. Hug. de Welles, LRS, i. 258; ii. 301) and in 1235-6 
John de Bachepuis held one fee there (Fees, 519), but in 1259 Peter de Bachepuis presented (Rot. Ric. 
Gravesend, LRS, 138). Nichols (iii. 5) cites a charter, penes S. Roper, by which John de Bachepuis gave 
his son Nicholas a virgate and a half in Allexton; that must be a different charter from this.

Possibly the artist’s need to get this charter into a small space induced him to suggest that the strip for 
seal and the riband were cut less far across the document than they were in reality. 


This charter and No. 105, the later and fuller confirmation by Roger, the second earl, must be read 
together in the light of Round’s article on ‘Walter Tirel and his Wife’ (Feudal England, 468-79), in which 
he treats at length of the alienation of Langham to Gervase of Cornhill by Hugh Tirel, the son and heir 
of that Walter Tirel who labours under the suspicion of having caused the death of William Rufus. 
Round describes a confirmatory charter of Earl Gilbert, then PRO Duchy of Lancaster; Grants in boxes, 
A 157. It is now DL 27-47, and the collation given above shows it to be for all practical purposes a dupli- 
cate of the present charter. It should be noted that both charters are sealed. We know from a letter of 
Louis VII of France to Odo, bishop of Beauvais, that Hugh Tirel went on crusade in 1147 (Rec. des Hist. de 
France, xvi. 10), and charter No. 105 below shows that the object of the sale of Langham was to provide 
the necessary money. That sale and consequently this charter cannot well be earlier than 1146; on the 
other hand, the first witness Gilbert, earl of Pembroke, died in 1148. For the Cornhill family see Round, 
Geoffrey de Mandeville, 304-12.

Hervey Bagot married Milisent daughter of Robert de Stafford, the grantor of No. 143. Her brother

Amaury was son of Ralf de St. Amand and Azeline sister and coheir of Robert d’Aubigny of Cainhoe 
(BHRS xix. 146). As his parents were married in 1234 or later this charter can hardly be earlier than 1256. 
In the British Museum (Harl. Chart. 50 H 41) is a notification that on 27 Dec. 1273 master Henry of 
Chesham in his hall beside the church of St. Peter in the East at Oxford delivered a charter conveying all 
his land in Bedfordshire to Amaury de St. Amand; it also states that Henry died on the Sth of January 
following. This conveyance shortly before his death suggests that the present charter, which must be earlier, 
represents a feoffment to uses. For Cotes see the note to No. 136.

Charter of Agnes de Mussegros, lady of Chinnor, Oxon. (Cennore), in her free widowhood giving to 
Thame abbey Oxon. one penny of yearly rent in Sydenham, Oxon. (Sydeham), in free alms for the health 
of her soul and that of Robert de Mussegros formerly her husband, being that penny of rent which Thomas 
de Duno used to render to her for the yearly rent of 100 shillings which the said Thomas used to receive 
annually from the abbot and convent of Thame, of the gift of Roger de Quincy, Agnes’s grandfather, 
sometime earl of Winchester, who gave the aforesaid rent of 100 shillings to Reginald de Duno, Thomas’s 
father. Sealing clause. ‘Hiis testibus domino Hugone de Pleciis . domino Roberto Malet domino Elya 
de Wytefeld . Thoma de Fell’ Nicholas Bursard . Johanne de Boys . Hugone Pirton de Tham’ . Ricardo
