SEAL on tag: pointed oval, 1} x ? in.; green. Three shields of arms suspended from a tree, (i) a lion rampant 
to sinister; (ii) and (iii) both vair; [SIJ]JGIVUVM IGDETI? DG& : MV : CAGRO. 


Agnes was the wife of Robert de Mucegros, who died 27 Dec. 1280 (CP, 2nd ed. v. 320-1). Chinnor 
with its hamlet Sydenham had been held by Roger de Quincy, earl of Winchester (see No. 67); he left 
three daughters and coheirs, Margaret wife of William de Ferrers, earl of Derby, Elizabeth wife of Alexan- 
der Comyn, earl of Buchan, and Helen wife of Alan la Zouche. In 1278-9 the verdict of a jury as to Chin- 
nor (Hundred Rolls, ii. 783) states Agnes to be daughter of Robert de Ferrers, earl of Derby, Earl William’s 
son and successor, and to have received Chinnor as her maritagium. She must, however, have been the 
daughter of Earl William since she calls Roger de Quincy her grandfather, and moreover, the affiliation to 
Earl Robert would involve the marriage of an uncle and niece, for Hawise de Mucegros, Agnes’s daughter, 
married John de Ferrers of Chartley, son and heir of Earl Robert (CP v. 307-8). A papal dispensation was 
obtained from the impediment of affinity in the third degree arising out of an unconsummated marriage 
between Hawise and William de Mortimer, then dead, John and William being first cousins once removed 
(ibid.; Cal. Papal Letters, i. 588), but no dispensation seems to have been obtained from the impediment 
of consanguinity in the second degree between John and Hawise.

The text in BS is much abbreviated; for instance, the dates for the payment of the rent are omitted, as 
also the warranty clause. For a pedigree of Montfichet see Feudal Cambridgeshire, 234; Richard de 
Montfichet the elder died in 1203 and was succeeded by his son, another Richard, who died in 1267. The 
witness Warin son of Ralf of Barrington occurs in 1279 (ibid. 236, 243), and in the same year William de 
la Haye was holding one hide in Shepreth (ibid. 232). The date of this charter cannot therefore be many 
years earlier than 1267, and this seems to be confirmed by the handwriting of the original.

in Wath, a name subsequently absorbed in Wentworth Woodhouse.

Notification by Sir John de Wahul that he is bound to his steward William St. John, son of John St. John, 
residing in Plumpton, Northants. (P/wmton’), to pay him the yearly sum of 5 marks sterling in equal 
amounts at Easter and Michaelmas for his service as steward while he shall hold that office; William is 
also to have 18 pence a day for his maintenance and expenses and for the maintenance of his grooms 
(garcionum) and horses, and in addition to the said 18 pence he shall have wood ‘&c.’ on all days that

mus liber quietus et absolutus ab omnimodis compotis permaneat inperpetuum absque aliqua calumpnia 
mei &c.’ Sealing clause. ‘Hiis testibus domino Willelmo de Gradden’ Watero de Gradden’. Willelmo le 
Waleys. Willelmo de Roddeston’ et aliis.’ (After 1288-96.) 


Tag only for SEAL. 


The transcript in BS is abbreviated. John de Wahull, then a minor, succeeded his father Walter in 1269; 
he died in the spring of 1296 (HKF i. 67). The next John to hold the honor was his grandson, who was 
under age in 1316 and died in 1336 (ibid. 68). William St. John, son of John, succeeded his grandfather 
William in or shortly before 1288, being then under age (ibid. 88). The present instrument therefore must 
be after 1288 and not later than the death of John de Wahull in 1296.

Isabel clearly outlived her husband, for she refers to his death in a charter reproduced in facsimile by 
Watson (op. cit. i. 169); the substance of the present charter points to its being made during her widow- 
hood. Alexander was prior of Lewes in 1201, and was succeeded by the witness Hubert, more correctly 
Humbert, in 1202, who was still prior in 1207 (VCH Sussex, ii. 70). As many of the witnesses also figure 
in Hamelin’s charter, No. 69 above, the present one was probably made not long after his death.

The most interesting feature of this charter is perhaps the appearance of John the nephew of St. Thomas 
among the witnesses; it is also the only criterion of date. He was the son of Rohese, the archbishop’s 
sister. At Michaelmas 1176 the sheriff of Kent accounts for a pension to Rohese of 11 pounds charged 
on the mill of Canterbury (PR 22 Hen. II, 205). The entry continues till Michaelmas 1185 when it is charged 
as paid to Rohese and her son John, Rohese having presumably died during the financial year (PR 
31 Hen. II, 224). Thereafter the pension appears on the rolls as paid to John until it disappears at Michael- 
mas 1201 (3 Joh.); John therefore presumably died towards the end of 1200. Becket was canonized in 
Feb. 1173, and the limits of date are that event and John’s death.

This charter and the next, No. 108, when read in conjunction with others referred to below, disclose a 
family originating in Rouen and connected with London, no doubt by trade, which as early as the reign 
of Henry I was holding Ashstead in Surrey of the chamberlains of Tancarville. The following pedigree 
shows the relationship of the persons mentioned in the two charters. 


Laurence of Rouen, alias de 
Sancto Sepulchro, living 1130 


Ralf, son of Robert of Rouen T Mary Robert, living 1175 


| 
William de la Mare, living 1180 = Lecia, living 1180 Laurence 


| $$ ____—_——, 


! 
William de la Mare 


A charter of Henry II (Delisle and Berger, Recueil, ii. 456), for which the limits of date are 1180-3, 
confirms to William de Mare and Lecia, his wife, Ashstead, Surr., as Laurence de Sancto Sepulchro held 
it of William the chamberlain of Tancarville (d. 1129); Mitcham, Surr., which Rabel the chamberlain 
(d. 1140) gave to Ralf son of Robert and his wife Mary, daughter of the aforesaid Laurence; and their 
land of Grantham, Lincs., viz. Harlaxton and Londonthorpe, which William the then chamberlain of 
Tancarville had restored to them as their inheritance. Another charter of Henry II (ibid. ii. 205) con- 
firms to the priory of St. L6 at Rouen a rent of 60 shillings in Rouen, the gift of Ralf son of Robert, and 
another rent of 60 shillings, the gift of his wife Mary. It will have been noted that in the first of these 
charters Laurence of Rouen is described as de Sancto Sepulchro; the church of the Holy Sepulchre at 
Rouen formerly stood between the Vieux Marché and the present Place de la Pucelle not far from the 
priory of St. Lé, and his daughter’s benefaction to that house suggests the origin of Laurence’s name. 
Farin (Hist. de Rouen, 1738 ed. ii, pt. i. 97) prints in translation an agreement between the chapter of 
Rouen cathedral and William de la Mare, by which the latter released to the chapter all his claim over the 
patronage of the church of St. Sauveur at Rouen, the chapter promising to commemorate William on 
the morrow of the Nativity of the Virgin (9 Sept.); and the necrology of the cathedral has the entry, 
‘9 Sept. Guillermus de la Mara’ (Rec. Hist. France, xxxiii. 366). The church of St. Sauveur in the Vieux 
Marché was about 200 yards distant from the church of the Holy Sepulchre. It seems safe to identify 
this William de la Mare with either the husband or son of Lecia, and this is additional evidence of the 
exact provenance of the family. 

Laurence of Rouen must have had considerable interests in England, for he occurs on the Pipe Roll 
of 1130 under Surrey, Essex, and London. The Pipe Roll of 21 Hen. II (p. 149) shows Mary’s brother, 
Robert, in possession of Harlaxton; he must have died without issue before 1183, by which time the over- 
lord had restored it to Lecia and her husband as their inheritance. The two charters are contemporaneous, 
and the handwritings both of the texts and the endorsements are identical, but their date is not easy to 
determine. Lecia’s grandfather Laurence was living in 1130, and her son William was old enough to 
consent to the grant here made; both Lecia and her husband were living at least as late as 1180. On 
these data it is difficult to put the charters earlier than the early years of Henry II. A later confirmation 
by Ralf the chamberlain of Tancarville of these English lands to Lecia’s son, William de la Mare, will 
be found at No. 281.

This charter, the earliest charter of Bordesley abbey, is prior in date to the ‘foundation’ charter of Earl 
Waleran (Mon. v. 410). It sets out the abbey’s original endowment. For Earl Waleran see G. H. White, — 
Trans. R. Hist. Soc. 4th ser. xvii. 19-48. Mr. White concludes that this charter must have been made 
either during Stephen’s visit to Lincoln before Christmas 1140 or before the siege of Lincoln began in 
Jan. 1141. He assumes that R. the chancellor is Ralf the chancellor who attested two charters issued 
by Maud while Stephen was in captivity. Since he wrote, another charter issued by Maud has been printed 
(B. A. Lees, Records of the Templars, Brit. Acad. 146) witnessed by ‘Ralf my chancellor’. There is no 
reason to suppose that Stephen ‘had appointed a ‘Ralf’ as his chancellor before he was taken prisoner. 
Philip de Harcourt had been appointed as chancellor after the fall of Roger the chancellor in 1139. In the 


1 BM 46; Wyon, Great Seals of England, No. 28.

spring of 1140 he was nominated by the king as bishop of Salisbury, although he never secured the 
election. Mr. Clay in commenting on this charter (Yorks. Arch. Journ. xxxiv. 366-7) suggests that Philip 
resigned or was removed from the chancellorship in the spring of 1140 and was succeeded in office by 
Robert de Gant before this charter was issued.

It is impossible to connect all the numerous Nevilles of the 12th and 13th centuries. A number of charters 
connecting Erneis de Neville with Habrough, Lincs., are printed in Stenton, Danelaw Charters, Nos. 273 
et seq.; one of Erneis himself, temp. Henry II, is witnessed by his brother Hugh and his sons Hugh and 
Walter (No. 275), and Erneis and his son Hugh witnessed one c. 1200 (ibid., No. 533). Turning to the 
present charter, the witness William de Percy of Carnaby was dead in 1219 and had been succeeded by 
his son Robert (Percy Chartulary, Surtees Soc. 56); seven out of the eight witnesses witnessed a charter 
of Walter de Ver, son of Adam of Goxhill, for Bridlington, of which the limits of date are 1200-13 
(EYC iii, No. 1344). It should be noted that as Erneis de Neville merely held the land at farm there is

Notification by John de Burgh that he has granted for himself and his heirs that Philip Basset shall during

76 . SIR HENRY ST. GEORGE 


Norf., which Philip holds of him, provided that John and his heirs shall not distrain on the manor for the

SEAL on tag: shield shaped, 18 x1 in.; green. Shield of arms, lozengy [gules] and vair, a label of five 
points; * SIGIUUVM : LOhANNIS . DE . BURGO. 

The seal and tag are now missing on the original. 

This somewhat clumsily expressed grant is clearly a reduction into writing of an agreement which had 
been arrived at as to the payment of castle guard. The grantor was the son and heir of the justiciar, 
Hubert de Burgh, earl of Kent, by his first wife (CP, 2nd ed. vii. 142, n. a). He did not succeed to the 
earldom, which was limited to the issue of Hubert’s third wife (ibid. 137, n. h). Beeston was a member 
of the honor of ‘Haganet’, ic. Haughley (Fees, 909, 1465); the honor had been held by the Montforts 
and their successors in the 11th and 12th centuries and thus had been connected with the constableship, 
a fact which accounts for the liability in respect of castle guard at Dover here in question (see Round, 
Geoffrey de Mandeville, 326). The date must be later than the death of Hubert de Burgh on 12 May 1243 
and earlier than that of the witness Paulin Peyvre in 1251 (Matthew Paris, Chron. Mai., RS, v. 242). For 
a charter of Hubert de Burgh to Philip Basset see No. 63. The original grant of Beeston by Hubert 
de Burgh to Philip Basset is PRO Ancient Deed A 5282. The present charter may be compared with 
A 5007.

This interesting charter appears to reveal the formal laying out of a village in his demesne land by its lord, 
rather in the manner in which a lord laid out a borough. Twenty-three separate holdings are described, 
only 2 of them amounting to as much as 3 acres. One of these is held by 2 men in common. One other 
tenant holds 2 holdings, one of 2 acres and another of 1 acre. The men named are free men and have 
given their lord a present of 3 shillings an acre down and promise to pay a rent of | shilling an acre. They 
undertake to pay the portion of royal service, that is, scutage, due from their land. The lord promises 
to warrant his grant to all these men. To them and ‘to all who shall afterwards take land there’ he 
promises rights of common. They are quit of attendance at the hall moot, and their lord promises that 
he or his ministers will hold a court for them on their free land. A very unusual feature of this document 
is the undertaking that each man shall put up a house on each acre of land. 

The lord, Robert Arsic, was the direct descendant of that Manasser Arsic who in 1103 founded a priory 
at Cogges, the head of his barony, giving his house at Cogges to the abbey of Fécamp to make a priory, 
with the church, and land for 2 ploughs, and all the wood necessary for the monks’ use (Round, CDF, 40; 
Dugdale, Baronage). In Domesday Book Wadard, whose land afterwards formed the Arsic barony, was 
holding Cogges, which was assessed at 5 hides. There was land for 8 ploughs. There were 2 in demesne 
with 3 slaves. The mill and the hay were both worth 10 shillings. There was a considerable amount of 
pasture and woodland. The village had been, and still was, worth £10. No tenants, either villein or free, 
are mentioned. Much of the village lands was still uncultivated woodland. 


It would seem that Robert was deliberately setting out to create a village of some importance, possibly 


inviting people to come in and take up these holdings. In the Hundred Roll account of Cogges descendants 
of some of these men appear. Of the 10 villeins noted in the Hundred Rolls one is Richard le Norreys, 
who held a half virgate, working at the lady’s will; she taking if she wished 2 shillings and 6 pence instead 
of work. Among the 13 free men, Thomas le Nappere, John de la Wike, and Richard de Wike appear 
as rent-paying tenants.

Joan de Valence, wife of William de Valence, was a coheir of the earls of Pembroke. William was never 
created earl of Pembroke or invested with the earldom, although he is sometimes called earl. He died 
18 May 1296. Joan survived him until 1307, retaining until her death the lordship of Pembroke and 
Goodrich castle (CP, 2nd ed. x. 381).

SEAL on tag: round, 27, in.; green. A wolf running to the sinister, two pieces of a broken spear above

The subject of the seal refers to the hunting tenure of Pytchley and Laxton. 


This charter is written in a curious hand which has the appearance of deliberate archaism. The warranty 
and sealing clauses suggest a date not earlier than the end of the 12th century. Richard Engaine is con- 
firming his father’s foundation of Fineshade priory and elaborating the original grant. His father, Richard 
Engaine I, died about 1177. In 1185 he had been dead 8 years and his widow had married Geoffrey 
Brito and was 50 years old (Rot. de dominabus, 24, 27). Richard, the grantor of the present charter, 
married Sarah, daughter and coheir of William de Chesney, sheriff of Norfolk. He died in 1209 (Mon. v. 
450). Robert de Courtney, who witnessed this charter, died in the same year, see CP, 2nd ed. v. 72-3, 
where a pedigree of the Engaine family is set out.

The manor of Claycoton and a part of Lilbourne together with other lands in Northants. were held by 
Thomas de Astley, who was slain fighting against the king at Evesham; the lands were forfeited and on 
25 Oct. 1265 granted to Warin de Bassingbourn (Cal. Chart. Rolls, ii. 56). Andrew son and heir of Thomas 
redeemed them from Warin under the Dictum de Kenilworth, and by letters patent of 10 July 1266 the 
king confirmed to him the lands thus regranted to him by Warin, the regrant not including the advowsons 
of the churches nor £20 yearly of land in Lilbourne and Claycoton which Warin had given to Laurence 
de Sancto Medardo (Cal. Pat. Rolls, 1258-66, 615). Dugdale (Baronage, i. 669) cites Warin’s charter to 
Andrew, then in the possession of Thomas Astley of Wolvey and therefore in proper custody, and says 
that Andrew paid Warin 320 marks. It should be added that subsequent presentations show the advowson 
of Claycoton to have remained vested in the Astleys down to the middle of the 15th century (Bridges, 
i. 549).

The grantor was Hugh de Neville, the king’s forester (CP, 2nd ed. ix. 479 et seq.). He married before 
30 Apr. 1200 Joan daughter and heir of Henry of Cornhill, and the property here dealt with was no doubt 
part of his wife’s inheritance; she was dead in Apr. 1230 when Hugh had married a second wife, and 
he died shortly before 21 July 1234. This charter can hardly be earlier than 1200, and if, as is probable 
but.not certain, the first witness is Hugh’s son and heir it must be substantially later.

The only indication of date is the episcopate of the grantor, who was consecrated on 23 Aug. 1164 and 
died 9 Aug. 1179. The bishop of Worcester had a soke in London, which was apparently formed out 
of the eastern portion of Edredshythe or Queenhithe and given to the see by King Alfred (W. Page, 
London, 131-2). 

St. Mary’s Southwark being a house of Augustinian canons, the position of Cristina is somewhat 
perplexing. We are indebted to Professor Hamilton Thompson for the following observations: 

‘Soror eorum cannot refer to anybody but the prior and convent, and conferre secum implies, I should 
say, a good deal more than confraternity. The only thing I can suggest is that Cristina gave herself and 
her property to the canons, probably at the foundation of the priory, and remained part of the establish- 
ment, perhaps enclosed as an “‘ankress’’, or as a sister in a hospital attached to it. There is an old tradition 


1 See CP, ut sup. 479, n. b. 3 meo BS. 
2 Picott BS. * Cf. BM 2275, obv. only. Now missing from original. 


SIR HENRY ST. GEORGE 85 


that the priory succeeded a community of women on the site, and this may point to some foundation 
in fact for the legend. In any case, attempts at combining communities of canons and nuns on the system 
which had some success in Gilbertine houses were not infrequent in the early part of the 12th century, 
as in the early Arroasian and Premonstratensian monasteries and in isolated instances, such as the double 
house at Marton-in-Galtres, of which the female portion migrated to Moxby. It is certainly not unlikely 
that, if a double house was not actually attempted at Southwark, Cristina and her household were allowed 
to reside for life in the monastery precincts and engage in pious duties.’

Miles de Bray the son died 1212-13 (Bracton’s Note Book, No. 1608) and it seems probable that Roger 
died c. 1205 (BHRS xiii. 320). The first witness acted as a judge in 1202 and survived till at least 1215

charter makes a date much before 1200 unlikely. The original gift of Othbert and his son was earlier 
than 1122, being confirmed by a charter of Henry I which probably passed at Easter 1122 (Von. v. 192). 
In the St. Andrew’s cartulary (Cotton MS. Vespas. E xvii, f. 143) are a number of charters confirming 
this same gift including the present one and one of Miles de Bray; in one of these Othbert is called 
‘de Mera’. The wood of Purnho is also mentioned in the cartulary under Horton (ff. 75v and 76), and 
is described as ‘Sithene Pornho iuxta boscum Simonis comitis’.

William de Auberville with the consent of his wife Maud founded Langdon abbey circa 1192 (Mon. 
vi. 898). He was succeeded by his son Hugh, who in 1221 had in his turn been succeeded by his son 
William, then under age (Bracton’s Note Book, No. 1506). The elder William was living in 1195 (PR 
7 Ric. I, 241) but dead before Michaelmas 1196, when scutage was due from his heirs (PR 8 Ric. I, 288); 
in 1202 Maud occurs as holding land in Swingfield (Cur. Reg. Rolls, ii. 121). This charter must be later 
than the death of Maud’s husband, but earlier than the election of Richard of Osney, who in 1213 succeeded 
Dunstan as prior of St. Gregory, Canterbury (VCH Kent, ii. 159).

In the Michaelmas term 1200 Robert son of Thorold of Bedfont restored to his lord Richard of Herriard 
half the village of Bedfont recovered against Henry of Bedfont as a result of a final concord in the king’s 
court. Richard gave Robert 30 marks and promised that he and his heirs would pay Robert a mark every 
Easter for clothes; payment to cease on Robert’s death (Cur. Reg. Rolls, i. 353). Richard of Herriard 
offered a half mark for the enrolment of this grant upon the Pipe Roll. The entry appears on the roll 
for 1 John, 1199 (p. 130), which was probably still open when the agreement was made at Michaelmas 
1200. Richard of Herriard must thereupon have given or sold the land to Thomas de Haverill and the 
present charter was an assurance necessary to complete the transaction.

The Northamptonshire fees of the family of Béthune are dealt with by Farrer in his account of the honor 
of Chokes (HKF i. 22-6); for an elaborate history of the family see A. Duchesne, Hist. généalogique de la 
Maison de Béthune (1639), with an account of the present donor at pp. 167-76. 

William, who held Tenremonde in right of his wife, succeeded as advocate of Arras and lord of Béthune 
on the death of his elder brother Robert, which occurred in 1193 or 1194, probably on 29 Apr. 1194 


92 SIR HENRY ST. GEORGE 


(Duchesne, op. cit. 148 and ‘Preuves’, 52). William himself died 13 Apr. 1213 (ibid. 175-6; ‘Preuves’, 
92 and 94). The Pipe Rolls show him to have been out of possession of these English lands from his 
accession, there being in particular a yearly render of the farm of Grimsbury by the sheriff, until in 1200 
he figures as owing £100 for having seisin (PR 2 John, 61); this gives possible limits of date 1200-13. 
He was, however, absent on crusade from 1203 to 1205 and thereafter does not seem to have had effective 
possession till 1209 (Farrer, op. cit. i. 25). Moreover, Simon of Pattishall who heads the list of witnesses 
did not become the advocate’s tenant till 1209, when he received a grant of Rothersthorpe (ibid. 44). The 
witness Walter of Pattishall was Simon’s son. The more probable limits are therefore 1209-13.

In the Northamptonshire Survey Roger de Camville held three hides and a half and one great virgate 
in Crick of Roger de Mowbray (VCH Northants. i. 379); at Michaelmas 1130 he was dead and Geoffrey 
de Trailli made fine for his widow and for the wardship of his son until he attained the age of 20 (PR 
31 Hen. I, 88). Since Nigel d’Aubigny, Roger de Mowbray’s father, died later in Noy. 1129, this entry 
must represent the position at the beginning of 1130 or later. In Domesday Book both Crick and Swinford 
were held by Geoffrey de Wirce, Mowbray’s ‘antecessor’. In 1166 Walter de Camville held nine fees of 
the old feoffment of Roger de Mowbray (RB 419), and he occurs on the Northamptonshire Pipe Roll of 
1167 in connexion with Cranford (PR 13 Hen. II, 119). Early in Henry II’s reign Roger son of Walter 
de Camville witnessed two contemporaneous charters for Nuneaton priory (Stenton, Danelaw Charters, 
Nos. 327, 328); as Ives de Harcourt is among the witnesses they are probably not later than 1166. In 
a charter of the late 12th century Roger de Camville at the desire of his father Walter confirmed lands 
in Theddingworth, Leics., to Leicester abbey (Stenton, op. cit., No. 420). In 1232-3 Crick was held of 
Nigel de Mowbray by the heirs of Roger de Camville (Fees, 1467). From the above we can infer that 
Walter was the son of the first Roger, and since there was clearly only one Walter the identity of the 
grantor 1s certain. The family of the grantee gave its name to Ashby Folville, Leics.

For the earlier history of these two manors see No. 85. Two documents in the Record Office also deal 
with this transaction: Ancient Deed A 514 is another charter of Robert de Guisnes giving these two 
manors to the bishop; it is less elaborate in phraseology though identical in substance with the present 
charter, and a number of witnesses are common to both, though the two lists differ materially. Ancient 
Deed A 508 is a letter from Robert to his men of Little Holland informing them that he has given the 
manor to the bishop and ordering them to attorn to him; it is dated at Tolleshunt on 17 Aug. 1248. The 
fact that both A 514 and A 508 are witnessed by the abbot of St. John’s Colchester, the prior of Hatfield, 
and the precentor and two canons of St. Paul’s, London, leaves no doubt that they are contemporaneous. 
The present charter seems to be an elaborated version of A 514, but seven witnesses are common to both 
and it can hardly be much later.

took the name of d’Aubigny. He died in 1235, and at an unknown date she married Dreux de Préaux

In No. 133 Adam de Port of Mapledurwell made a grant of the church of Hatley; it is witnessed by his 
brother Henry de Port. In 1171-2 Adam suffered forfeiture and exile, and at the same time Hatley que fuit 
Henrici de Port was in the king’s hand (PR 18 Hen. II, 49). It appears therefore that Adam conveyed 
Hatley to his brother Henry and that the latter was involved in Adam’s misfortune. Henry, however, 
must have recovered Hatley, which continued to be held by this branch of the family until the close 
of the 13th century. The present donor must be Adam son of Henry de Port who in 1205 was in possession 
of Hatley (Cur. Reg. Rolls, iv. 24).

An agreement between the prior of Newark, near Guildford, Surr., and the prior of Selborne, Hants. 
It recites that King Henry III is exacting from the prior of Newark a debt of Roger de Lymesye amounting 
to £276, 14 shillings, and 3 pence by reason of a tenement in West Tisted, Hants, which was Roger’s and 
is held by the prior; that the prior by his friends had procured from the king that the debt should be 
discharged by the yearly payment at the Exchequer of one mark, half at Easter and half at Michaelmas, 
until the whole amount be paid; that the prior of Newark had impleaded the prior of Selborne that as 
he holds a portion of the land that was Roger’s he should help to discharge the debt. The land of the — 
prior of Newark having been valued at £4 a year and that of the prior of Selborne at 8 shillings a year ; 
it is agreed that the prior of Selborne shall acquit his proportion of the debt by paying yearly 144 pence 
to the prior of Newark or his attorney at West Tisted, half at Easter and half at Michaelmas as from 
Easter 1266 until the debt be discharged. If the prior of Selborne make default the barons of the Exchequer 
_ May distrain on his lands and chattels, and if the prior of Newark make default so that the king’s debt 
be not discharged in the manner aforesaid he shall make good any damage suffered by the prior of Selborne 
by the award of good men. Sealing clause. 1266.

The donor was the son and successor of the Nicholas de Stafford of No. 130.. In his note on this charter 
Eyton identifies the King Henry who is mentioned as dead with Henry II’s son, the young king, and on 
that ground dates the charter 1183, the year of his death. The conjecture seems somewhat far fetched; 
the more natural interpretation is an allusion to Henry I; moreover, Robert de Stafford uses precisely 
the same language in No. 197, which is later in date than this one. Robert was succeeded by his son Robert, 
and there is no evidence available for the date of his death, with the consequence that it is impossible 
to date this charter with anything approaching precision. It is later than the accession of Henry II and 


SIR HENRY ST. GEORGE 101 


since this gift is not mentioned in the king’s charter of confirmation (Cal. Chart. Rolls, ii. 64) it would 
appear to be not earlier than 1156, the earliest possible date for that charter. On the other hand, Engelrand 
de Dumart, who is here mentioned as living, was dead in 1185 (Rot. de Dominabus, PRS, 23). The wording 
of the charter may suggest that Avice was not the mother of Nicholas, Robert’s younger son. The writing 
and style of the charter suggest a date in the earlier half of Henry II’s reign.

Ernald del Bec was enfeoffed of half a knight’s fee by Robert de Ferrers, the first earl of Derby, between 
1135 and 1139 (RB 338) and was still living in 1177 (PR 23 Hen. I, 61). After his death Geoffrey del Bec, 
son of Ernald, and his mother Margaret confirmed to Rocester abbey land in Hilton, Derbs., given by 
Ernald (W. Salt Soc., N.S. vii. 175-6). In 1242-3 Robert de Tuke and a later Geoffrey de Bec held a third 
of a fee in Hilton of the earl of Derby (Fees, 994). ‘Comes de Ferrariis’ is the style used by the first 
Earl William, who died in 1190; his son William styles himself earl of Derby except that for his first few 
years he occasionally uses the same style as his father. The Hatton of the present charter adjoins Hilton, 
which identifies the donor with Geoffrey the son of Ernald. An Ernulf de Bec who may be identical with 
the witness of that name occurs in 1189 (PR J Ric. I, 160). Nothing is known of the donee, but it may 
be noted that a charter of the first Earl William is witnessed by Robert Calcun, abbot of St. Pierre-sur- 
Dives, the mother house of the Ferrers foundation of Tutbury priory (Jeayes, Gresley Charters, 2).

The donor, who was the daughter of Simon de Senlis I, earl of Northampton, must have been born about 
1100. She married as her first husband Robert fitzRichard, of Dunmow, son of Gilbert of Clare, from 
which marriage descended the baronial house of fitzWalter. The statements of the chronicle of Dunmow 
priory (Mon. vi. 147) as to the early history of the family are quite untrustworthy: Maud de Senlis is 
there said to have died in 1140, whereas she was living in 1158 (PR 4 Hen. II, 133); again, her son Walter 
fitzRobert is said to have married firstly Maud de Bohun and secondly Maud daughter of Richard de Lucy, 
but in an original charter (BM Cott. Chart. xxv. 23) he speaks of his ‘late’ wife Maud de Lucy and his 
wife Maud de Bohun. The witness ‘Saher my son’ was the offspring of Maud’s second marriage to 
Saher de Quincy, as to which see No. 282 below. 

Maurice son of Geoffrey, also known as Maurice of Tiltey and Maurice the sheriff, was the founder 
of Tiltey abbey, Ess., and sheriff of Essex and Hertfordshire from 1158 to 1164. In 1166 he held one fee 
of Walter fitzRobert (RB 347), a third of a fee of the earl of Essex which was in the king’s hand (ibid.), 
and half a fee of Earl William de Ferrers (ibid. 339) having given to Tiltey abbey another fee which his 
father had held of the earl in 1135 (ibid. 337). Three interesting charters of Earl Robert de Ferrers Me 
one of them dated 26 Sept. 1139, dealing with Maurice’s Essex lands are printed in Hist. MSS. Com. 
Var. Coll. vii. 310-12; further light is thrown on these lands by a paper of J. H. Round (Essex Arch. Soc. 
Trans. x. 303). The London land mentioned in the present charter was part of the fitzWalter soke of 
Castle Baynard’s, for which see W. Page, London, 190 et seq.

In 1135 Henry de Boscherville held 3 knights’ fees of the Ferrers honor. In 1166 they were held by 
his son John (RB 337). Two charters printed by Nichols (iii. 5) relate to the present transaction: 

1. A charter of Aeleza daughter of Robert de Bachepuis giving her land in Allexton to her brother 
John with the consent of the lord thereof, Robert Grimbald her uncle (avunculi), and of her son John 
de Boscherville. ‘Hii sunt testes Nicholas de Jubria(? Turnebi) Guillelmus Grimbaldi et tota curia Roberti 
Grimbaldi.’ This would seem to be contemporaneous with John de Boscherville’s livery of seisin in 
Robert Grimbald’s court. 

2. A charter of John de Boscherville confirming to John de Bachepuis his mother’s gift of Allexton. 
This must have passed in the court of the Earl Ferrers, as there are a number of Ferrers under-tenants 
among the witnesses, including Roger the chaplain and Robert de Piru the steward, who witness charters 
of Robert the second earl and William the third. The attestations to Ferrers charters show that Robert 
de Piru was succeeded as steward by William fitzHerbert about 1165, and William by Richard de Fifehide 
about 1168. Robert Grimbald was sheriff of Hunts. in 1154-5 (PR 2 Hen. I, 41); the last mention of 
him as living is in 1160 (PR 6 Hen. II, 2), and in 1163 the sheriff of Northants. accounted for a debt of 
his wife (PR 9 Hen. IT, 36). He was, presumably, then dead. A charter in BM Facsimiles, No. 49, shows 
Robert de Bachepuis the elder giving lands in Berkshire to his son, this John; see also Jeayes, Derbyshire. 
Charters, Nos. 238, 239. Robert Grimbald was succeeded by his son William, but this charter shows an 
elder son Simon who must have died s.p.

SEAL:' round, 1? in.; red. A figure sitting upon what seems to be a cask, a reference to the assistant 
butlership; he is holding a knife or sword in each hand and is wearing puff breeches. The design has 
evidently been given an Elizabethan flavour by the artist. “4 SIGI....... ELIS BE" KES 


West Sheen, now Richmond, was held by the Belet family by the serjeanty of the assistant butlership ; 
see Round, The King’s Serjeants, 165 et seq. The charter is not easy to date Owing to the difficulties 
presented by the descent of the manor, and to the fact that there seem to have been two contemporary 
Michael Belets, one a magister and the king’s clerk, and the other a knight, both of whom occur in con- 
nexion with Sheen and the butlership. In 1206 Master Michael Belet paid £100 to have the butlership 
as his right (Rot. de Oblatis, 358); in 1212 Michael Belet held Sheen by the serjeanty of the butlership 
(Fees, 70), and in 1215 the king committed to Hugh de Neville the land which had been (fuit) that of 
Michael Belet, knight, in Sheen (Rot. Lit. Claus. i. 237b). In 1219 Wimund de Ralegh is returned as having 
the custody of the daughter and heir of Michael Belet with her inheritance in Sheen (Fees, 273); this must 
have been the daughter of the knight, and she was apparently that Maud Belet for the succession to 
whose land in Surrey her kinsman John Belet paid a relief of 10 marks in 1229 (Excerpta e Rot. Fin. 
i. 190). John was dead in 1231 when Henry son of Nicholas paid 50 marks for the wardship and marriage 
of his heirs (ibid. i. 218), and accordingly in 1235 Henry is holding the serjeanty of Sheen by the king’s 
grant (Fees, 1363). The heirs in question were Emma Oliver and Alice her sister, daughters of John Belet, 
who in 1250 were holding the serjeanty of Sheen jointly (ibid. 1237). In the meanwhile, however, Master 
Michael Belet officiated at the queen’s coronation in 1236 as assistant butler de iure ueteri (RB 758), and 
in 1244 Michael Belet is returned as holding Sheen by serjeanty (Fees, 1153). The witness Herbert 
de Alengon occurs in 1203 (Cur. Reg. Rolls, ii. 160) and was still living in 1238 (Bracton’s Note Book, 
No. 1240), but in 1210 he occurs in conjunction with the second witness Robert of Cockfield (Cur. Reg. 
Rolls, vi. 79), while the witness Gilbert Mauduit occurs in 1217 (Rot. Lit. Claus. i. 326). On these grounds 
it seems justifiable to assign the charter to Michael Belet the knight and to the reign of John.

Notification by John son of Warin of Great Hormead (Magna Horemeda?), Herts., that he and his heirs 
are bound to find and maintain for ever a lamp burning day and night before the rood in the church of 
Great Hormead and a wax candle before the altar of the blessed Mary burning at the mass of the blessed 
Mary only, for the health of the soul of Lorette de Sanford and of the souls of her predecessors and heirs. 
For this Lorette has given him 22 acres of land in Great Hormead, on the condition that if by the default 
of John or his heirs the said lamp and candle be not so maintained it shall be lawful for Lorette or her 
successors to distrain and retain the chattels both movable and immovable on the said 22 acres until he 
or his heirs shall have paid 2 marks of silver to Lorette or her successors in full satisfaction. Sealing clause.

Great Hormead with other lands was held by the Sanford family by the serjeanty of the queen’s chamber- 
lainship (Round, The King’s Serjeants, 132 et seq.). An account of the manor and family will be found 
in VCH Herts. iv. 71, from which the following facts are taken. Gilbert de Sanford held the manor in 
1247-8 but died in or shortly before 1250 leaving a widow, the Lorette of this charter, who had Great 
Hormead in dower. She was living in 1287, but must have died soon after when the manor reverted to 
her daughter Alice de Sanford, the wife of Robert de Vere, earl of Oxford, who was holding it jointly 
with his wife on his death in 1294 (CP, 2nd ed. x. 217). The limits of date are those of the deaths of 
Gilbert and Lorette.

Charter of Roger de Montbegon giving to Sulby abbey, Northants, Simon son of 
Henry with his chattels and issue. (1171-81 ) 7 


ORIGINAL: Harl. Chart. 53 E 14. 
BS FACSIMILE, first 12 words. 
PRINTED: Stenton, Danelaw Charters, No. 403. 


SEAL on tag: round, 23 in.; yellow-brown. Equestrian, armour to which the artist has given an Elizabethan 
flavour, rounded helmet, kite-shaped shield, with non-armorial bars bendwise or palewise over a studded 
border, and sword; ** SIGIUUVM ...... GVM. BM 6232 


An account of the family of Montbegon which held lands in Lancashire and Lincolnshire will be found 
in VCH Lancs. i. 319 et seq., and a pedigree in EYC iii. 318. Roger de Montbegon temp. Henry I was 
succeeded at an unknown date by Adam, who first occurs as a witness to a charter of his lord William, 
count of Boulogne and Mortain and Earl Warenne, between 1154 and 1158 (Farrer, Lancs. Pipe Rolls, 308). 
Adam was living at Michaelmas 1171 (PR 17 Hen. II, 30) but dead at Michaelmas 1172 when a debt due 
from him was forgiven to John Malherbe (PR 18 Hen. II, 65), who married Maud, Adam’s widow. Adam 
left a son and heir Roger, who was probably under age at his father’s death and who died in 1227. John 
Malherbe died in 1181 (PR 27 Hen. II, 61) leaving by Maud a son, John, who could not have been born 
before 1173. Since.Sulby abbey was founded circa 1155 the donor must be the younger Roger de Mont- 
begon. The form of the charter strongly suggests the time of Henry II, and since John Malherbe the 
younger could not have been of age till 1194 at the earliest, the witness John Malherbe can safely be 
identified with the donor’s stepfather who died in 1181.

Hugh de Dive witnessed a Norman charter of Robert count of Mortain about 1095, and in 1103-6 one 

of William count of Mortain, his son (CDF, Nos. 1205, 1210). Ata later date the family is found holding 

East Haddon, Northants., and land in Eastbourne and Horsted Keynes, Suss. In each case the Domesday 

tenant-in-chief was the count of Mortain, East Haddon being subsequently granted to the earl of Leicester 

after the forfeiture of William count of Mortain in 1106, and similarly the Sussex lands to the family of 

Laigle. It would seem therefore that the subinfeudations to Dive must have been earlier than 1106. The 
? Jnterlined in original. 2y Sic: 3 Herford BS.

earliest mention of the family in Northants. is in 1130, when the heir of a deceased William de Dive was 
in the wardship of Geoffrey of Glympton (Clinton’) (PR 31 Hen. I, 83). The early descent is by no means 
clear, but the subsequent alternation of the names Hugh and William in the family makes it not unreason- 
able to suggest that Hugh the father of the donor of the present charter was the son of the William of the 
1130 Pipe Roll entry and grandson of the Hugh of the 11th century. Besides the present benefaction 
William de Dive gave the church of East Haddon to Sulby abbey which was founded circa 1155 (Mon. 
vi. 904). He married Maud daughter and coheir of Geoffrey de Waterville, who had Corby, Lincs., in 
marriage (Rot. de Dominabus, 14): living in 1181 (PR 27 Hen. IT, 68) he was dead in 1185 leaving two sons 
and two daughters, his son and heir, Hugh, being aged 10 or 12 and in the wardship of another William 
de Dive (Rot. de Dominabus, 14 and 27). 

Turning to Sussex, a charter of William count of Mortain, and therefore not later than 1106, confirms 
gifts of Hugh de Dive to Lewes priory (Cartulary, f. 44; Sussex Rec. Soc. xxxviii. 75); this must be 
Hugh I. At a later date William son of Hugh de Dive gave to the priory land in Horsted Keynes and 
Bromham or Burneham, i.e. Eastbourne (ibid., f. 89, p. 160); the occurrence of a Northamptonshire man, 
Robert of Holdenby, among the witnesses should be noted. As the donor mentions benefactions of his 
grandfather he must be the William of the present charter and not the William who was dead in 1130. 
These gifts are confirmed by a charter of King Stephen for Cluny (CDF, No. 1391), from which it would 
seem that Hugh I, the present donor’s father, died before 1155. 

The present charter cannot be later than 1185 when William was dead. The earlier limit is difficult to 
determine; in the Northants. Survey temp. Henry I a Coleman held half a hide in Nortoft of the fee of 
Peverel (VCH Northants. 1. 378); the document seems to have been ‘written up’, and this may be an 
addition, but if he is identical with the Coleman of Lamora of the charter a limit near the beginning of 
Henry II’s reign is suggested.

The grantor was son and heir of William son of Corbucion, the Domesday tenant-in-chief. As Peter son 
of William he witnessed a charter of Henry earl of Warwick (died 1119) for St. Mary’s, Warwick (Mon. 


110 SIR HENRY ST. GEORGE 


vi. 1326) and one of Roger earl of Warwick for the same dated 1123 (ibid. 1327). In 1130 he figures on 
the Pipe Roll as Peter de Stotleia, Studley in Warwickshire, held in 1086 by his father, being his principal 
residence (PR 31 Hen. I, 108): he had yet a third designation, for in a Worcestershire survey of the last 
years of Henry I he occurs as Peter Corbezun holding 2 hides at Witton in Droitwich (VCH Worcs. i. 330); 
these hides were held by his father in 1086. He or his son occurs three times in the returns of knights’ 
fees of 1166 in RB; as Peter de Stodleia holding 10 fees of the earl of Warwick (p. 325),' as Peter Corbuzone 
5 fees of the honor of Walter Giffard, the deceased earl of Buckingham (p. 312), as Peter de Stodlega 1 fee 
in Worcestershire of the abbot of Westminster (p. 188), this last being Dormston which William son of 
Corbucion held of the abbot in 1086. These returns indicate that on the formation of the earldoms of 
Warwick and Buckingham in the reign of William II the overlordship of lands held in chief in 1086 by 
William son of Corbucion was divided between the two earls. Peter son of William was succeeded by 
his son another Peter, generally known as Peter Corbezun but occasionally as Peter of Studley. The date 
of the elder Peter’s death is unknown and consequently it is not easy to distinguish between father and 
son; if, as appears likely, William son of Corbucion is identical with the man who in Aug. 1060 witnessed 
a confirmation by William the Conqueror for the abbey of St. Pére of Chartres (CDF, No. 1256), it is 
probable that the Peter son of William died before 1166. Peter his son was living in 1200 (Cur. Reg. Rolls, 
i. 116) and his son William in 1212 (RB 604). Charters of Peter the son and of his son William are printed 
in Staff. Coll. ii. 202-5. The grantor must be Peter the elder since his son Geoffrey Corbezun, a witness, 
occurs on the Pipe Roll in 1171 (PR 17 Hen. II, 94). The grantor gave 10 acres at Hillborough in Temple 
Grafton to Bordesley by a charter (Madox, Formulare, No. 406) addressed to John bishop of Worcester 
(1151-8), a gift confirmed by his son Peter Corbezun (ibid., No. 87). That gift was confirmed by charters 
of the empress and Henry II, both of which passed at Rouen in 1156? (Cal. Chart. R. ii. 63-4). The gift 
here in question is not confirmed by either of these charters, but is confirmed by a charter of Richard I 
(ibid. 65). The earliest limit of date for the present charter is therefore 1156. The date of the grantor’s 
death being unknown, it is impossible to fix the later limit definitely, but four of the six witnesses also 
witness Formulare No. 406, and when one also takes into account the facts that the grantor witnessed 
a charter in 1119 or earlier and his father one in 1060, it seems difficult to place it much later than 1160. 
The land in question probably lay in Bearley, a manor which was held by William son of Corbucion in 
1086 and from which the acutal donor took his name: the abbey held land there at the Dissolution (Mon. 
v. 411). No. 528 is a much earlier charter of Peter of Studley.

By a charter passing at Dover in Jan. 1156 Henry II confirmed to the abbey ‘ex dono Willelmi de Kereby 
unam carucatam terre in Thingworth’ (Cal. Chart. Rolls, iii. 381). In a late 12th-century charter (Stenton,

and the request of William de Karebi confirmed to the abbey a carucate and four tofts in Theddingworth, 
the gift of William. If, as seems to be the case, the carucate and the four virgates are identical, the original 
gift must have been earlier than 1156; the present charter, however, appears to be a confirmation. .

The following charters throw some light on the present one: 


1. A gift by Robert de la Mare, with the consent of his wife Wimarc and his brother Geoffrey, of 
various lands in Over Rendcombe to Bruern abbey; being witnessed by Richard archdeacon of 
Poitiers, its date is 1163-73. (Madox, Formulare, No. 426.) 

2. Confirmation of the above by William earl of Gloucester witnessed by Robert de la Mare, the donor. 
and by William and Robert his sons. (Ibid., No. 83.) 

3. A gift by William de la Mare, with the consent of Amfelisa his wife and Thomas his son and heir, 
to Bruern abbey of all Over Rendcombe; there is also mention of the donor’s brothers Simon de 
Solers and Robert de la Mare. (Ibid., No. 460.) 

4. A gift by William de la Mare, with the consent of his lord, William earl of Gloucester, to Bruern 
of 66 acres in Over Rendcombe, the limits of date being 1171-83. (Ancient Charters, PRS, x. 72.) 

Exact limits of date for the present charter are not easy to fix. It must be later than 1163 since the donor’s 

father was then living. Two other charters of William for Bruern, No. 4 above and that confirmed by 
No. 288 below, cannot be later than 1183. If, as is probable, he is the man who paid scutage on the 


Gloucestershire Pipe Roll of 1196 (PR 8 Ric. I, 103), one can only date this charter as probably some time 
after 1163 and before 1200.

An account of the Takeley family up to the beginning of the 13th century will be found in HKF iii. 175-6; 
and a number of charters dealing with them are printed in the Colchester Cartulary, ed. S. Moore, Rox- 
burghe Club, 340-5. William son of Adeliz of Takeley, Muriel his wife, and Elias their son gave land in 
Takeley to Colchester abbey before 1151, the gift being witnessed by Robert bishop of London (ibid. 340); 
this is followed by charters which show Elias to have been succeeded by his son William, and him by 
his son, another William, the present donor. A charter of Lecia prioress of Ankerwyke of the year 1194 
shows William son of Elias to have then succeeded his father (BM Campb. Ch. x. 7), and he was still 
living in 1199 (Rot. Cur. Regis, i. 353-4, 398). On the other hand, the fact that the witness William 
de Hauville is described as ‘junior’ suggests that his father William who died before 1208 (see note to 
No. 157) was alive or only lately dead.

The family of Hauville held Dunton, Norf., by a falconer serjeanty which has been discussed by Round 
(King’s Serjeants, 311-17); it originated in a grant by Henry II to Ralf de Hauville, descending to his son 
Ralf II, and to Ralf IPs son Henry who held it in 1212 (Fees, 129). The present donor represented what 
seems to have been another branch. By a charter dated 2 June 1200 King John confirmed to this William 
de Hauville Takeley which had been his father Ralf’s and his grandfather William’s (Rot. Chart. i. 68). 
There is no chronological difficulty in identifying Ralf the father of the present donor with the original 
grantee of Dunton, but the fact that at the beginning of the 13th century Dunton and Takeley were in 
different hands is against such identity. Numerous charters of the Takeley Hauvilles are printed in the 
Colchester Cartulary, 345-65, and from these it appears that William son of Ralf was succeeded by his 
son William. By a charter dated 1208 (ibid. 371) Adam abbot of Colchester quitclaimed to Geoffrey 
de Hauville son of William the right to lands in Takeley which Geoffrey had by gift and sale either from 
William de Hauville son of Ralf or from William’s son and heir William; William son of Ralf therefore 
died before 1208. Geoffrey was brother of William the younger and succeeded him in or before 1223, 
William dying without issue (Excerpta e Rot. Fin. i. 103; PRO Ancient Deed A 11850). In Trans. Essex 
Arch. Soc. xxii. 68 et seq. is a paper on Colchester Hall, Takeley, in which is printed a number of unpub- 
lished Hauville charters. 

Charter No. 156 shows that the wife of William son of Elias of Takeley was Alice who survived him, 
since she held land in dower; the same charter shows her son, the younger William, to have succeeded 
his father and been of full age some time before 1208, so that Alice cannot have been married much later 
than 1180. If Deudaune had been a first wife of William son of Elias this charter would be 1180 or earlier, 
but the form of warranty against all men and women negatives so early a date. The donee is therefore 
William of Takeley the younger and since he is described simply as William of Takeley, and not as William 
son of William, the charter must be later than the death of his father who was alive in 1199 (note to 
No. 156). The donor died before 1208, and this charter can be referred to the opening years of the 13t 
century. .

For the history of this transaction see VCH Herts. ii, sub ‘Shenley’, in particular p. 265. At Michaelmas 
1179 William de Chenduit made a render of £133. 6s. 8d. pro fine terre sue (PR 25 Hen. II, 56); this is 
the earliest entry on the rolls and as it works out at the round figure of 200 marks it suggests that his 
father Ralf must have lately died. Roger de Somery was dead at Michaelmas 1190 (PR 2 Ric. I, 2). The 
witness Henry son of Ailwin was later the first mayor of London. The conveyance by William de Chenduit 
to Richard son of Reiner is PRO Ancient Deed A 5434: William’s son, Ralf de Chenduit, confirmed it to 
Henry son of Reiner, Richard’s brother, Ancient Deed A 5438. 

For the different branches of the Somery family in Shenley see note to No. 79 above. In the Michaelmas 
term 1204 the present grant was the subject of litigation between Miles de Somery, Roger’s brother, and 
Henry son of Reiner, Richard’s brother (Cur. Reg. Rolls, iii. 168).

The interesting history of Hasculf the forester and his descendants may be read in a record of the Rutland 
Eyre of 1269, which is largely occupied with the misdeeds of his great-grandson Peter de Neville (Select 
Pleas of the Forest, Selden Soc. 44 et seq.). Hasculf was appointed forester in Leicestershire and Rutland 
by Henry I at some date before 1130 since he occurs as forester on the Pipe Roll of that year (p. 87); he 
was killed in his own house by Bartholomew de Verdun in the reign of Stephen. His son Peter was 
appointed by Henry II and occurs as forester on the Pipe Roll of 1167 (p. 125); he lived till the reign of 
John and married a niece of Ives son of Alan de Neville by whom he had a son Hasculf, father of Peter 
de Neville. The chronicler Roger of Howden records that in 1194 on 6 Apr. Richard I and the king of 
Scots ‘came to the house of Peter the forester of Rutland’ (RS iii. 243). 

Since Peter’s father Hasculf was already a forester in 1130 and died before 1155 the bishop of Lincoln 
here mentioned may safely be identified with St. Hugh (1186-1200) rather than Hugh of Welles, con- 
secrated at Melun 20 Dec. 1209. The only other occurrence of Hamo archdeacon of Leicester so far 
noted is in a charter in the Boarstall cartulary (Ox. Hist. Soc. 7), the date being 1186-9. For a list of 
archdeacons see Registrum Antiquissimum (LRS iii. 230n.). The only time when Hamo can be fitted in 
with any probability is after Baldric de Sigillo and before Roger of Rolleston, who first occurs in 1191. 
A Hamo was dean of Lincoln 1189-95 and it seems probable that he is the same man as this archdeacon 
of Leicester. 1189 seems therefore the latest limit of date.

Charter of William of Wentworth (Wyntewrth’) the elder quitclaiming to Joan daughter of John le Heyr 
whom Bertram of Bolingbroke has taken to wife and the heirs of the body of the same Joan all right 
or claim which he had has or may have in 100 shillings’ worth of rent receivable yearly from the manor 
of Sutton Veney, Wilts. (Fenny Sutton), at the octave of Michaelmas and at Easter in equal portions with 
all wardships, marriages, &c., arising therefrom. If Joan die without an heir of her body the aforesaid 
rent to revert to the grantor and his heirs. Sealing clause. ‘Hiis testibus Thoma de Lungeuilers Edmundo 
de Cressy Hugone de Hercy militibus Johanne Power Hugone de Tothill’ Iohanne Fouler de Stokhith’ 
et aliis.”. (Mid 14th century.) 


SEAL on strip: round, }2 in.; red. Within a cusped panel with a leopard’s face at top a shield of arms, 
a chevron between three leopards’ faces [WENTWORTH]; no legend. 


The possession of the original charter by the earl of Strafford shows the grantor to have been a Went- 
worth of Wentworth Woodhouse. The best account of the family is in Hunter’s South Yorkshire, and the 
pedigree on p. 89 shows that from the time of Edward I Wentworth was held by six Williams in succession, 
the third of whom married Isabel daughter and coheir of Walter of Tinsley. In 1327 there was a partition 
of Walter’s lands between his daughters, (1) Isabel wife of William of Wentworth, and (2) Joan, who 
married first John Eyre of Chesterfield, Derbs., and secondly Hugh of Toothill in Rastrick, Yorks. (Hunter, 
op. cit. ii. 32). John Eyre or Le Heyr had a daughter Joan who married Bertram of Bolingbroke (ibid.) 
and is the grantee here; she was therefore William’s niéce by marriage. The connexion of Wentworth 
with Sutton Veney is obscure. In 1195 a William of London made a render for half a knight’s fee and 
for land held by serjeanty in Nettleworth and Warsop, Notts., and Tinsley, Yorks. (PR 7 Ric. I, 21). In 
1242-3 a William de Lundoniis and two others held a knight’s fee in Sutton Veney of Henry Huse (Fees, 
718). Lastly, in 1371 there is a fine between Bertram of Bolingbroke, querent, and John son of Bertram 


THOMAS EARL OF STRAFFORD 123 


of Bolingbroke, deforciant, of the manor of Ordsall and a moiety of the manor of Nettleworth, Notts., 
and of land in Greasborough and a moiety of the manor of Tinsley, Yorks. (Yorks. Arch. Soc., Rec. Ser., 
Yorks. Fines, 229). This suggests that Nettleworth may have passed from the London to the Tinsley 
family and have been partitioned in 1327 between the Tinsley coheirs; a possible London-Tinsley-— 
Wentworth succession may have given Wentworth an interest in Sutton Veney, if only a contingent one.

The grantee was Robert son of Hugh son of Robert son of Sewin of a well-known Northampton family

the occasion to extort £30 from Robert.

Elizabeth was daughter of John Comyn of Badenoch, the claimant to the throne of Scotland, who was

The grantor, a great-grandson of Richard son of Scrob, was lord of Richard’s castle and a considerable 
tenant-in-chief. The grantee was Walter Cumin of Snitterfield, Warw. The limits of date are supplied by 
the attestation of Richard of Ilchester, archdeacon of Poitiers; he first appears as such in 1163 and was 
elected to the see of Winchester in 1173. 


* The clerk wrote p for per and corrected it by deleting the tail to 0. Correctly written BS. SiC. 


JOHN PHILIPOTT, ESQ. 127 


The charter is of interest as affording a possible clue to the origin of John Cumin, archbishop of Dublin, 
who was already a royal official in 1164 and who died in 1212. The grantee, a Warwickshire landowner, 
is somewhat surprisingly described by his relationship to a man who was apparently his younger brother. 
The first witness, Richard the archdeacon, however, was an important royal official, and if John Cumin 
be identical with the future archbishop of that name, the explanation may be that the charter was drafted 
from, so to speak, an official point of view. The hand in which the charter is written and the general format 
of the document are very reminiscent of the royal charters put out by the chancery clerks.

Charter of Baldwin de Reviers, earl of Devon, confirming to Quarr abbey the land 
of Luccombe, Isle of Wight, which he had given to Hugh de Mandeville and which 
Hugh gave to the abbey with himself. (1141-4) 


ORIGINAL: Harl. Chart. 55 D 21. 
BS FACSIMILE. 


Ego Bald’ de Riv’ . comes Exonie - pro salute anime mee . dono & concedo & hac mea 
cartula confirmo deo & abbatie sancte Marie sanctique Johannis euangeliste de 
Quarraria . totam terram de Louecumba cum omnibus pertinentiis suis » liberam & 
quietam ab omnibus terrenis seruitiis. Quam quidem terram donaueram Hugoni de 
Mandauill’ pro seruitio suo ? & ipse postmodum hanc eandem terram per manum 
meam donauit secum in elemosinam predicte abbatie » concedente Ricardo de Riv’ . 
filio meo. Testibus Willelmo de Moreuill’ . Gaufrido de Fornell’ . Hugone Peverello . 
Sanson Foliot . Pagano Trenchart Peuerello de Arg’. 


Endorsed: Carta de Louecumba . comitis Baldewini. (12th century.) 
No seal or tag is shown. Slits only for tag on original. 


Hugh de Mandeville must have been a junior member of a family which was closely connected with that 
of the Reviers, earls of Devon, and which came from Magneville (dép. Manche, arr. Valognes, canton 
Bricquebec) about 3 km. north-east of Néhou, the caput of the Reviers barony in Cotentin. In 1093 
Richard de Reviers and Roger de Mandeville assisted the future Henry I to obtain the comté of the 
Cotentin (William of Jumiéges, Gesta Normannorum Ducum, lib. viii, cap. 4, by Robert of Torigny; ed. 
Marx, 271). Roger and his brother Geoffrey both came to England early in Henry I’s reign, the former 
being the ancestor of the Mandevilles of Erlestoke, Wilts., and the latter of those of Marshwood, Dors. 
Both of them witness in Normandy a charter for the abbey of St.-Sauveur-le-Vicomte (Delisle, Hist. du 
Chateau de St.-Sauveur-le-Vicomte: *Preuves’, 55), and in England one of Richard de Reviers (d. 1107) 
for Christchurch priory, Hants (Mon. vi. 304). This charter must be later than the creation of the earldom 
of Devon in 1141; on the other hand, Hugh de Mandeville’s gift of Luccombe here confirmed is among 
the numerous benefactions confirmed by Earl Baldwin’s ‘foundation’ charter of 1141-4 (see V. H. 
Galbraith, Cambridge Historical Journal, iv. 217, 297). After the gift had been thus included in a general 
confirmation a specific grant would be unnecessary, and it is therefore presumably the earlier of the two. 
Hugh died before 1162, since a gift of his son Symeon to Quarr is confirmed by Richard de Reviers, earl 
of Devon (Mon. v. 317).

Alan la Zouche, Roger’s father, was a younger son of Geoffrey vicomte of Porhéet (Mon. vi. 263). A 
charter of Alan’s for the abbey of Savigny (Morice, Hist. de Bretagne, ‘Preuves’, i, col. 656) shows that 
he married Alice daughter and eventually heir of Philip de Belmeis (cf. Mon., loc. cit.; HKF i. 129) and 
that his son and heir was William. Alan was dead at Michaelmas 1190 when William who had taken 
his mother’s name of Belmeis paid 100 marks for his relief (PR 2 Ric. J, 130). William died before 
Michaelmas 1199, when his brother Roger la Zouche made a render of £100 for his land (PR I John, 197). 
The present charter is presumably later than this, and must be earlier than 15 May 1227, when Henry III 
confirmed the gift in question (Cal. Chart. Rolls, i. 41). Letters of protection were issued in favour of 
Humphrey de Scoville, described as a knight of Roger la Zouche, in 1215 (Rot. Lit. Claus. i. 231 b). He 
witnessed William Burnel’s charter for Monkton Farleigh priory, No. 173 above.

Notification that Ansketil (de Saucy) has granted one half of Newbold Saucy, 

Leics., to Robert son of Osmund (of Leicester) and has pledged the other half to him 

for two marks. The agreement was made in the presence of Ansketil’s lord Ives de 
Harcourt who is surety for its performance. (Not later than 1166) 


ORIGINAL: Harl. Chart. 45 C 40. 

BS FACSIMILE. 

PRINTED: Stenton, Danelaw Charters, No. 461. 
Fragment of seal on tag: brown. 


The grantor was the ancestor of the family from which Newbold Saucy took its distinguishing appellation, 
and they presumably came from La Saussaye (dép. Eure, arr. Louviers, cant. Amfreville-la-Campagne), 
a fief of the Norman branch of the Harcourts (Le Prevost, Notes sur l’Eure, iii. 220). A charter of the 
grantee for Nuneaton priory is printed in Danelaw Charters, No. 316, in which he is described as ‘of

also cites from the register of Owston abbey a charter of Robert son of Osmund giving his moiety of 
Newbold to that house. The fact that Ives de Harcourt is a witness means that the charter was granted 
before his death in the latter part of 1166.

Charter of Rannulf de Bayeux and Margaret his wife confirming to Alan of 
Rippingale, Lincs., and the heirs of his body the land which Swein of Kirkby held, 
Swein himself, with his heir, consenting. (1130-58; probably circa 1140) 


ORIGINAL: Harl. Chart. 45 F 16. 
BS FACSIMILE. 
PRINTED: Stenton, Danelaw Charters, No. 468. 


SEAL on strip: round, 2% in.; yellow. A lamb walking to dexter, supporting with right forefoot a staff 
with cross formy at top and a banner with two streamers and charged with a saltire. 


A later addition to the Lindsey Survey states that Rannulf de Bayeux married Margaret daughter of Alan 
of Lincoln (LRS xix. 246), and on the Pipe Roll of 31 Hen. I (p. 111) Rannulf proffers 20 marks for the 
daughter of Alan of Lincoln. This charter cannot therefore be earlier than 1130. Rannulf must have died 
not long before Michaelmas 1158, when his son Hugh made a render of 20 marks pro terra sua (PR 
4 Hen. II, 137). There are two joint charters of Rannulf, his wife Margaret, Hugh his son and heir, and 
another son for Newhouse abbey, one of which, addressed to Alexander bishop of Lincoln, cannot be 
later than the beginning of 1148 (Stenton, Danelaw Charters, Nos. 244, 255); since no son joins in the 
present charter there seems reason to place it substantially earlier than these. A charter of Rannulf’s son, 
Hugh, is printed by Stenton in English Feudalism, 274.

A notification addressed by Ralf de Boscheville to Richard bishop of Coventry shows this grant to have 
been made in furtherance of an agreement between the priory and Henry the clerk (Madox, Formulare, 
No. 4). A confirmation by Bishop Richard is also printed by Madox (ibid., No. 507): it is witnessed by 
Hervey de Stretton, sheriff of Staffordshire. Richard Peche was consecrated bishop of Coventry and 
Lichfield in 1161 and died 6 Oct. 1182; Hervey became sheriff in 1166 and served continuously until after 
the bishop’s death. In 1166 Ralf the grantor held one knight’s fee of Ferrers, being one of the three which 
his father William de Boscherville held in 1135 (RB i. 337). Ralf was dead in 1202 (Earliest Northampton- 
shire Assize Rolls, NRS v, Nos. 208, 440). The rectory of Sutton belonged to the priory at the Dissolution 
(Mon. vi. 398).

Richard of Fleet occurs as witness to a charter for Sixle priory in which land in East Rasen held of his 
fee is mentioned and of which the limits of date are 1153-62 (Stenton, Gilbertine Charters, LRS, 21). He 
first occurs on the Pipe Roll in 1170, and again 1175-7. In 1195 he paid 100 marks which he had owed 
for some years, ‘ut filia sit deliberata de Radulfo de Chandos qui dicebat se eam desponsasse’ (PR 7 Ric. I, 
160). At some date before 1185 he gave 50 acres in Fleet to the Templars (Lees, Records of the Templars, 
96). An Alger of Fleet appears intermittently on the Pipe Roll from 1165 to 1186; in 1188 Walter of Fleet 
occurs on the roll, as also on the Curia Regis Roll of 1194 (PRS xiv. 35).

In 1212 Geoffrey of Titsey was holding land in Titsey, of the king as of the honor of Gloucester and 
4 fee in Camberwell by the same tenure (Fees, 69). He died before 1242-3, when the land was held by

of Titsey had called to warranty for 2 acres of land in Camberwell (Cur. Reg. Rolls, vii. 119); these are 
clearly the donee and the first witness. This charter can therefore be assigned to the earlier part of the 
13th century.

The charter is now in a far worse condition than it was in 1640. It has been rebacked and several letters 
legible in 1640 are now gone. They have been printed within square brackets. 

For Robert, the last count of Meulan, see CP, 2nd ed. vii. 739-41. Holding, as he did, lands in France, 
Normandy, and England, he was placed in a difficult position by Philip’s conquest of Normandy, and it 
was to meet this that by a charter dated 1 May 1204 he granted to his daughter Mabiria, wife of William 
earl of Devon, all his lands in France, Normandy, and England (La Roque, Hist. de la Maison de Harcourt, 
iv. 1966, from the cartulary of Beaulieu priory; reprinted, without the witnesses, CP, 2nd ed. iv. 315 n. f). 
The present instrument appears to be a letter notifying the above-mentioned grant, which, however, never 
took effect. In the king’s court on 21 June following William the Marshal claimed against the earl of 
Devon and the countess of Meulan seisin of Sturminster and he produced a charter of the count of Meulan 
granting it to him; this charter was presumably earlier than that of 1 May. After argument the case was 
adjourned (Cur. Reg. Rolls, iii. 124). Thereafter there seem to have been negotiations with Count Robert, 
for by letters patent of 9 Sept. 1204 the king commanded the men of Sturminster to do homage to the 
Marshal as they had been directed by the letters they had received from the count of Meulan. It is to be 
noted that the count’s sons Henry and Peter mentioned in this letter were already dead. In the course 
of the year Philip Augustus confiscated both the county of Meulan and the Norman lands, and Count 
Robert died a ruined man; he was living in 1210, apparently as a pensioner of King John (Rot. de Liberate, 
226), and probably died not long before 1219, when his widow claimed the manor of Sturminster as dower 
(Cur. Reg. Rolls, viii. 116). Previously, in 1201, Count Robert executed a charter, known by a copy in 
Dodsworth MSS. xc, f. 114, by which he granted one-third of all his lands in France, Normandy, and 
England to his grand-daughter Mary, daughter of the earl of Devon, in marriage with Peter de Préaux. 
It is a curious feature of the count of Meulan’s attempts to dispose of his lands that his grandson and 
heir, Ralf, the son of his eldest son Waleran, was throughout entirely passed over (see CP, vii. 741). In 
the present charter Moreis may possibly be More’s Court, a manor in Sturminster Marshall (Hutchins, 
Dorset, iii. 31). Redelestun has not been identified.

No seal or tag shown. Slit only for tag on original. 


The grantor is Geoffrey of Glympton, the younger, son of Henry I’s well-known minister. In 1166 he 
held 17 knights’ fees of the earl of Warwick (RB 325). Sometime in the reign.of Stephen he married Agnes 
daughter of Roger earl of Warwick, and William son of Ralf was one of Geoffrey’s witnesses to the 
marriage settlement (Ancestor, xi. 153). He held no land in chief and does not occur on the Pipe Rolls; 
the date of his death is unknown, but it must have been before 1175 when his son and successor occurs 
on the Pipe Roll (PR 21 Hen. II, 34, 98). A Hugh son of Hermenfred and a Henry son of Boscher who 
witnessed a charter of Henry earl of Warwick (d. 1119) for St. Mary’s, Warwick (Mon. vi. 1326) seem 
to be identical with witnesses to this.

For an account of the family and honor of Courcy see HKF i. 103 et seq., also a paper on the family by 
Sir H. Maxwell Lyte in Somerset Arch. and Nat. Hist. Soc. Proc. \xvi. 98. Nevertheless there remain 
obscure points in the descent and chronology due principally to the difficulty of distinguishing between 
members of the Norman and English branches of the family who at times bore the same Christian names. 
The attestation of Jordan de Courcy ‘my brother’ shows the grantor to be William III of the English 
branch. Robert was consecrated bishop of Bath and Wells in 1136 and died 31 Aug. 1166.

A charter of Richard I dated 15 Sept. 1189 confirms to Bruern abbey ‘in territorio de Middlintonia terras 
quas Willelmus filius Ricardi scripto suo dedit et confirmavit’ (Cal. Chart. Rolls, v. 221). Milton under

Stow on the Wold, the ‘Edwardesstowe’ of this charter, to Burford; Littlehill is the name of a farm still 
existing in Milton. These details identify the present charter with that confirmed by Richard I. William 
son of Richard occurs on the Oxfordshire Pipe Roll of 1 183 (PR 29 Hen. II, 103). The latest limit of date 
is 1189 and the warranty clause suggests the later part of Henry II’s reign.

Since the witness Walter de Amundeville had sons he cannot be the steward of the bishop of Lincoln 
who died 1166-7 and was succeeded by his brother (Reg. Antiquiss., LRS iv. 157 n.); he seems to be the 
man who occurs on the Lincolnshire Assize Rolls of 1202 and 1206 (LRS xxii, Nos. 189, 1462); Simon 
de Blia occurs on the roll of 1202 (ibid., No. 495). Among the duke of Rutland’s charters at Belvoir is 
one of William de Coleville giving a mill at Muston, Leics., to Owston abbey, which Round dates circa 1200; 
the donor mentions his father William, and it is witnessed by Simon de Blia and Geoffrey de Perfite 
(Rutland Report, iv. 12). Maude de Coleville occurs in 1191 as a large debtor of Aaron the Jew of Lincoln 
(PR 3 & 4 Ric. I, 20), and the debts continue on the rolls till 1202, when her son William de Coleville 
produced documents showing that Maud had repaid the money to Aaron himself (PR 4 John, 223). 
Aaron died in 1186 and, however these debts may have originated, Maud’s husband William de Coleville 
the elder was presumably dead when Maud dealt directly with Aaron. The present charter, therefore, 
must be earlier than 1186; on the other hand, the occurrence of two of the witnesses in the early 13th 
century suggests a date in the latter part of the reign of Henry II.

For the succession to the earldom and honor of Huntingdon, of which Draughton was held, see CP, 
2nd ed. vi. David, younger brother of Malcolm and William kings of Scots, succeeded to it in 1185 
(ibid. 646). Stephen of Ecton the father made a render at Michaelmas 1187 pro pace regis habenda 
(PR 33 Hen. IT, 100); at Michaelmas 1188 his son Stephen is entered as liable for the balance of his father’s 
debt (PR 34 Hen. II, 129); the father therefore died 1187-8. The caput of the honor was Fotheringhay, 
and a court was sometimes held there (Stenton, English Feudalism, 43), but the court of the honor also 
met at Earl’s Barton (HKF ii. 300); the presence among the witnesses of Thomas the clerk of Barton and 
his brother and of Robert of Wilby, an adjacent parish, suggests that the present charter passed at Earl’s 
Barton. For a slightly later charter of William de Audre or Aldri dealing with this same matter see 
No. 220 below.

Charter of Henry Biset giving to Ralf de Aureville 100 ‘solidatae’ of land in his 
manor of Kidderminster, Worcs., namely 14 shillings in his demesne mill of Kidder-

Comberton. (1187-1205)

-H. Biset omnibus hominibus suis Francis et Anglis salutem. Sciatis me dedisse et con-

JOHN PHILIPOTT, ESQ. 145 


suis . et totam uillam de Cumbrintun’ cum omnibus pertinenciis suis. Tenend’ sibi 
et heredibus suis . de me et heredibus meis . annuatim reddendo j hostorium sor . 
uel v solidos pro omni seruicio . et hoc sit in electione predicti Radulfi? utrum eorum

The rest of the charter is not reproduced and consequently there is no indication of a seal. 


The donor’s father Manasser Biset was a royal steward from the beginning of Henry II’s reign; he married 
Alice de Cany, the heiress of extensive lands in Caux in Normandy (Le Cacheux, Chartes du Prieuré de 
Longueville, Soc. Hist. Norm. 43-6). He was living at Michaelmas 1176 (PR 22 Hen. IT, 188), but was 
dead at Michaelmas 1177 (PR 23 Hen. II, 165), leaving a son and heir, this Henry Biset then a minor 
(PR 32 Hen. II, 168). Henry seems to have come of age in 1187, when he obtained possession of Kidder- 
minster (PR 33 Hen. II, 216): at first sight he appears to have been out of possession between 1199 and 
1201 since Geoffrey fitzPeter makes a render for the farm of Kidderminster for the first two years of 
John’s reign (PR 3 John, 116) and in 1201 Henry paid 200 marks to have it (ibid. 117), but a note on the 
roll of 1202 (p. 18) states Henry to have had the land during these years, and it is clear that Geoffrey 
made no payment. The date of Henry’s death is uncertain; on 17 Sept. 1207 he witnessed a royal charter 
(Rot. Chart. 170 b) and as he appears no more on the rolls he probably died soon after: he was certainly - 
dead in 1212 (Fees, 74-5). His widow Iseult was living on 9 Dec. 1213 (Rot. de Oblatis, 511). 

Of the places named, ‘Muct’ is Mitton 3 miles south of Kidderminster, and ‘Cambrintuna’ is Comber- 
ton, a farm just east of Kidderminster, rather than Comberton near Evesham. Aldimun’ has not been 
identified; it is possibly a corrupt form of Oldington, between Kidderminster and Mitton. The date 
cannot be earlier than 1187, when the donor attained his majority; nor, being addressed to his men 
French and English, is the charter likely to be later than 1205, by when Henry would have lost his 
Norman lands.

scilicet ad festum omnium sanctorum. Hiis testibus . Radulfo Gocelin . Simone 
de Croprie . Thoma de Willecote® . Fuche Bassat . Rogero Murdach filio Rogeri . 
Philippo persona de Eindona . Willelmo fratre eius. 


No ancient endorsement. 
No seal or tag shown. Slit only for tag on original. 


This charter relates to the one fee held by Murdac of the honor of Huntingdon (HKF ii. 324-6). The family 
also held one fee of the earl of Warwick in Compton Murdak, now Compton Verney, Warw.: a pedigree 
in Dugdale’s Warwickshire, 1765 ed. 404) is defective and is of no help in dating this charter. Roger 
Murdac and Ralf Gocelin appear on the Assize Roll of 1202, and Simon of Cropredy on that of 1203 
(VRS v. Nos. 598, 304, 765). Philip had ceased to be rector of Eydon by 1220 (Rot. Hugh de Welles, 
Cant. and York Soc. ii. 98). The form of the charter and the absence of a sealing clause suggest the 
late 12th century rather than the early 13th. Attention may be called to the very rare personal name Flaut, 
a variant of Flaald, that of the Breton ancestor of the royal house of Stewart (Round, Peerage and Family 
History, 120 et seq.).

Charter of Thomas de Charleton of Apley (Appeleye) giving to John Attewode, knight, and Alesia his wife, 
the daughter of John of Ludlow (Lodelawe), knight, the manor of Apley beside Wellington with all rents, 
services, &c., and also all lands and tenements being his demesne within the said manor together with the 
reversions of all lands and tenements in the same village held of him for the term of their lives by Thomas 
Makkesson, William of Tong, chaplain, Philip Fissher, John Malpas, Margaret Pors, John Michel and 
Alice his wife, John of Tong, Richard de Atton, John Mercer, John de Morton, Thomas Aleyn, John 
Pereweye and Isabel his wife: granting also the reversion of 2 messuages, a virgate of land and 2 meadows 
in Wappenshall (Wapmondeshale) beside Apley held by John Herdeman for the term of his life: giving 
also to the said John and Alesia all the lands, tenements, demesnes, services, &c., which he has within 
the manor of Preston upon the Weald Moors (Preston iuxta Wyldemor) with the reversions of the lands 
and tenements held by Thomas Smot, John Palmer (Palmarius), John the smith of Preston, William the 
tailor of the same, Thomas of Kinnersley (Kynerdesleye), John de Grene, and Margery Palmer for the 
term of their lives: giving also to the said John and Alesia the reversion of his lands and tenements in 
Haughton (Halgton) and Trilwardyn held by Thomas Cresset and Rose his wife for the life of the said 
Rose: to hold all the aforesaid lands, tenements, &c., to the said John and Alesia jointly and severally 
for their lives and for the life of the survivor of them and for a further year from the death of such survivor, 
of the donor and his heirs by the payment of one peppercorn at Christmas and performing for the donor 
and his heirs to the chief lords of the fee the services due and accustomed. At the end of the above-mentioned 
term all the aforesaid lands, tenements, &c., together with all reversions shall revert to the donor and his 
heirs. Warranty by the donor and his heirs for the above-mentioned term. Sealing clause. ‘Hiis testibus 
Ade de Peeshale chiualer Thome de Glasleye et Petro de Eyton’ et aliis.” Wellington: 27 July 1384. 


Endorsed: Indentura Johannis del Wode cheualer et Thome de Cherleton’ de Appleye. (Contemporary.) 
No seal! or tag is shown. 


All the places mentioned are in Shropshire. Haughton is near Shifnal, and a family of Cresset is found 
there in the Middle Ages (Eyton, Shropshire, viii. 285-7): Trilwardyn is a lost place-name in Shifnal 
(ibid. ii. 311-12).

Master Roger de Martivall was the son of Anketin de Martivall and his successor in the lordship of the 
village of Noseley, Leics. He had succeeded him in 1278. By this time he was, as this document shows, a 
master. In 1294 he became archdeacon of Leicester, in 1310 dean of Lincoln, and in 1315 bishop of 
Salisbury. He died in Mar. 1330 (Nichols, ii, pt. ii. 739 and 756). Nicholas de Martivall has no place 
in the pedigree in Nichols (p. 756), but he states that in 1277 Goadby was of the inheritance of Nicholas 
de Martivall (p. 438). It is possible that he was an elder son of Anketin, and that his death brought 
the inheritance to Roger, destined as a younger son for the Church.
