Notification by William, earl Warenne and (count of) Boulogne and Mortain, that 

he has granted permission to the monks of Furness abbey to take in his forest of 

Lancaster the material which they may need, in particular for their fishery at 
Lancaster. Singleton (1153-9) 

BS FACSIMILE. 


PRINTED: Coucher Book of Furness Abbey (Chetham Soc., N.S. 74), ii, pt. i. 184, from the cartulary; first 
two witnesses only: Farrer, Lancashire Pipe Rolls, 309, from the cartulary. 


Willelmus comes Warennie et Bolonii et Moretonie . omnibus justic’ suis et bauilliis! 
et hominibus suis de honore Lanc’ . salutem. Sciatis me dedisse et sigilli mei munimine 
confirmasse deo et monachis sancte Marie de Furn’ in perpetuam elemosinam . ut in 
foresta mea de Lanc’ accipiant materiem . et cetera que ad usus suos sunt necessaria . 
et nominatim ad piscariam suam de Lanc’ faciendam quicquid eis ad hoc opus fuerit ’ 
inde accipere permitto. Testes . Reginaldus de Warenn’ . Eustachius cancellarius . 
Willelmus Malebisse . Faramus apud Singeltun. 


SEAL on tag: pink; much broken. Equestrian, lance, horse walking. 


The grantor was the younger son of King Stephen and had married Isabel daughter and heir of William 
de Warenne, the third earl of Surrey; for an account of him and his vast possessions see Round, Peerage 
and Family History, 167-71. The fishery at Lancaster was a part of the original endowment of the abbey 
(charter No. 423 post); timber would be required for the construction of the weirs. The witness Reginald 
de Warenne was a younger brother of the third earl and ancestor of the Warennes of Wormegay, Norf. 
He seems to have played an important part in the management of the Warenne lands (see BM Facsimiles, 
No. 31). Faramus is the well-known Faramus of Boulogne, as to whom see Round in Genealogist, 
N.S. xii. 145 et seq. This instrument cannot be earlier than 6 Nov. 1153, the date of the treaty between 
Stephen and the future Henry II by the terms of which Henry undertook to restore to William the lands 
in Normandy including the comté of Mortain which Stephen had possessed (Delisle and Berger, Recueil 
des Actes de Henry II, i. 62). The grantor died in 1159 on the Toulouse expedition.

et si infra xl dies se nollet erga comitem Gloecestrie erigere ’ se comiti Gloecestrie

This important feudal document has been printed by Round (see above) with a commentary. Round 
(p. 379) suspected that Dugdale’s transcript was incomplete and that the provisions to be observed by 
the earl of Hereford had been omitted therefrom; the transcript, however, agrees with the facsimile except 
for minor inaccuracies and is complete. The agreement is mentioned by Dugdale in his Baronage (i. 537), 
and it is significant that he describes it as ‘ex ipso autographo penes Joh. Philipot Somerset Heraldum, 
an. 1640’, the year in which this facsimile was made. The date assigned is that proposed by Round. 
Although there is no indication that a chirograph was drawn up, it seems arguable that each earl would 
have desired to hold a copy of the agreement sealed with his ally’s seal.

The donor took his name from Whitefield in the Isle of Wight; his father Robert witnessed Earl Baldwin’s 
‘foundation’ charter for Quarr between 1141 and 1144 (Cambridge Hist. Journ. iv. 297). Earl Richard, 
here clearly mentioned as dead, died Apr. 1162, but this is the only indication of date. Simon is a hitherto 
unrecorded abbot of Quarr. In connexion with this transaction there are two subsidiary instruments of 
interest: a notification by Warin de Aula that he was present and heard the gift and affidatio (Madox,

Guarinus and the Gaufridus of the affidatio. The witnesses show all three documents to be contempor- 
aneous. Hugh also gave Whitefield to Quarr (Madox, op. cit., No. 84).

A charter of Hubert Walter, archbishop of Canterbury (1193-1205), confirms this gift, describing the

de Holmia gave to Langley half a thousand eels or alternatively a rent of 3 shillings from her fishery of

Stoke Ferry, which Basilia daughter of Roger of Holme held at her death (Blomefield and Parkin, Hist. 
of Norfolk, 8vo ed. vii. 438); here we seem to have the donor’s son and granddaughter. The charter 
contains no very clear indications of date, but the pedigree outlined above suggests the second half of the 
12th century.

Charter of Sampson Foliot giving to Quarr abbey a house in Barfleur, Manche, and 
confirming the gift of his father in the same place. (circa 1200) 


ORIGINAL: Harl. Chart. 50 D 4. 
BS FACSIMILE. 


Sciant presentes et futuri quod ego Sanson Foliot dedi et concessi in elemosinam per- 
petuam sancte Marie de Quadraria et monachis ibidem seruientibus unum mesuagium 
in uilla de Barbeflet scilicet unum de tribus quod Matheus clericus tenuit scilicet 
medium illud libere et quiete ab omni seruitio. Donum etiam patris mei in pre- 
nominata uilla de Barbeflet eis concessi libere et quiete. His testibus . Driwone 
de Vernon . Herberto Goldewino . Rodberto pincerna . Willelmo Coffin. et aliis multis. 


Endorsed: Carta Sansonis Folioth de mesuagio in Barbeflet. (Contemporary.) 
No seal or tag shown. A fragment of seal remains on its tag on the original. 


Sampson Foliot was lord of Montfarville, close to Barfleur; by another charter he gave two houses in 
Barfleur to Quarr (Madox, Formulare, No. 419); they were probably the remaining two of the three here 
mentioned. The family were benefactors of the abbey of Montebourg, another foundation with which the 
earls of Devon were closely connected. A charter of Henry II confirms to Montebourg the gift of the church 
of Montfarville made by an earlier Sampson Foliot concessu Roberti de Novoburgo and therefore before 
1159 (Delisle and Berger, Recueil, ii. 152); this Sampson must be identical with the witness to charter 
No. 178. Between c. 1165 and 1190 William Foliot, the then lord of Montfarville, twice occurs as a 
benefactor of the abbey of Le Vceu at Cherbourg (L. Couppey, L’ Abbaye de N.-D. du Veu de Cherbourg, 
11, 22), and in 1190 he took the cross (ibid. 34). He is apparently the father whose gift is here confirmed. 
In 1213 Sampson Foliot, the present donor, confirmed a gift to Cherbourg (ibid. 43), and in 1223 Richard 
Foliot, son of Sampson Foliot, confirmed to the Maison-Dieu at Barfleur a gift by his brother William 
of land at Le Vicel (P. Le Cacheux, L’H6tel-Dieu de Coutances, i. 20). In May 1231 Louis IX gave to 
John de Fricamps ‘terram que fuit Richardi Foliot in omnibus apud Carnanvillam, Morfarvillam et terram 
Sansonis Foliot in omnibus ibidem’ (Delisle, Cartulaire Normand, No. 379). The family does not seem, 
however, to have lost its lands finally and completely, for in 1278 Richard Foliot, son of the late Sampson 
Foliot, confirmed to Montebourg lands in Montfarville among other places (Delisle, loc. cit., citing the 
cartulary of Montebourg). 

In Oxfordshire in 1235-6 a Sampson Foliot held 3 knights’ fees of the earl of Devon in Fritwell, Noke, 
and Aldbury (Fees, 447), and in Wiltshire Chilton Foliatt and Draycott Foliatt of the king as of the 
honor of Wallingford (ibid. 423). When in addition we find a William Foliot party to a fine concerning 
land in Aldbury in 1197 (PRS xx, No. 79) it is tempting to identify the Oxfordshire Sampson of 1235-6 
with the man mentioned in St. Louis’s charter of 1231. They were, however, different persons, for the 
Oxfordshire tenant in a charter giving land at Chilton to St. Frideswide’s priory, Oxford, describes himself 
as son of Henry Foliot (Cartulary, Ox. Hist. Soc. ii. 361), which Henry had succeeded an elder brother 
Ralf (ibid. ii. 359). At the same time all the circumstances suggest a relationship between the two families. 
The history of these Norman Foliots is not without interest as affording a clue to the origin of Gilbert 
Foliot, bishop of London, who had a nephew, another Gilbert, who held land at Vauville in the Cétentin 


(Delisle et Berger, Recueil, Introduction, 376, n. 5).

et presenti carta mea confirmaui . ecclesie sancti Dionisii iuxta Suhanton’ . et canonicis

domino Johanni Norewicensi episcopo presentauit. Hiis testibus . Gilone Hosato . 
Waltero de Wike . Hilario de Bacamtone . Ricardo de Stutescumbe . Rocelino Husato .

SEAL on green and white cords: pointed oval, c. 2} x 1} in.; uncoloured; much broken. A lady standing, 
a hawk on her left hand; no legend. BM 6732 


Gundred de Warenne married firstly Peter II de Valognes, who died without issue (HKF iii. 393); secondly 
William HI de Curcy of Stogursey, who died 1170-1 (ibid. i. 112) and to whom she bore a son William, 
aged 20 in 1185 (Rot. de Dominabus, 73) and a daughter named Alice; her second marriage therefore 
cannot have been later than the beginning of 1165. She married thirdly Geoffrey de la Huse, who seems 
to have been dead by Michaelmas 1198 (PR 10 Ric. I, 69), and by whom she had a son Geoffrey. She 
died in 1224 (HKFi. 112). There is no direct evidence as to her parentage. The date of her second marriage 
suggests that she was born before 1150. She could not be a daughter of the second Earl Warenne who 
died in 1138 and who moreover had a daughter Gundred who married Roger earl of Warwick; nor of 
the third earl who left an only daughter and heir, the countess Isabel. The only available father for her 
would seem to be Reginald de Warenne, a younger son of the second earl, who married Alice daughter 
and heir of William of Wormegay, lord of a considerable honor in the eastern counties. Some little support 
for this conjecture is afforded by a charter of William de Warenne, son of this Reginald, in the Lewes 
priory cartulary which is witnessed by William de Curcy, apparently either Gundred’s second husband 
or her son (Suss. Rec. Soc. xxxviii. 55); it should also be noted that Gundred’s daughter bore the name 
of Alice, that of Reginald’s wife. 

In Domesday Book Little Fakenham was held by Peter of the abbey of Bury St. Edmunds (f. 367 5), 
and the corresponding entries in Abbot Baldwin’s Book of Fees (Feudal Documents from Bury St Edmunds, 
23-4) show him to have been Peter I de Valognes, grandfather of Gundred’s first husband. This suggests 
that Gundred held it as dower and not as maritagium, a marriage portion from her father. The subsequent 
history of the land, however, seems to negative this idea. On 9 May 1225 there is a royal writ to the sheriff 
of Suffolk to give Hugh de Neville and Joan his wife and Margaret de Reviers seisin of the land in Faken- 


JOHN PHILIPOTT, ESQ. 159 


ham of which Gundred de Warenne was seised at her death and which belonged by inheritance to Joan and 
Margaret (Rot. Litt. Claus. ii. 37). They were daughters of Alice, Gundred’s daughter by her second husband, 
William de Curcy; Joan by Alice’s first husband Henry of Cornhill, and Margaret by her second, Warin 
fitzGerold (HKF i. 108); Margaret was the widow of Baldwin, son of the earl of Devon, and of Fawkes 
de Breauté. Later, in 1236, in a list of knights’ fees of the barony of Valognes (Fees, 579) Margaret 
de Reviers is entered as holding 1? fees in Little Fakenham and elsewhere. An interest which thus descended 
to the grandchildren by the second husband could not have originated in dower from the first, and in 
view of the fact that in the present charter Gundred herself describes Little Fakenham as her maritagium, 
the most probable explanation seems to be that her father held it of Valognes by subinfeudation and when 
his daughter married into the family of his overlord gave it her as a marriage portion. No very definite 
evidence of date is forthcoming for this charter, but from its substance it was probably issued not long 
after the death of Geoffrey de la Huse.

This charter carries the history of the land dealt with by No. 200 above a stage farther. As shown in the 
note to the previous charter, Stephen the father died 1187-8, and the subject-matter of the present charter, 
in particular the mention of the relief, shows it to be soon after that event. The local character of some 
of the witnesses suggests that this charter also was executed at Earl’s Barton; indeed, the correspondence 
between the witnesses to the two charters is such that but for their subject-matter they might well be taken 
to be contemporaneous; in this connexion it may be noted that the originals are in different handwritings. 
Fackeley soke was in Rothwell hundred.

Crowhurst and Guestling lie in the Rape of Hastings and were held of the count of Eu. The present gift 
was confirmed by the donor’s son, Ralf de Dene—the usual name of the family—by a charter which 
cannot be much later (PRO Ancient Deed A 15483; see Lewes Cartulary, ed. L. F. Salzman, Suss. Rec. 
Soc. xxxviii, pt. i. 137). A charter of John, count of Eu, confirms what appears to be a different gift by 
Robert to the priory (ibid. i. 147). Roger Hai became sheriff of Sussex after Michaelmas 1163 and con- 
tinued to Easter 1170. Ralf de Dene, Robert’s son, held 6 knights’ fees of Richer de Laigle in 1166 (RB 
204); as Robert the butler witnesses two charters of Richer for Lewes priory (Salzman, op. cit. i. 159-60) 
he must have preceded his son in this holding and died before 1166. No holding by the family is shown 
in the count of Eu’s return of 1166. The press-mark xviij—o on the endorsement is a serial number and as

Loxley in Uttoxeter, Staffs., was held of the earls of Derby by the service of a quarter of a knight’s fee 
by a younger branch of the Ferrers family. Although the earlier pedigree of this branch has not been 
established, it seems probable that the original sub-feoffee was Robert de Ferrers, a younger brother of 
William the third earl. In 1266 the honor of Tutbury, of which Loxley was a member, was given to the 
grantor’s father, Edmund second son of Henry III (see No. 411 and note).

Henry II gave Ravensmeols and other lands in Lancashire to Warin of Lancaster to hold by a falconer 
serjeanty, and this grant was confirmed to Warin’s son Henry, the present donor, by John count of 
Mortain between 1189 and 1194 (Farrer, Lancashire Pipe Rolls, 432). Forton, in Cockerham, Lancs., had 
been given by William of Lancaster I to Warin (VCH Lancs. viii. 106), and Warin gave a moiety to Aldred 
son of Hamlet, the Haldred of this charter (ibid.). In the Coucher Book this charter is immediately 
preceded by that of Haldred of Forton giving to Furness the other moiety of the land in question; and except 
for necessary variations the two are verbally identical; unfortunately the cartulary omits witnesses and 
consequently it is not certain that they are contemporaneous. The extreme limits of date seem to be after 
1194, when Thomas the predecessor of the witness Roger abbot de Marisco (i.e. Cockersand abbey) was 
certainly living (Farrer, op. cit. 339), and before 1216, when Roger had been succeeded by Hereward 
(VCH Lancs. ii. 158). Farrer (ibid. viii. 107 n.) says of this charter that ‘it may be dated about 1206’.

Margaret, wife of the famous John Talbot, earl of Shrewsbury, was daughter of Richard Beauchamp, 
earl of Warwick, by his first wife. By his second wife, Richard had a son Henry who succeeded him in 
the earldom and died leaving an only daughter Anne who died an infant. By his second wife Richard 
had also a daughter Anne married to Richard Neville, ‘the king-maker’, earl of Warwick. This Anne 
countess of Warwick was sole heir of her brother Henry and would take all of which he had died seised, 
but only coheir with her half-sister Margaret of her father and would take only a moiety of that of which 
Henry had not had seisin. This may well have given rise to disputes.

Charter of Thomas of Poynings, Lord St. John, confirming to the prior and convent of the Blessed Mary 
of Boxgrove all the alms, foundations, gifts, grants, and exchanges made by Robert de [la] Hay, William 
de St. John, Robert de St. John, and his other predecessors lords St. John; to hold to the aforesaid prior

or that of his heirs, and also all right and claim that two monks should celebrate divine service in the 
chapel of Halnaker, notwithstanding any, grant or long possession or custom. Warranty and sealing

The grantor was the son and heir of Luke de Poynings by Isabel, sister and coheir of Edmund de St. John, 
which Isabel became sole heir on the death of her elder sister (CP, 2nd ed. xi. 293-4), thus inheriting the

assigns, and of their tenants both free and serf. Within the enclosure (defensum) in the aforesaid wood 
Roger and his heirs may make their profit both from herbage and soil as also from hunting and sale of 
wood, so that they leave sufficient pasture (limited as above) to Thomas, &c., and the tenants; and neither 
the aforesaid Roger, his heirs or assigns, shall enfeoff any one of the village of Swarland of herbage of the 
aforesaid wood nor allow them to have entry without the consent of Thomas, his heirs or assigns. Warranty

The grantor of the inspeximus was Roger Bertram III of Mitford, and the grantor of the charter inspected 
and confirmed, his niece, the daughter of Thomas fitzWilliam of Emley and Sprotborough by Agnes 
daughter of Roger Bertram II and sister of Roger III. An inquisition taken in 1311 shows that Roger III 
had a daughter Agnes who survived him but died without issue, whereupon Roger III’s four sisters became 
coheirs, of whom Agnes fitzWilliam was the eldest (Cal. Ing. p.m. v, No. 294). An accurate account of 
these Bertrams will be found in CP, 2nd ed. ii. 161-2. For the fitzWilliams see W. P. Baildon, Baildon 
and the Baildons, i. 366. Woodhall in Darfield parish, Yorks., W.R., was held by Thomas fitzWilliam, 
but passed to his younger son, Roger. The Northumberland County History, vii. 385-6, gives an account 


* BM 5706, description ‘an orle between eleven crosses land and Durham, No. 71 and pl. i, description ‘crusilly an 
crosslet’; and cf. C. H. Hunter-Blair, Seals of Northumber- _ orle’. is

of Roger Bertram III’s dealings with his lands and cites this inspeximus, but it errs in making Agnes the 
wife of Thomas fitzWilliam Roger III’s daughter instead of his sister. The inquisition of 1311, which is 
the crucial evidence, had not been printed when this volume was compiled. Thomas of Carlisle and also 
his son and grandson were mayors of Newcastle (ibid. vii. 389). Guichard de Charron was sheriff from 
Nov. 1267 to Nov. 1272. ‘Ouergares’ is Overgrass in Swarland and the wood called ‘Le defens’ appears 
to be that now known as Swarlandfence. The original charter and the inspeximus must have passed at 
the same time, which can be explained by the fact that as certain provisions of the former are expressly 
binding on Roger it was probably desired to show beyond doubt that he consented to them.

An indenture witnessing that Anne, queen of England and France and lady of Ireland, has granted and 
leased at farm to Matthew Swetenham and [blank] the manor of Weedon Lois, Northants. (Wedon’ 
Pynkeny), with its appurtenances, except the fees, advowsons, wardships, marriages, reliefs, heriots, and 
escheats of all the free tenants of the manor, to hold with all profits as John Porter and Adam Selby 
the last farmers held it; from the Michaelmas next after the date of these presents for the term of 10 years, 
rendering yearly into the Receipt of the queen at London 28 marks sterling by equal portions at the two 
accustomed terms, namely, the Annunciation and the Nativity of Our Lady, and bearing at their own cost 
all other charges pertaining to the said manor and its appurtenances during their term, both repairs of 
houses, walls, and enclosures as also any other charges, except that they ought to have from the queen 
the necessary timber (moryn) and this by the view of the queen’s seneschal or surveyor. At the end of 
their term they shall leave the said manor and houses with their appurtenances in as good condition or 
better than at their first entry. They shall not during their term permit any waste in the said manor nor 
in the woods or other things pertaining to the manor. 

The said Matthew and [b/ank] grant that if the said farm be either in whole or in part 20 days in arrear 
after any of the aforesaid term days, it shall be lawful for the queen to distrain on the said manor or any 
parcel thereof or on any other lands and tenements of the said Matthew and [blank], and to take and 
retain such part of the distress as she shall see fit so that full satisfaction be made for the said farm and 
its arrears: and if the said farm be four weeks in arrear the said Matthew and [blank] bind themselves 
their heirs and executors to pay to the queen double for the term so in arrear, and so for each term so 
often as they shall be in default; and equally it shall be lawful for the queen to re-enter and hold the 
said manor and thereafter deal with it as she please. It is agreed that they shall not cut or fell any of the 
wood except by the queen’s licence and warrant. Sealing clause. London: 15 July 1391.

The name of the second farmer has been left in blank throughout, and there is therefore no evidence as 
to him; in the event it may have been a venture of Swetenham alone. Matthew Swetenham was a yeoman 
of the chamber and occurs on the rolls as holding various offices including the constableship of North- 
ampton castle which he surrendered in 1391 (Cal. Pat. Rolls, Richard II, v. 325, 425). ‘Moryn’ is a corrupt 
form of the Old French mairain, marrien, Latin maremium, meaning building timber.

This agreement failed to effect a final settlement of the disputes between William de Fougéres and 
Geoffrey, for a further agreement was made in J uly 1204 (Morice, Hist. de Bretagne, ‘Preuves’, i, col. 798), 
and as late as 1208 Philip Augustus ratified a later agreement (ibid. i, col. 810). It will be noted that the 
annual payments of £100 to the earl of Chester are to run from Christmas 1201 and that the first payment 
was to be made at midsummer; also that William was to hold the land of Fougéeres for five years from 
Christmas 1201. It seems unlikely that the time thus specified in the agreement should run from a date 
more than a year later than its execution, or that the first payment to the earl should be postponed for 
more than twenty months; consequently the parties must, like so many contemporary chroniclers, have 
been considering the year to begin on Christmas Day. The charter of Geoffrey de Fougéres giving the 
lands in marriage to his sister as provided in this agreement is printed in Ormerod, History of Cheshire, 


2nd ed. i. 39. Since Geoffrey failed to keep his agreement William du Hommet gave the earl land in 
Normandy (PRO Ancient Deeds LS (DL 27) No. 26).

174 JOHN PHILIPOTT, ESQ. 


The grantor, Reginald son of Peter son of Herbert, was the descendant in the male line from Herbert the 
chamberlain of Henry I who died circa 1129. Herbert’s son, another Herbert, died before 1154. Herbert 
the chamberlain’s grandson, Herbert, married Lucy, daughter and eventually coheir of Miles earl of 
Hereford. He died 1203-4 and was the grandfather of Reginald, the grantor. Reginald succeeded his 
elder brother, Herbert, who died without issue in 1248 and himself died in 1286 (CP, 2nd ed. v. 465). 
Reginald’s son John was summoned to the Parliaments of 1299 and 1307 by writ ‘whereby he is held - 
to have become Lord Fitzreynold’ (ibid. 466).

ORIGINAL: Harl. Chart. 46 E 9. 
BS FACSIMILE, first 10 words. Indented. 


Indenture of Henry de Bissheburi, sheriff of Staffordshire, recites a writ of Edward II dated at Greenhow 
29 Aug. 1323 ordering him to cause John son of Thomas de Ferrers to have seisin of a messuage, 20 acres 
of land and 2 acres of meadow in Great Loxley, Staffs., as the king learns by inquisition taken by the 
sheriff that William son of Richard le Hore of Frodeswell and Alice his wife, who were outlawed for 
felony, held the premises of the said John, and that Robert le Hunte has had the king’s year, day, and 
waste and ought to answer to the king for the same. Pursuant thereto he, the sheriff, has delivered to 
John full seisin of the tenements which had been taken into the king’s hand on 29 Aug. 1322; to hold to 
John, his heirs and assigns, saving whatever Robert le Hunte, the coroner, has to answer for to the king 
in respect of the year, day, and waste. Sealed in the presence of ‘Thome de Pype Roberti de Dotton 
militum . Rogeri Hillary Rogeri de Aston et Ricardi de Kyngeston et aliorum’. Stafford: 15 Sept. 1323. 


Strip only for seal, riband below. 


John son of Thomas de Ferrers was half-brother of the Thomas son of Thomas of No. 223. On Thomas’s 
death without issue in or shortly before 1312 there followed long and complicated litigation between John 
and his aunt Margaret, wife of Richard de Calewich, who claimed to be the heir of Thomas, the person 
last seised to whom she was related in the whole blood (Selden Soc. xviii. 155 et seq.). John was ultimately 
successful but died without issue in 1326-7, when Loxley passed to his sister and heir, Joan wife of John 
de Kynnersley. The family of Kynnersley of Loxley continued in the male line till 1815. Robert le Hunte, 
the coroner, who had the king’s year and day is no doubt identical with Robert le Veneur of No. 223. 
The king’s writ here recited is entered on the Close Roll (Cal. Close Rolls, Edw. I, iv. 20).

No seal. 


A part of Mollington was formerly in Warwickshire. Bridges (Northamptonshire, i. 254) and Baker 
(Northamptonshire, ii. 96) give pedigrees of the family of Plumpton of Plumpton, Northants., in both of 
which this marriage is shown. The chronology of the pedigree suggests it to have taken place early in 
the reign of Henry III, in which case the Robert Wandard who held Shotteswell in 1235-6 and 1242-3 
(Fees, 508, 957) was probably Robert Wandard, the son of the present grantor. Robert of Plumpton died 
in 1256, leaving three married daughters by Alice (HKF i. 88). Hence the charter may presumably be 
dated before 1240.

Ballincreif and other lands in Scotland came to Henry de Pinkeny, Robert’s grandfather, through his 
marriage with Alice daughter of David de Lindsay of Crawford of the first line, Alice being ultimately

The nature of this agreement suggests that the financial difficulties of the family, which ultimately led to 
the sale of the English lands to the king by Robert’s brother and heir, Henry, had already begun.

No seal is shown in BS, but a seal in poor condition, on a tag transversely, survives; a capital P, device 
above. No legend. 


The number of extant 13th-century instruments by which a man makes a suitable provision for his mistress 
and illegitimate children must be limited. There seem to be some grounds for identifying the donor with 
a Philip Pantulf, clerk, who by a covenant dated 23 June 1256 made his peace with the prior of Monks 


JOHN PHILIPOTT, ESQ. 189 


Kirby and terminated a long dispute which had originated in the death of Geoffrey de Craft, husband 
of Maud, Philip’s sister. She had ‘maliciously defamed’ the prior and his men in regard to her husband’s 
death. Philip himself had blamed the prior for his imprisonment at Warwick, which he, by this agree- 
ment, acknowledged was done in accordance with the king’s mandate. Philip’s fidejussores were John 
de Awers, John of Warwick, husband of Isabel Pantulf, and John Rag of Lawford; the first and last of 
whom witness the present charter. The case for the identification seems to be strengthened by the remark- 
able exception contained in the final clause: ‘Nolo tamen quod ego Philippus et fidejussores mei pro 
aliquo peccato carnali cum aliqua parrochiana predicti prioris a me commisso per presentem litteram 
obligatoriam predicto priori obligemur’ (Madox, Formulare, No. 158). Philip’s father was apparently 
the Roger Pantulf who in 1209-10 made an agreement with the abbot of Pipewell as to rights of pasture 
in Long Lawford (ibid., No. 47).

Hawise was dowered in Dodford, and her elder son, Robert, released to her the reversion, whereupon she

Acknowledgement by John of Pattishall of Crawley, Bucks. (Craule), that he has received from Robert 
son and heir of John de Wylleby £20 sterling for which Robert was bound to him by a recognizance in 
chancery in the Easter term 3 Edw. III (1329) payable at Michaelmas next after the date of such recog- 
nizance. A further acknowledgement that he has received from Robert, as son and heir and also executor 
of the said John, a final account of all lands, goods, and chattels which belonged to Walter Langton, 
bishop of Coventry and Lichfield, in the county of Northampton and which by the king’s writ were in 
the custody of the said John de Wylleby when sheriff of the said county. Crawley: 8 July 1329. - 


SEAL: round, 7§ in.; red. Shield of arms, a fess between three crescents [PATTESHULL]; no legend. 


192 JOHN PHILIPOTT, ESQ. 


Walter Langton, bishop of Coventry and Lichfield, treasurer under Edward I, was removed from office 
22 Aug. 1307 by Edward II and on 20 Sept. his lands were taken into the king’s hands. He was not 
restored to office until 14 Mar. 1312. He died 9 Nov. 1321 (DNB). John de Wylleby was sheriff of North- 
ampton 1308-12 (PRO List of Sheriffs). It seems probable that his acknowledgement records the belated 
settlement of the treasurer’s property held by John during the time Langton was out of favour with the 
king. John of Pattishall was the direct descendant of Simon of Pattishall, the judge, of the reigns of 
Richard I and John. Simon was the founder of the family (CP, 2nd ed. x. 311-16).

The grantee was elder brother of the whole blood to the famous William the Marshal, earl of Pembroke. 
_ In the Academy of 9 July 1892 (p. 33) Round deals with the succession to the marshalship at this time. 
John the Marshal the elder, who distinguished himself as a partisan of the empress during the civil war 
of Stephen’s reign, died in 1165 before Michaelmas (PR 11 Hen. II, 56) leaving a son and heir, Gilbert, 
by his first wife. Gilbert died before Michaelmas 1166 (PR 12 Hen. II, 95) and John the younger, the 
eldest son by the second wife, became heir to his father and brother (ibid. 74). The king was in England 
from May 1165 till Mar. 1166. He was at Rouen in Nov. 1166 and there met the archbishop of Rouen 
and the bishop of Lisieux. This seems to be the earliest possible date for the present charter; the latest 
limit is the adoption of the style dei gratia in 1172-3. The witnesses are consistent with these limits, but 
the subject-matter makes the date almost certainly 1166 or 1167. The priory of Notre-Dame du Pré or 
Bonne-Nouvelle, a dependency of the abbey of Le Bec, was situated in the faubourg of Emendreville 
across the Seine from Rouen. The phrase concessisse et reddidisse is also used in the charter of Conan IV, 
duke of Brittany, restoring the constableship of Richmond to Alan son of Roald in 1158 (EYC iv; Rich- 
mond, pt. 1, 48). It would appear to be the correct technical term for the admission to an inherited office 
of this kind.

The latest mention of William the chamberlain of Tancarville is June 1191, when he arrived with other 
crusaders at’ Acre (Landon, Jtin. 50): the earliest mention of Ralf his son and successor seems to be 
16 Sept. 1197 (ibid. 122). The latest limit of date is 1200, in which year William fitzRalf ceased to be 
seneschal of Normandy. The subject-matter of the present charter suggests that it was executed not long 
after Ralf’s succession. For the family of the grantee and the lands involved see the annotation to charter 
No. 107.

The ancestry of Saher de Quincy, first earl of Winchester, is obscure. A Saher de Quincy appears in the 
Northamptonshire Survey (VCH Northants. i. 379) as tenant of Anselm de Chokes at Long Buckby. The 


taste. court-en-Caux. 

2 The contraction is the usual one for er, but the conjunc- 3 There is no stop between clerico and Joh’: the latter has

witness is Robert de Harcourt, a well-known royal official, words also supports this reading. ;

date of the survey is 1124-9, but as interpolations were made later it is uncertain whether this entry belongs 
to the time of Henry I. In 1158 Saher de Quincy was pardoned 25 shillings danegeld in Northamptonshire 
(PR 4 Hen. II, 142). He probably took his name from Cuinchy near Béthune, less than 10 miles from 
Chocques, the original home of his Northamptonshire overlord. At some time after the death of her first 
husband in 1136 Saher married Maud de Senlis, daughter of Simon I, earl of Northampton, and widow 
of Robert fitzRichard of Dunmow. In the register of Daventry priory is a joint charter of the husband 
and wife (Cott. MS. Claudius D xii, f. 5). Maud apparently had Daventry as her marriage portion 
(HKF ii. 395) and a charter of 12 Jan. 1146 is attested by ‘Seerus de Quinci dominus de Daventre’ (Mon. 
v. 182). It ultimately passed to the issue of Maud’s son, Walter fitzRobert, by his second wife, Maud 
de Bohun. No. 145 above is a charter of Maud witnessed first by her son Walter fitzRobert and, almost 
at the end of the witness list, by her son Seher. There is no evidence about the date of her husband 
Saher de Quincy’s death. Possibly the fact that he is not mentioned in No. 145 implies that he was dead 
when the charter was made. If so, he probably died between 1154 and 1166 and the Saher de Quincy, 
who held 1 fees of Robert de Chokes and 14 fees of the new feoffment of Walter fitzRobert, was his son. 
In 1208 Saher de Quincy, earl of Winchester, in a plea as to the advowson of Wimpole, Cambs., said that 
his grandfather, Saher de Quincy, had held it in Henry II’s reign (Cur. Reg. Rolls, v.231). It seems probable 
that the earl was the grandson of the Saher who married Maud de Senlis, although it is possible that 
another generation should be inserted in the pedigree and the earl is referring in 1208 to Maud’s son. 
The grantor of this present charter would seem to be Maud’s son. Geoffrey Pecche was son of Hamo 
Pecche and occurs late in Henry II’s reign (Eyton, Itin. 277; Liber Memorandum ecclesie de Bernewelle, 
ed. J. W. Clark, 47). Roger of Huntingfield is said to have succeeded his father in 1155 and died in 1204 
(CP, 2nd ed. vi. 671). Various lands in Tuddenham are confirmed to Sibton abbey by a charter of Henry II 
in 1163 (Cal. Chart. Rolls, ii. 96). Saher is not mentioned as a donor, and although plots of 20 and 30 acres 
are confirmed, they cannot be certainly identified with those of this deed, an indication that it was made 
after 1163. 

The 30 acres of broken heath were assart, measured, as was customary, by a longer perch than that 
used for ancient ploughland. The purpose of the longer perch was apparently to encourage the bringing 
of new land into cultivation by increasing the size of the acre, the ancient unit of assessment (Maitland, 
Domesday Book and Beyond, 376).

Tedelingham is not shown on the 1-inch Ordnance map, but it appears to have been not far from Budbridge 
in the parish of Arreton, Isle of Wight: see PRO Ancient Deed B 3091. The original gift to Quarr must 
have been early, for it is confirmed in Earl Baldwin’s charter of 1141-4 (Cambridge Hist. Journ. iv. 297). 
The circumstances of Quarr’s loss of Tedelingham to Christchurch do not appear, and it is impossible 
to assign fixed limits of date for the present charter narrower than those of Earl Richard de Revier’s 
tenure of the earldom, but it was doubtless late in that period. The first and second witnesses are the 
grantor’s brothers; the second ultimately succeeded to the earldom.

near Gommerville, Seine-Inférieure, a fief which passed by marriage to the family of Estouteville (CDF, 
No. 212). Robert and his brother Roger appear on the Pipe Roll of 1130 (p. 54) as each owing £50 for 
the lands of their father William; the amount shows William to be recently dead. Robert must have died 
without issue before 1142, when his lands were held by the sons of his brother Roger (Round, G. de M. 
402). Another version of this charter, making the same gift with the same witnesses but with slight 
differences in the formal wording, is printed in Mon. v. 149 as ‘Inter collectanea Jac. Strangeman in bibl. 
Cotton sub effigie Vitelli F. 4’. This second version is also found in Dodsworth MSS. xc, f. 107 v., a copy 
in Dodsworth’s writing professing, apparently, to be taken from BS. Its origin appears to be a bad copy 
of the present charter. See No. 354 below.

No. 282 above. For the early history of the Huntingfield family see CP, 2nd ed. vi. 671 et seq.

Catteshill in Godalming, Surr., was held by the serjeanty of keeping the door of the king’s chamber (see 
Round, The King’s Serjeants, 98-108). Robert of Gatton had married Mabel the eldest of the five daughters 
and coheirs of Stephen of Thornham and Edelina del Brok, the heiress of Catteshill, which on her death 
descended to Mabel. Robert, however, was never in possession, for he was dead at Michaelmas 1219 
(Cur. Reg. Rolls, viii. 24), in which year Edelina is returned as holding it (Fees, 273). There is no trace 
of Nicholas de Wancy having had any hereditary interest in Catteshill, and this quitclaim was probably 
a step in the settlement of the reversion. The witness Hamo of Gatton was Robert’s son and heir, and 
as he is described as a knight the date is probably late in Robert’s life. The hand in which the charter 
is written has the appearance of being considerably later in the 13th century than it actually is.

The earlier history of the land and rights here confirmed can be traced in the Clerkenwell cartulary (Cott. 
MS. Faustina B II) and have been set out in Robinson, History of Tottenham High Cross, 2nd ed. (1840) 
257-9. Between 1136 and 1146 Henry earl of Huntingdon, son of David I of Scotland, gave them to 
Uchtred of London (Cartulary, f. 10 v.). Between 1157 and 1165 King Malcolm gave them to Robert 
son of Sewin, to whom Uchtred’s heirs had quitclaimed them (Cott. Chart. xv. 19). William the Lion, 
probably soon after he had succeeded to the earldom in 1165, confirmed them to Robert, to whom the 
heirs of Uchtred had quitclaimed them. Thereafter Robert gave them to the priory. Since his gift was 
confirmed by William the Lion it is not likely to have been made later than 1174, when he lost the earldom. 
In 1818 the original charter was in the possession of Thomas Astle, F.S.A. (Robinson, loc. cit.). David, 
brother of Kings Malcolm and William the Lion, held the earldom from 1185 to 1216 (CP, 2nd ed. v. 646). 
The present charter is later than No. 200, since Robert de Basingham has succeeded Hugh Ridel as. 
steward. Peter was instituted to the church of Great Paxton about 1185 (Reg. Antiq. Linc., LRS, iii. 159) 
and was living as an old man 1223-7 (ibid. 165). Robert Basset, Simon de Senlis, and William Burdet 
witness a charter of Earl David 1191-4 (ibid. 147). The date of.the present charter seems to lie between 
circa 1188 and circa 1200. Robert son of Sewin held one knight’s fee of Robert de Chokes in 1166 (RB 
334), probably in Rothersthorpe, Northants. (HKF i. 41). From 1155 to 1174 he accounted for the farm 
of Northampton at the exchequer. See also No. 174 and note.

FitzRoscelin was adopted by the grantee as a surname and was so used by his son and heir John. William 
was living in 1230 (PR 14 Hen. III, 354), but dead by Trinity 1230, when his heir John fitzRoscelin was 
suing Lecia, William’s widow, for waste (Bracton’s Note Book, No. 632). In 1206 William le Blund sued 
William fitzRoscelin for the manor of Hainton, Norf. (Cur. Reg. Rolls, iv. 107). There is no evidence 
that the plaintiff was connected with Peter le Blund, but he is probably identical with the first witness. 
Richard of Seething was a royal official and judge who first appears in 1190-1; see No. 405 below. He 
acted as undersheriff for Hubert de Burgh in Herefordshire in 1201. He does not appear later than 1226 
(Foss, Judges of England). For the descent of Seething see HKF iii. 135-7. A list of fitzWalter fees in 
1236 shows that Fulk Baynard and William of Wheatacre were alive, but Robert son of Thomas and 
Walter de Valognes were dead (Fees, 576). Walter was living in 1233 (Excerpta e Rot. Fin. i. 109). Walter 
de Caen and Geoffrey of Loddon occur in 1221 (ibid. i. 73). The earlier limit of date is difficult to fix, 
but the handwriting suggests the middle of the period assigned.

Gilbert de Gant was son of Robert de Gant and nephew of Gilbert de Gant, earl of Lincoln, and inherited 
the Gant honor; an account of him will be found in the CP, 2nd ed. vii. 674. In 1166 David de Armenteres 
(Armere) held 10 fees of the old feoffment of the honor of Gant then in the hands of Earl Simon de Senlis 
(RB 383). Henry de Armenteres, Geoffrey’s father, was living at Michaelmas 1207 (Cur. Reg. Rolls, v. 41), 
but died before Hilary 1214, when his widow Reine was party to an assize of novel disseisin (ibid. vii. 63); 
at Trinity of that year Geoffrey occurs as party to a fine to be made at Michaelmas and was therefore 
of full age (ibid. vii. 218). A document forming part of this transaction was copied by Dodsworth (vol. 
68, f. 3). It shows that the present charter was made earlier, probably by several years, than June 1210. 
See Introduction. A similar case in which Roger earl of Warwick provided a marriage portion for his 
daughter Agnes on her marriage with his undertenant Geoffrey of Glympton the younger by releasing 
the service of 10 knights has been dealt with by Round (Ancestor, xi. 153).

SEAL on cord: round, 2} in.; green; broken on sinister side. Ona chair with animal-head terminals, a seated 


figure wearing robe and mantle, a sword in his right hand; in the field on his right a pig rampant to the 
RIOR LOD ea SS 5 gtk eG DE ANISI REGIS DI[SPENS]JATORIS.1 


From the point of view of the organization of feudal society in England this is one of the most interesting 
charters in the whole book, for it displays the composition of the honorial court and sets it in motion 
before our eyes. The witnesses to the charter were the members of the court and the surrender and regrant 
were made, the charter records, with the counsel of the grantor’s friends and peers (see Stenton, English 
Feudalism, 58-60). The land was the grantor’s own acquisition de acato meo. A man had a better right 
as against his expectant heir to alienate land he had himself acquired than that which had come to him 
by inheritance (see Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law, 2nd ed. ii. 308). The surrender to 
the lord who thereupon regrants to the man to whom the tenant wishes to give or sell the land was a means 
of avoiding a sub-tenancy. The grantee became the immediate tenant of the chief lord of the fee. In the 
carta of John de Port, son and heir of the Henry de Port of this charter, Richard de Anesia is returned 


1 The letters in square brackets are inserted in the drawing in pencil. 


208 SIR WILLIAM LE NEVE 


as holding one fee of the old feoffment (RB 208). He must be the grantee of this charter, or his successor. 
The elder line was at that time represented by William de Anesye, who occurs on the Pipe Roll under 
Wiltshire in 1165 and 1167 (PR 11 Hen. II, 59 and 13 Hen. II, 131). William de Anesye, the grantor 
of this charter, describes himself on his seal as regis dispensator. Among the Wiltshire serjeanties in 1198 
is the entry ‘Willelmus de Anesya iij carucatas et valent vj li.’ (Fees, 12). The Wiltshire list in the returns 
to the 1212 inquest records ‘Willelmus de Anesy iiij hidas per serjanteriam dispensatoris larderii’ (RB 
486). The despenser serjeanty is carried back to Henry I’s reign by the seal of the grantor of this charter. 
The subsequent history of the knight’s fee here granted raises a curious problem, for it looks as if the 
mesne tenancy, so laboriously prevented when this present charter was made, ultimately came into being. 
The returns of 1242-3 record that Robert de Anesya holds one fee in Sherfield of the old feoffment of 
Richard de Anesya, who holds of the chief lord who holds of the king (Fees, 694). There seems to have 
been no other Anesya tenure of Port save this one fee. The intermediate tenant, Richard de Anesya, of 
the 1242-3 return is the representative of the elder line. He occurs under Wiltshire in 1236 as holding 43 
hides by serjeanty (Fees, 586). 

The limits of date are not easy to determine. The fact that the fee is described as of the old enfeoffment 
in 1166 suggests that the charter was made before 1135.. It is, however, most likely that in 1166, the date 
of the original enfeoffment of William de Anesye by his lord was regarded as marking the creation of this 
fee rather than the present charter. A comparison of the witnesses with those of a charter of Henry de Port 
printed by Mr. Salter (Oxford Charters, No. 14) and dated by him 1120-30 suggests that the two charters 
are not very far separated in time. The present charter seems a little the later of the two, for the sons 
of Roger de Scures and Henry de Breiboue witness with their fathers. The period 1120-40 is therefore 
tentatively suggested.

SIR WILLIAM LE NEVE 209 


established, the view put forward that Bernard I was immediately succeeded by his fourth son, Bernard II, 
seems to require reconsideration. The last certain date in the life of Bernard I is 27 Apr. 1147, when at 
Paris in the presence of Pope Eugenius III he granted land near Hitchin to the Templars with the consent 
of his eldest son Ingelram (Lees, Records of the Templars, 213). There is no evidence that Ingelram 
succeeded his father and if, as is likely, he predeceased him the death of Bernard I probably occurred 
some little time after 1147. By a charter dated 1171 Bernard de Baliol II confirmed to the abbey of Selin- 
court the gifts of his father Bernard and his brother Eustace (Cartulaire, No. 112, printed Mém. Soc. 
antiq. de Picardie, x\. 189); this shows Eustace to have succeeded his father in the French lands and 
himself to have been succeeded by his brother. Turning to England Guy de Baliol confirmed to St. Mary’s 
abbey, York, the church of Gainford which his father Bernard had previously confirmed, and thereafter 


_ Bernard II also confirmed (EYC i, No. 561 n.). Again by a charter which Farrer dates circa 1150-5 Adam of 


Ingleby gave the mill of Ingleby to Whitby abbey (ibid. i, No. 569); this gift was confirmed by Guy de Baliol 
by a charter of about the same date (No. 570), and subsequently Bernard II confirmed it for the souls of 
his father and mother and of his brother Guy (No. 571). Here there seems an equally clear succession 
by Guy to Bernard I, and by Bernard II to Guy. Whether Guy and Eustace each in turn held both the 
English and French lands, or whether there was a partition, Guy taking the English and Eustace the 
French, may be doubtful, but Bernard II ultimately succeeded to both and was already in possession 
of the English lands in 1162 when the sheriff of Yorkshire made a render of £20 for his scutage (PR 
& Hen. IT, 52). 

The present charter states that Gerold de Dumart and his father should have held land overseas of the 
grantor, and this enables us to trace the family to Dumart-en-Pontieu (dep. Somme, arr. Doullens); a 
Bernard de Domno Medardo is mentioned as a donor in a charter of Guy I, count of Ponthieu, of 6 Oct. 
1100 (Brunel, Recueil des actes des comtes de Pontieu, 13). The subsequent devolution of Faxton has 
been exhaustively treated by Mr. Baker-Cresswell and Dr. Craster in a paper on the manor of Ellington 
in Northumberland (Archaeologia Aeliana, 4th ser. v. 1). It should be noted that the manor of Faxton 
included lands in Walgrave, Moulton, and Mawsley (Fees 941; Stenton, English Feudalism, 158). The 
kinship between Baliol and Dumart referred to in the present charter was through Gerold’s mother, since 
his brother and successor Ingelram de Dumart refers to a certain Walter de Baliol as his avunculus in 
a charter printed by Sir Frank Stenton (op. cit. 275), but Walter’s place in the Baliol pedigree has not 
been determined; see further Rot. de Dominabus, PRS, v. 23 and n. Since both Bernard de Baliol I and 
his eldest son Ingelram are alive this charter cannot be much later than 1150; on the other hand, it can 
hardly be much earlier since Gerold’s sister Emma lived till 1211 (Arch. Aeliana, loc. cit. 3).

For Walter fitzRobert, the ancestor of the fitzWalters, see CP, 2nd ed. v. 472 n. The evidence of date 
is somewhat scanty since Walter succeeded his father in 1136 and lived till 1198, and though he was twice 
married both his wives were named Maud. An Ernisius Ruffus occurs in Essex in 1162 (PR 8 Hen. IT, 70), 
and at Michaelmas 1165 Jordan nephew of Gervase of Cornhill owed £100 for marrying the widow of 
Ernisius Ruffus without licence (PR 11 Hen. II, 33). The witness Odo of Cockfield held one knight’s fee 
of Walter fitzRobert in 1166 (RB 348), and no other man of that name seems to occur. Roger son of 
William of Huntingfield would have been of an age to witness charters in the early years of Henry II’s 
reign (see No. 355 below). No holding of one-fortieth of a knight’s fee is included in Walter’s return 
of 1166, but in 1236 Robert de Hauville held that amount of Robert fitzWalter in Ubbeston (Fees, 577).

This charter by no means represents a simple gift. In the Public Record Office there is a charter by which 
Richard son of Simon with the advice and assent of Agnes his wife gives to William son of Adam Agnel 
for his homage and service the virgate which Ralf son of Emma held in Hemel Hempstead and which 
Richard had bought of Gilbert son of William Stiward; rendering therefor 2 shillings yearly to Gilbert 
and doing the service due to the court of Hemel Hempstead (Ancient Deed C 1933; Cat. ii. 464). By 
another charter Henry son of Geoffrey son of Simon quitclaims the same virgate to William Aignel, as 
the charter of Richard son of Simon, his uncle, and the confirmation of Geoffrey son of Simon, his father, 
witness; he also quitclaims the assart which his uncle Richard had held; for this William gave Henry

12 shillings (Ancient Deed C 3918; Cat. vi. 19). Some witnesses are common to all three charters. No 
charter dealing with the remaining parcel of a messuage, six acres, and three roods has been traced. The 
present charter would seem to be in effect a confirmation and consolidation by the chief lord of the several 
holdings which the grantee had acquired. It may be noted that Agnell’s Farm still exists in Hemel Hemp- 
stead (PNS Hertfordshire, 42). The limits of date assigned are those of Geoffrey fitzPeter’s tenure of

Hubert de Rye gave 10 carucates of land in Aslackby to the Templars before 1185 (Records of the Templars, 
96). In the Easter term 1201 John Marshal and Geoffrey of Chester, who had married the daughters and 
coheirs of Hubert de Rye, entered into a judicial agreement with the Templars whereby the latter acknow- 
ledged their hereditary right to Aslackby (Cur. Reg. Rolls, i. 439). Geoffrey died in 1206 and his widow 
married Roger de Cressy (HKF iii. 279). The present charter must be later than the agreement of 1201, 
to which it refers: Alexander of Pointon was already holding land in Graby at the close of the 12th century 
(Danelaw Charters, No. 467) and that being so, a confirmation such as this is not likely to have been long 
delayed after John Marshal had recovered seisin.

William de Braiose, lord of Bramber and Gower, died shortly before 1 May 1326, leaving two daughters 

and coheirs, Alina, wife of John de Mowbray, and Joan, who married firstly James de Bohun of Midhurst 

and secondly Sir Richard Foliot of Gressenhall (CP, 2nd ed. ii. 302-4). After the death of her first husband 
5172 Ff 


Ly 


218 SIR WILLIAM LE NEVE 


John de Mowbray, executed on 23 Mar. 1322 after the battle of Boroughbridge, Alina married Sir Richard 
de Peshale; her son John de Mowbray succeeded to Gower. Humphrey de Bohun, earl of Hereford and 
Essex, was slain at Boroughbridge 16 Mar. 1322. He was grandson of Humphrey de Bohun (d. 1265) 
by Eleanor daughter and coheir of William de Braiose of Brecknock, lord of Abergavenny (ibid. vi. 462), 
which William was first cousin of the present grantor’s grandfather, John de Braiose of Bramber and 
Gower, both being grandsons of William de Braiose (d. 1211), lord of Bramber and Brecknock, and his 
wife Maud de St. Valery. The remainder over in default of issue of John and Alina was therefore to 
a very distant relation to the exclusion of the issue of Joan, the younger daughter, and her. husband James 
de Bohun of the line of Midhurst. William de Braiose was still in possession of Gower in Aug. 1318, for 
on 3 Aug. there is a royal mandate to Hugh le Despenser to keep the peace in the dissension which had 
arisen between him and his men of Glamorgan and William de Braiose and his men of Gower (Cal. Close 
Rolls, Edw. II, iii. 96); this charter, however, is earlier than 26 Oct. 1320, when the escheator was ordered 
to take into the king’s hand the land of Gower which William de Braiose gave to John de Mowbray with- 
out the king’s licence (ibid. 268). The present charter was cited in a plea between Thomas de Beauchamp, 
earl of Warwick, and John de Mowbray in 1353 (Clark, Glamorgan Charters, iv. 1392). For John 
de Mowbray see DNB.

The family of Avranches inherited through females the barony of William of Arques, the Domesday lord 
of Folkestone (Stapleton in Archaeologia, xxxi. 216 et seq.; Round, Geoffrey de Mandeville, 397). Simon 
d’Avranches, the father of William the grantor, was living at Michaelmas 1202, when he made a payment 
on account of scutage on 214 knights’ fees (PR 4 John, 217); but was dead at Michaelmas 1203, when 
Cecily his widow owed 100 marks and 2 palfreys not to be compelled to marry (PR 5 John, 27). Cecily 
was still living and unmarried in 1219 (Fees, 275). The witnesses suggest this charter to have been executed 
in William’s court at Moreton, Ess. Northeye has not been identified; the fact that the prior of Blackmore, 
a small Essex house, held land in it points to that county. There was a Northeye in Belchamp Walter, 
now represented by Northey’s Farm, but no evidence has been found to connect the Avranches family 
with it.

The donor belonged to a family originating at Craon in Anjou. Guy de Craon was a considerable Lincoln- 
shire tenant-in-chief in 1086 and was succeeded by Alan, apparently his son; Alan’s son, Maurice de Craon, 
was the father of the donor (BM Facsimiles, No. 45: Mon. iv. 125 et seq.). Maurice died in 1188 and was 
succeeded by this Guy (PR 34 Hen. II, 25, 81), who was living in 1196 (PR 8 Ric. I, 232); thereafter 
although sums due from him continue to be entered on the rolls up to at least 1203, a suit of the Michael- 
mas term 1201 shows him to be then dead (Cur. Reg. Rolls, ii. 13), and since William son of Henry 
de Longchamp who married Parnel, Guy’s daughter and heir, owed 300 marks in 1197 for having his 
land in Lincolnshire of which the king had disseised him (PR 9 Ric. I, 114; 10 Ric. I, 62), he seems to have 
died in 1196-7. Vivian was succeeded in this land by Peter the Angevin, possibly the witness, who in 
1212 was holding a ninth of a fee in Burton of the fee of Craon (Fees, 179). It so happens that exactly 
contemporary with Guy’s father, Maurice, was another Maurice de Craon of the Angevin line, lord of 
Craon itself (Bertrand de Broussillon, La Maison de Craon, i. 71 et seq.): this has been the source of a 
confusion which numbers among its victims the editors of BM Facsimiles and Léopold Delisle (Receuil 
des actes de Henri I, Introduction, 405).

SEAL On tag: green; fragmentary. The Virgin seated. Cf. BM 2884 


Roger of Huntingfield was the son and heir of William of Huntingfield, who had founded the priory of 
Mendham as a cell of Castle Acre about the middle of the 12th century. This charter though in form a 
grant by the prior of Castle Acre is in substance the record of an agreement between the mother house 
and the patron. The land of Mendham was temporarily lost to the family during Henry II’s reign. The 
Pipe Rolls show Stephen de Sackville holding it as terrae datae from 1172 to 1181. Thereafter it seems 
to have been in the king’s hand and in 1191 it was tallaged along with the royal demesne (PR 3 Ric. I, 41). 
Roger did not recover it till 1198-9, for on the Pipe Roll of 1 John (p. 72) he accounted for 200 marks 
for it. The present charter is subsequent to his recovery of Mendham, for its witnesses are identical with 
those to a charter printed in the Mon. v. 58, No. iv, in which he gives land in Mendham to the priory. 
On the other hand, Hugh had ceased to be prior of Castle Acre by 1203 (VCH Norfolk, ii. 358). Robert 
son of Roscelin witnessed No. 355 in the middle of the 12th century.

In addition to this Le Neve charter there is another original charter, Harl. Chart. 54 D 15, also sealed, 
printed in Mon. iv. 45. It follows the Le Neve charter practically word for word with two exceptions: 
(1) a clause is added by which the abbot and convent give the countess the benefit of their prayers, &c., 
according to the tenor of their charter which she has; (2) the witnesses differ materially and run as follows: 
‘domino Rogero de Mortuomari . et magistro Ricardo de Stanes . magistro Radulfo de Fremingeham . 
domino Radulfo de Hengeham justic’ . dominis Adam Gurdun . Grimbaldo Paunceuot . Ricardo Sturmy . 
Rolando de Erle . Johanne de Thedmers . Thoma Dauuers . Oliuero Punchardun . Bartholomeo de 
Tatingeden’ militibus . Thoma Hurschal . Nigello de Saundreuile . et multis (sic)’. It is endorsed ‘Carta 
domine Ele comitisse de Warewyck de marisco de Suthwode in insula de Ely’. It is evident that the 
Harleian charter was later than the Le Neve charter and superseded it, but the fact that seven witnesses 
are common to both suggests that they are practically contemporaneous. Ela was a daughter of William 
Longespée, earl of Salisbury, by Ela daughter of William earl of Salisbury (see No. 62); she married first 
Thomas earl of Warwick, who died in 1242, and secondly Philip Basset, the justiciar, who died in Oct. 
1271; she herself died 6 Feb. 1297 and was buried at Osney priory, Oxon. Ralf de Hengham, a witness 
to the Harleian charter, was appointed a judge in 1270 and was dismissed in 1289 or 1290, not being 
restored to office till 1301. The date therefore of the Harleian charter, and consequently of the Le Neve 


' Cf. the seal to No. 370 below. 


SIR WILLIAM LE NEVE 227 


charter, must lie between the death of Philip Basset in 1271 and the dismissal of Hengham in 1290. These 
limits can, however, be narrowed, for as stated above, the Harleian charter refers to a charter of the abbot 
and convent already in the possession of the countess by which they bind themselves to give the countess 
the benefit of their prayers, &c. This charter is now Add. Chart. 19633 and is dated 30 Dec. 1284; it 
refers to certain rents bestowed by her but not to the present gifts, which therefore are subsequent to it, 
as indeed the language of the Harleian charter seems to imply.

Manasser de Dammartin was the son and heir of Odo de Dammartin, who was enfeoffed of Mendlesham, 
Suff., by Henry I (Fees, 138; RB 409). Manasser died between Michaelmas 1178 and Michaelmas 1179 
(PR 24 Hen. II, 36; 25 Hen. II, 9) and was succeeded by his son Bartholomew who was dead without 
issue in 1190 and succeeded by his brother William (Cur. Reg. Rolls, vi. 21; PR 2 Ric. I, 102). William 
died in 1195, for at Michaelmas the sheriffs accounted for the farm of Mendlesham for a quarter of the 
year and for the farm of Norton Mandeville, Ess., also held by William, for part of the year (PR 7 Ric. I, 
51-2). He was succeeded by his daughter Galiena, for whom see No. 409. Baleshangre is now lost. 
A family of Cordebeof held land by serjeanty in Mendlesham (Fees, 138) and the grove of John Cordebeof 
probably lay in that village. Cotton is the next village on the north-west and Braiseworth lies between 
4 and 5 miles to the north-east of Mendlesham. The minster is presumably Mendlesham church.

A Richard son of Peter le Brun is recorded as having given land at Dullingham to the priory of St. Mary 
of Thetford, but no date is given (Mon. v. 143). The priory of St. Sepulchre of Thetford was founded 
before 1147 (see No. 416 below). The first known prior is Richard in 1202. A Gilbert occurs as prior 
between this Richard and another Richard in 1228 (VCH Norfolk, ii. 393). The formulas of this charter 
suggest a much earlier date than this. The hand of the few words in facsimile, the * at the beginning, 
the low price of the palfrey, the attestation in the nominative case of God and St. Mary and the chapter 
of Thetford, all strongly suggest a date near the middle of the 12th century.

1189, and since he is not here described as earl the date must lie between the date of his father’s death 
and that of his accession to the earldom.

SEAL on tag: round, 14 in.; green. Shield of arms, a saltire on a chief a lion passant; a wyvern on either 
side of the shield; « S’.. ROBERTI . DA BRVS COMITIS DE CARRIR. 


The grantor was son and heir of Robert de Bruce, lord of Annandale, the competitor for the throne of 
Scotland. In 1271 he married Margaret suo iure countess of Carrick, thereby becoming earl; in 1292 he 
resigned the earldom in favour of his eldest son Robert, afterwards king of Scotland, but is said to have 
continued to be styled earl; his father, the lord of Annandale, died 1 Apr. 1295 (CP, 2nd ed., iii. 55—6). 
It is impossible with any certainty to narrow the limits of date to less than his accession to the earldom 
and his own death.

within the last ten years of the 12th century.

SIR WILLIAM LE NEVE 239 


The donor was the son of Simon de Senlis II, earl of Northampton or Huntingdon. The evidence suggests 
that in the 12th century these two territorial styles were alternatives for the same earldom. The lands seem 
usually to have been described collectively as the honor of Huntingdon, but it is to be noted that the caput 
of the honor was at Fotheringhay and that the court of the honor was usually held at Earl’s Barton, both 
of which are in Northamptonshire: furthermore, the exhaustive account of the fees of the honor by Farrer 
(HKF ii. 294-416) shows that the greater amount of the lands lay in Northamptonshire. For the complicated 
devolution of the earldom alternating between the family of Senlis and the royal house of Scotland, who 
descended respectively from the first and second marriages of Maud, the daughter of Waltheof and the 
countess Judith, see CP, 2nd ed. vi. 638-47. The Senlis earls are generally styled simply ‘comes Simon’, 
but when they use a territorial style it is almost invariably that of Northampton; with the Scottish earls, 
on the other hand, it is Huntingdon in the few instances where a territorial style is used. On his father’s 
death in 1153 the donor was a minor and did not obtain the honor till 1174, the lands and earldom till 
then being held by the Scottish line. In 1156 he married Alice, daughter and heir of Gilbert de Gant, 
earl of Lincoln (Robert de Torigny, ed. R. Hewlett, 189), thus obtaining possession of those lands in right 
of his wife; for the fees in 1166 see RB 381-4. It should be noted, however, that during that period he was 
styled “comes Simon’ (see e.g. PR 1] Hen. II, 49). The donee can be identified by means of a charter of Earl 
Simon for St. Peter’s hospital, York (EYC ii, No. 1186), among the witnesses to which are ‘ Willelmo filio 
Walteri, Roberto filio ejus de Wella’. The father, William son of Walter, held one-fifth of a knight’s fee of 
Earl Simon as of the honor of Gant in 1166 (RB 382). In 1242-3 his descendant, another Robert of Well, 
held more than three knights’ fees and a half in Well and other places of the honor of Gant (Fees, 1058). 
Little Paxton, on the other hand, formed part of the honor of Huntingdon, and the date of the present 
charter therefore falls between 1174, when Earl Simon obtained that honor, and his death in 1184. The 
witness William Mauduit, the king’s chamberlain, had married the earl’s sister Isabel (Ancestor, v. 210).

Wollaston was a member of the honor of Chokes, and an account of it will be found in HKF i. 39-41. 
In 1166 Roger de Neufbourg held two fees of Chokes (RB 334); this family had held Winfrith Newburgh, 
Dors., by chamberlain serjeanty since the days of Henry I (Round, King’s Serjeants, 123), and must not 
be confused with the Norman house of that name which was a younger branch of the family of the earls 
of Warwick. The present charter records that this Roger, or a successor of the same name, gave the mill 
of Wollaston to Peter son of Adam, but the precise nature of the interest of the Neufbourgs in Wollaston 
is not clear; in 1208 William de Béthune sued Robert de Neufbourg for the manor on the ground that 


SIR WILLIAM LE NEVE 241 


he held it under a mortgage which he, William, was willing to repay (Cur. Reg. Rolls, v. 233), and the 
plaintiff seems to have recovered possession. The origin of the claims of the family of Béthune on the 
honor of Chokes is obscure and has been dealt with by Farrer (HKFi. 22-6). In 1194 William de Béthune, 
advocate of Arras, succeeded to these claims (see note to No. 131 above), but apparently failed to make 
them effective. On the Pipe Roll of 1 John we find the sheriff accounting for the tallage of the men of 
Wollaston (p. 17) and William de ‘Mallium’ accounts for the farm of Wollaston (p. 20); no such entries 
appear on the previous or succeeding rolls. In 1199 therefore Wollaston was in the king’s hand and its 
custody committed to William de Mauleon, a Poitevin follower of Richard I. This state of affairs is 
consistent with the terms of the present charter and fixes its date. 

The grantee, Peter son of Adam of Northampton, was the founder of the ‘hospital of the Holy Trinity- 
without Northampton in the parish of Kingsthorpe. He died in 1200 during the process of the foundation 
of the hospital which was completed by his son Henry (Mon. v. 193). William de Béthune had confirmed 
the mill to Peter (PRO Ancient Deed C 1897); for the reasons given in the note to No. 131 above it is 
unlikely that William was actually in possession of Wollaston at so early a date, and this confirmation 
was probably obtained as a precaution. The mill was given to the hospital by either Peter or his son 
Henry; the instrument is not forthcoming but early in the 13th century the hospital took the precaution 
of obtaining a confirmation from Robert de Neuf bourg, son of Roger de Neuf bourg (PRO Ancient 
Deed C 1909).

This charter should be compared with the charter of Robert de Rames, No. 291 above, on which the present 
charter is obviously modelled. Yet a third charter to the same effect must have existed, since Henry II 
by a charter, which having passed at Thetford and being witnessed by Thomas Becket as chancellor cannot 
be later than 1158, confirmed to the priory, ‘ex dono Willelmi filii Eadmundi ecclesiam de Minori Brisset 
cum omnibus pertinentiis suis et cum duodecim acris terre de dominio eiusdem uille’ (Mon. v. 151). 
Though in form a gift the present charter would appear to be really a confirmation: there does not seem 
to be sufficient evidence to determine whether the original donor was Robert de Rames or William son 
of Eadmund. John of Tuddenham occurs under Suffolk in 1191 and 1197 (PR 3 Ric. I, 47, 9 Ric. I, 247).

The early history of the Cluniac priory of Mendham, a cell of Castle Acre, is obscure. It was founded 
by William of Huntingfield, the present grantor, either towards the end of the reign of Stephen or early 
in that of Henry II. The foundation charter is printed in the Mon. (v. 58, No. 1) from the Castle Acre 
cartulary, and the present charter appears to be only slightly later. It seems to be an amplification of the 
original endowment, and appears to attempt to make provision for building a stone church. The founder 
married Sybil daughter of Roger de Gigny, with whom he obtained Harlton, Cambs., held of the honor 
of Giffard. She was living in 1185, aged 70 and more (Rot. de Dominabus, PRS, 85). In the return of 
knights’ fees of the honor of Giffard in 1166 is the entry, ‘Filius Willelmi filii Rogeri j militis’ (RB 312). 
Assuming, as is extremely probable, that Farrer (Feudal Cambridgeshire, 256) is correct in identifying this 
entry with the Huntingfield fee in Harlton, William was dead in 1166; on the other hand, the present 
charter was made with the consent of his son Roger, who lived until 1204. A charter of William for 
Kirkstead abbey is printed in Stenton, Danelaw Charters, No. 157, and from a confirmation (ibid., No. 158) 
we learn that he was a kinsman of Maurice de Craon. No. 292 above is a charter of his son Roger for 
Mendham. The spelling ‘Rorbert’ for ‘Robert’ must be a transcriber’s error for ‘Rotbert’. The name 
of the last witness is thus correctly spelt. ‘Benedicto sacerdoti’ and ‘Macharii’ are so written.

For a pedigree of Burnel see Eyton, Shropshire, vi. 134; see also CP, 2nd ed. ii. 434 et seq. Edward 
Burnel was the son and heir of Philip Burnel, who was nephew and heir of Robert Burnel, Edward I’s 
chancellor; he died s.p. shortly before 1 Sept. 1315 (Cal. Ing. p.m. v, No. 611). Maud was Edward’s sister 
and heir; she married firstly John Lovel of Titchmarsh, who died 24 June 1314 and by whom she had 
a son and heir John Lovel; and secondly John de Haudlo (CP viii. 217 and vi. 400). Aliva was daughter 
of Hugh le Despenser of Loughborough and sister of Hugh le Despenser ‘the elder’, created earl of 
Winchester in 1322 (ibid. iv. 262-6). Although the eventual heir was John Lovel, Maud’s son by her first 
husband, the bulk of the Burnel lands passed to Nicholas, her son by John de Haudlo, who assumed the 
name of Burnel and was summoned to Parliament as Lord Burnel (ibid. ii. 435), Bedhampton belonged

About the year 1160 William de Lisewis founded at Normansburgh in South Rainham, Norf., a small 
religious house for canons; the evidence available is insufficient to show whether the foundation was 
regular or secular, but at this period secular corporations were not being founded with any frequency 
and it was probably Augustinian. The house must have languished and possibly died out, for Geoffrey 


. 2 ° 
1 ¢ interlined. Sic. 


246 SIR WILLIAM LE NEVE 


de Lisewis, the founder’s son, transferred it to Castle Acre priory, whereupon it became Cluniac, and if 
any canons survived they were displaced by monks. This was not earlier than 1186, since Geoffrey’s 
charter (Mon. v. 69) is witnessed by William prior of Lewes, a successor of Hugh who resigned in that 
year (VCH Sussex, ii. 70). The transfer is confirmed by John bishop of Norwich in a charter (Mon. v. 70) 
witnessed by master Reiner, almost certainly the Reiner who became an archdeacon probably circa 1187 
and who had ceased to be an archdeacon by 1195 (see ‘Early Archdeacons of Norwich Diocese’, in Proc. 
of Suffolk Institute of Archaeology &c., xx. 25). On the whole the transfer may with reasonable safety 
be placed between 1186 and 1189. The gift of the mill and land in Tittleshall here confirmed was originally 
made by Michael Capra and William his son and heir to Stephen the canon of Normansburgh and his 
brethren (Add. Chart. 24307). Michael held 4 knights’ fees of Walter fitzRobert in 1166 (RB 347) and in 
1236 Hamo Chevre held 2 fees in Tittleshall and Wixoe of Walter’s successor (Fees, 577). Geoffrey must 
be a younger son of Michael and the William Capra who witnesses and confirms this charter Michael’s 
son and heir. The date must be later than the death of Michael and earlier than circa 1189, by which 
time the house had been transferred to Castle Acre.

SEAL on tag: round, central portion only; green. An eagle displayed. 


It is impossible to determine the donor’s place in the Valognes pedigree. David of Flitwick was holding 
half a knight’s fee in Harlow of Margery de Reviers circa 1236 (Fees, 608). Since between 1200 and 1311 
four successive members of the family were called David, this is not much use for dating purposes, although 
it seems probable that he is the second David who died in 1247 (BHRS x. 272). Richard de Canne takes 
his name from Great Canney and was living in 1224 (EPNS' Essex, 221). The formulas suggest a date 
in the latter part of the first half of the century. The manor of Weld or.Sewells in Harlow was written 
Walda in medieval records (Morant, Essex, ii. 485).

The donor is the Walter of Clifford who married Agnes daughter and heir of Roger de Condet and who

charter was confirmed by Henry III on 20 Aug. 1227 (Cal. Chart. Rolls, i. 58).

Letter of Joan de Mortemer, countess of March. Whereas Thomas de Breouse, son of Peter de Breouse, 
is bound to her by a recognizance in chancery to pay 3,000 marks at Michaelmas next coming, Joan 
grants for herself, her heirs, and executors that if the said Thomas take money or other castles in settle- 
ment of the dispute between Thomas, son of the king of England Earl Marshal, of the one part, and Beatrice, 
Joan’s daughter, of the other as to the manors of Bosham and its members, Suss., Hinton Waldrist, Berks., 
(Henton), and Ascot and Deddington, Oxon. (Dadington’), and if the money so received, together with 
money to the value of other castles received on the same account, be deposited in a fitting place agreed 
on by Thomas de Breouse and by Joan, or friends appointed by her, to remain so deposited until Thomas 
with the said money purchase within three years of its receipt lands and tenements, fiefs and advowsons 
to him and the said Beatrice and the heirs of their bodies with remainder in default of such heirs to the 
right heirs of Beatrice, then the said recognizance for 3,000 marks shall be void and of none effect. She 
further grants that the force (execucion) of the said recognizance shall cease if Thomas shall have received 
in whole or in part the money on the account aforesaid, provided that he shall not be found guilty of 
default or slackness (Jachesse) in his attempt to recover the aforesaid manors, or other lands and tenements, 
fiefs or advowsons, or money or other castles equivalent to the said manors by the judgement and assent 
of Joan or her friends, appointed by her thereto. Sealing clause. ‘Ay ceux tesmoignes Mons’ Johan 
de Breouse Mons’ Thomas de Blauncfrount . Mons’ Rauf Bygot Sir Michel de Wach Sire Johan de Seynt 
Poul . Willem’ Skot sergaunt . Johan de Bray de Middelsex et plusours austres.’ Grays Thurrock, Ess.: 
9 Aug. 1334. 


SEAL on tag: round, c. 14 in.; red; chipped. Within a cusped and pointed panel a shield of arms, barry 
a chief paly and corners gyronny, an escutcheon [MorTIMER], dimidiated by three brays in pale, on a chief 
a demi-lion rampant issuant [JOINVILLE]. 


Joan daughter of Peter de Joinville of Ludlow (CP, 2nd ed. v. 634) married Roger de Mortimer, earl 
of March, hanged in 1330 (ibid. viii. 441); their daughter Beatrice married Edward, son and heir apparent 
of Thomas of Brotherton, earl of Norfolk and Marshal, fifth son of Edward I (ibid. ix. 599). Beatrice 
married as her second husband Thomas de Braiose (ibid. ii. 308). At his death in 1361 Thomas de Braiose 
was holding the manor of Bosham in right of his wife Beatrice who had it for life by the gift of Thomas 
of Brotherton (Cal. Ing. p.m. xi, No. 38); such gift must have been a term in the settlement of the dispute 
mentioned in this instrument. It is clear that the marriage of Thomas and Beatrice was shortly to take 
place, and this fixes its approximate date; it follows that Edward, Beatrice’s first husband, must have died 
not later than the first half of 1334.

cum omnibus pertinentiis . in villa in pratis in pascuis in in* campis . in viis in semitis 
et in omnibus libertatibus eidem terre pertinentibus. Tenendas de me et heredibus 
meis ille et heredes sui libere et quiete pacifice et honorifice ab omni seruicio excepto 
forinseco seruicio domini regis reddendo inde annuatim mihi et heredibus meis ille et 
heredes sui xij denarios scilicet ad Pascha. Hiis testibus . Willelmo sacerdote de 
Milton’ Ricardo de Leonibus . Jordano de Curcy . Ricardo Chaudel . Godardo 
Ricardo filio Roberti Jordario de Harewod’ . Radulfo Passelewe Henrico de Gatwod’ 
Radulfo de Longauilla . Ada camerario . Traci. Philippo Chaudel . Oseberto de Hunet .

SEAL on cord: round, 28 in.; brown; chipped at side. A boar to the sinister; scrolled background; 
i SIGIULUVM IORANNI.... CVRCI 

Besides the manor which gave Middleton its surname Cheney there was a Curcy holding in that village. 
The Northamptonshire Survey temp. Henry I records, ‘In Middleton William Meschin i hide and a half 
and one small virgate of the fee of William de Curcy’ (VCH Northants. i. 368). Round (Feudal England, 
222) points out that this entry is misleading, since William Meschin was the tenant in Henry I’s reign and 
his barony was held by his grandson William de Courcy in Henry II’s reign. At Michaelmas 1201 the 
sheriff accounted for £4 the farm of Middleton, the land of John de Courcy (PR 3 John, 187); in 1202 
the render was for the full year (PR 4 John, 152). This identifies John de Curcy with the conqueror of 
Ulster who fell into disgrace with the king in 1201 (Orpen, The Normans in Ireland, ii. 136); this being so, 
the witness Jordan de Curcy can be identified with John’s brother who was slain in Ireland in 1197 (ibid. 
ii. 134). The witness Richard de Leonibus occurs on the Northamptonshire Assize Roll of 1202 (VRS, 
v, No. 598). No definite evidence is forthcoming for the earlier limit of date. The identity of Midilton 
with Middleton Cheney seems certain. Baker (Hist. of Northamptonshire, i. 650) cites a charter in the 
Canons Ashby priory cartulary by which John de Curcy gave a virgate in Middleton to that house: at 
the Dissolution the priory possessed a rent of 13s. 4d. from land in Myddleton Chaynay (on. vi, pt. i. 444). 
Baker (loc. cit.) cites this charter from the ‘Hatton Portfolio of Deeds’, but does not give the number. 
No. 270 was made at Middleton Cheney 14 May 1310. One of the witnesses is William le Bruton of 
Middleton, doubtless a later member of the grantee’s family.

The hand of the few words in facsimile, the absence of a warranty clause, the spelling of Netheravon, 
the type of seal, and the way it was attached, all suggest a date early in the 13th century. Richard of 
Coombe had been succeeded by Simon of Coombe by 1220, when he sued Thomas Makerel for a mill 
in Fittleton which John of Coombe, Simon’s grandfather, had mortgaged to him for a term which had 
expired (Excerpta e Rot. Fin. i. 46). Simon was holding Fittleton in 1235 (Fees, 423). The seal on the 
present charter shows that Richard’s father was John, presumably the John of Coombe, Simon’s grand- 
father, mentioned in 1220. See No. 378 below.
