For the Marines family see VCH Herts. iii. 400. The grantor’s father, Werric, first occurs on the Pipe 
Roll in 1194 (PR 6 Ric. I, 38). In 1196 he was sheriff of Cambs. and Hunts. He was succeeded by his 
son Hugh, who in 1217 recovered his lands in Gloucs., Ess., and Herts. taken into the king’s hands 
(Rot. Lit. Claus. i. 326 b). He was living in 1230, when he was in debt to the Jews (PR 14 Hen. III, 148). 
Among the Ancient Deeds in the PRO are many relating to Westmill and the Marines family. William 
son of Benedict, a London citizen and moneylender, last occurs in 1235 (Close Rolls 1234-37, 84). The 
reference to a quit-rent is a very early one and should be compared with the quit-rent in Surrey, which 
was the subject of a suit in 1222 in which William son of Benedict was plaintiff (Bracton’s Note Book, 126). 
Hugh de Marines mortgaged land in Westmill to Thomas de Neville, chancellor of Lichfield, for 10 years 
from the Purification next after the consecration of Eustace de Fauconberg, bishop of London, i.e. from 
2 Feb. 1222, Thomas to take the crops (Ancient Deed A 8907). His servant witnessed this charter and 
supplies a limit of date.

Hubert Walter became archbishop in 1193 and died 13 July 1205, but Bletsoe being then in the diocese 
of Lincoln this confirmation must have been during the vacancy of the see between the death of St. Hugh 
on 17 Nov. 1200 and the consecration of William of Blois on 24 Aug. 1203. The archbishop is not styled 
legate, an office he ceased to hold on the death of Celestine III, Jan. 1198. For the Broy family see 
BHRS xiii. 352-4. The charter here confirmed must be after the death or cession of Osbert prior of 
Cauldwell, predecessor of Hugh. Osbert occurs in 1186 (VCH Beds. i. 384), but the confirmation by the 
archbishop suggests a date little earlier than 1200. The hermitage was subsequently placed under the 
control of the hospital of the Holy Trinity at Kingsthorpe outside Northampton (BHRS xiii. 354), 
the bulk of whose title-deeds are among PRO Ancient Deeds: see in particular Ancient Deed C 5842.

- For Cockenhatch see VCH Herts. iv. 32. St. Guenolé (in Old Breton Winwaloe) was the founder of the 
abbey of Landevenec in Brittany. Early in the 10th century the monks of Landevenec, fleeing from the 
Viking invaders, carried the relics of the saint to Montreuil in the Pas de Calais, where his name was 
added to the dedication of the monastery of St. Sauve (A. de La Borderie, Hist. de Bretagne, ii. 369, 
510-12). The charters of Robert de Buron and of the abbot of Montreuil cited in this charter are printed 
in Mon. iv. 151; the latter is by Abbot Robert, whose predecessor occurs in 1177 and who himself occurs 
in 1182 and 1201, but had ceased to be abbot in 1203 (Gallia Christiana, x, col. 1298). These are followed 
(p. 152) by one of Roger de Buron, son of Robert, confirming the cession to Walden, from which we learn 
that the chapel at Cockenhatch was dedicated to St. Guenolé. Roger must have died without issue and 
been succeeded by his brother Walter, the present grantor. Walter’s filiation is confirmed by a suit at 
Hilary 1206, in which a later Roger de Buron mentions his father Walter and his grandfather Robert 
(Cur. Reg. Rolls, iv. 71). Walter must have been dead in 1203, when his son, this Roger, was claiming 
land in Bengeo, Herts. (ibid. ii. 114; cf. iii. 272). This family must be distinguished from Roger de Burun, 
the Nottinghamshire tenant-in-chief who returned his carta in 1166 (RB 342).

A manor of Scales lay in Tilney cum Islington, Norf. (Blomefield, Norfolk, viii. 469). Hugh de Montfort, 
the constable, was the tenant-in-chief in 1086. In 1325 Robert de Scales died seised of land in Islington, 
held of the honor of Haughley, Suff., or of the constable, by the service of half a knight and the payment of 
10 shillings for the guard of Dover castle (Cal. Ing. p.m., Edw. I, ii, No. 593). For the Scales family see 
HKF iii. 149. The donor succeeded his father in 1215, being under age (Rot. Lit. Claus. i. 217). He was of

Charter of Nicholas of Kennett, Cambs. (Keneht), son of Peter of Kennett, giving to Sibton abbey, Suff., 
in free alms half a mark of yearly rent which the monks used to render from the tenement which they 
held of him in Kennett, namely, from all the land which lies between the road of the ford of Kennett 
and the road of the ford of Freckenham, Suff., with meadow, water, and all appurtenances, and with 
all rights from any tenement or thing which the monks hold of him or his ancestors, so that they shall 
hold free from all secular service or claim. He has made this gift for the health of his soul and those of 
his father and all his ancestors. Warranty clause. ‘Testibus domino Euerardo le Franceys . Roberto et 
Henrico fratribus eius Ricardo de Banham Willelmo fratre eius Johanne de Mora Willelmo filio Walteri 
Waltero Torel Admundo de Suhet . Petro filio Ricardi . Thoma Blundo . Ranulfo Wysman et aliis.’ 
1252-3. 


SEAL on tag: round, 14, in.; grey-green. Shield of arms, three hounds statant; +4 S.? NICROUAL DE 
Roo. NET 


The ree of this charter is confused; the grantor is clearly releasing besides the rent all rights which 
he may have against the monks, but these rights are introduced as if they were part of the description 
of the particular tenement. The grantor’s family had held Kennet of Warenne from the time of Domesday; 
see Feudal Cambridgeshire, 148 et seq., and HKF iii. 342 et seq. By a charter dated 1161 (Harl. Chart. 
83 F 54, see HKF iii. 343) an earlier Nicholas of Kennet gave the tenement here in question to the abbey, 
reserving a rent of half a mark; Henry II confirmed this in 1163 (Cal. Chart. Rolls, ii. 96). The present 
charter releases this rent.

The donor must be the William who held Attleborough from circa 1217 to 1242-6. The handwriting 
suggests the middle part of this period. For the family see CP, 2nd ed. ix. 243 et seq. and HKF iti. 385 
et seq. Its tenure under Warenne in Norfolk can be traced back to at least the reign of Henry I, so that 
the name is derived from Mortemer-sur-Eaulne, Seine Infér., which was given to William de Warenne 
after the forfeiture of Roger de Mortemer in 1055. He was the ancestor of the Mortimers of Wigmore. 
There is no reason to suppose a blood relationship between the two families.

BS FACSIMILE, first 11 words.

et pedes' usque ad vicum quo itur ad ecclesiam de Sopiland’ . habendas et tenendas 
in feodo et hereditate . sibi et suis heredibus de me et meis heredibus per seruicium

satum de latitudine quinque pedum ad faciendum cursum aque a fonte de Stanwelle

cione dedit mihi prefatus Laurentius xxv solidos. Quare uolo et concedo quod ipse 
et heredes sui habeant et teneant predictam terram cum pertinentiis libere et hereditarie 
de me et meis heredibus per seruicium prenominatum. Et ego et heredes mei waranti- 
zabimus illi et heredibus suis hoc tenementum uersus omnes homines et feminas. Testibus 
Gilberto de Estewd’ . et Antonio de Sopiland sacerdotibus . Willelmo filio Willelmi . 
Henrico de... Johanne de Fleta . Willelmo Butelar’ Rogero filio Serlonis Gralanc’ 
Bruno Henrico de... Nicholas de Paclesham . Rogero de Berges . Si... Bald’ filio 
Radulfi. Waltero Muluell’ . Godefrido et Waltero de Sopiland’. 


SEAL on tag: round, 2 in.; red. Shield of arms, barry dancetty; no legend. 


The constables of Boulogne took their name, de Osterwic, from Austruy in the Boulonnais; they held 
Shopland of the honor of Boulogne (Round, Peerage and Family History, 158). The Pipe Rolls show 
Shopland to have been in the king’s hand and at farm from 1194 to Easter 1199. The constable seems to 
have lost it temporarily during the troubles at the end of John’s reign, but to have recovered it before 1219 
(Fees, 278) and to have been in possession in 1221-2 (ibid. 1435). By 1230 he was finally out of possession, 
and in 1236 the king granted it to Henry de Tybetot (Close Rolls, 1227-31, 429; Cal. Chart. Rolls, i. 220). 
The land in question was the manor of Butlers, held in 1261 by William le Botyller of Robert de Tybetot 
(Morant, Essex, i. 310); the name survives in Butler’s Farm (EPNS Essex, 201). The form of warranty 
against all men and women makes it unlikely that the charter is before 1194, and the limits of date are 
therefore 1199-1230. The handwriting suggests a date in the early part of the period.

For the donor see CP, 2nd ed. ix. 418-20. He was the younger son of Warin de Munchensy by Agnes, 

~ daughter and coheir of Payn fitzJohn. His elder brother Ralf was living in 1185 (Rot. de Dominabus, 50),

The stipulation that William should make an annual payment from his chamber is noteworthy. It would, 
however, probably be going too far to see in it evidence of an elaborate financial organization analogous 
to the public and private finances of the king, although something of the sort may have existed in the 
case of a great magnate like the earl of Gloucester (Stenton, English Feudalism, 68-9). The phrase here 
used probably means no more than that, the payment being temporary in nature, it would be made from 
petty cash and not charged on land or rent.

The charter here confirmed seems to have been made in 1277. It is recited in an inspeximus of Roger

Lathom. Tarbock was held of the earl of Lincoln (Fees, 1105). Henry de Lacy succeeded his father 
Edmund de Lacy in 1258, being then under age.

Basset, abbot 1127-34, was a kinsman. The document is not entered in the cartulary, but the writ of

It is not easy to date this charter closely. Roger succeeded his father J ohn as constable in 1190 and died 
in 1211. Moreover, the witness Philip de Orreby is not described as justiciar, an office which he held 
as early as Nov. 1207; this gives the limits of 1190-1207. In 1194 Roger succeeded to the Lacy honor of 
Pontefract and took the name of Lacy; on the Pipe Roll of 1196 he occurs as Roger de Lacy in one entry 
(PR 8 Ric. I, 174), though in others as Roger the constable, so on the whole it is not safe to draw an 
inference as to date from the absence of the new surname.

SEAL on tag: pointed oval, 13 x14 in.; brown. Beneath an estoile a shield of arms curved at top and 
sides, quarterly, 1, a lion passant guardant; 2, vair; 3, pily; 4, barry; + SIGIUL’ : GALUIENE : DE 
‘DAMMARNT, 

Galiena was daughter and heir of William de Dammartin (see note to No. 332 above). A jury in 1275 
gave a detailed account of her marriages (Rot. Hundred. ii. 193). On her father’s death in 1195 Richard I 
gave her wardship to William Briwerre, who married her to his brother John (Rot. Chart. i. 60, 123) 
in or before 1197 (PR 9 Ric. I, 239). John was living in Mar. 1210 (Cur. Reg. Rolls, vi. 21), but died 
without issue before Michaelmas 1210 (Fees, 61 n., citing PR 12 John).. At Michaelmas 1210 Robert of 
Burgate offered 700 marks for her and her land and in 1212 is returned as holding Mendlesham in his 
wife’s right (Fees, 138). According to the jurors in 1275 Galiena was still under age when married to 
Robert; if so she can hardly have been 7 years old when married to John Briwerre. Robert of Burgate 
died at some time after Easter 1220, when he occurs under Suffolk (Cur. Reg. Rolls, viii. 320). The 1275 
jurors said that on his death she married Ernald de Mandeville, whose name suggests that he was a 
descendant of Ernulf or Ernald de Mandeville, the disinherited son of the first earl of Essex (Round, 
Geoffrey de Mandeville, 227 et seq.). He may be the Arnulf de Mandeville, son of Arnulf de Mandeville, 
who occurs in Middlesex in 1219 (Cur. Reg. Rolls viii. 110). Galiena had two sons by her third husband: 
John, the donee of the present charter, and Hugh, to whom she gave the manor of Mendlesham (Rot. 
Hundred. loc. cit.). In 1228 Ernulf de Mandeville and Galiena his wife had a plea with Isabel countess 
of Oxford as to the custody of the land and heir of Robert of Burgate (Close Rolls, Hen. ITT, 1. 92). He 
_was Peter of Burgate, son of Galiena by Robert. In 1242-3 Peter held 2 fees in Burgate, Suff., of the 
earl of Oxford (Fees, 916), and in 1257-8 he consented to a gift of land in Great Missenden made by 
Galiena (Cartulary of Missenden Abbey, Bucks. Arch. Soc. 74). 

Norton Mandeville had been held by Galiena’s father (PR 7 Ric. I, 52). The mention of Waleran 
de Monceaux assists in dating this charter. In 1212 Compton Monceaux, Hants, was held by Waleran 
de Monceaux (Fees, 75), in 1219 and 1242-3 by William de Monceaux (ibid. 258, 705), and in 1256 by 
Waleran de Monceaux (see No. 479 below). This means that the charter was made about the middle of 
the 13th century.

No clue has been found to the identity of the persons or place mentioned in this charter. The only Wiche 
occurring in Domesday (i, f. 176) as on the fee of Tosny is Droitwich, but whereas there Tosny held only 
one hide out of ten, here the gift is one of the whole village. The British Museum Index Locorum (i. 21) 
tentatively suggests Ash Wicken in Norfolk, but there is no trace of its having been held of Tosny. A 
Silvester son of Simon occurs under Essex in 1156 and 1158 (PR 2-4 Hen. II, 18, 134), but no place of 
this name in that county seems to have been on the Tosny fee. Since the land had been held by the donor’s 
great-grandfather, this charter can hardly be earlier than the reign of Henry II; on the other hand, its 
form makes a later date unlikely.

This document represents the conclusion of the first stage in the process by which the king and his council 
contrived to deprive the untrustworthy holder of a great position of his title and lands. For the facts see

clearly the characteristic 13th-century reliance on the forms of legal process rather than on violent direct 
sentence against an enemy of the State. :

Letters of attorney of Peter son of Robert de la Mare, knight, to Philip le But to put Adam of Stratton 
into full seisin of the hundred shillings of yearly rent which Peter was wont to receive from Isabel de 
Fortibus countess of Aumale in Cricklade, Wilts. London: 22 Apr. 1279. 


SEAL On strip, a riband apparently torn off: round, 1} in.; brown. Shield of arms suspended by a hook, 
two lions passant guardant; a wyvern on either side of the shield; * SE..... ET ....T1.D. MARA. 


The charter conveying this rent to Adam is also in the Cottonian Collection (xxvii. 31). Adam paid 100 
marks sterling and was to hold the rent by a service of rendering a rose yearly at midsummer. It is dated at 
London a day earlier than these letters of attorney, but is in the same handwriting; no doubt they were 
both executed at the same time, but dated on consecutive days, a practice still followed in modern con- 
veyancing in cases of a similar nature. For the career of Adam of Stratton see N. Denholm-Young, 
Seignorial Administration in England, 77-84. At the time he acquired this rent he was the steward of the 
countess of Aumale.

This charter bears on its face the suggestion of forgery. That it was compiled in the 12th century there 
seems little doubt, but it was certainly not written, as its beginning implies, in the early years of Nigel’s 
episcopate. It may be that the monks forged it when Nigel was incapable of action in the last years of 
his life, for his seal is attached to the document. It should be compared with No. 420 which purports 
to be a similar grant from Hervey, the first bishop.

The grantor of this confirmation was the last earl of Surrey of the second house of Warenne. Maud 
de Nereford, for whose salvation it is said to be, was the mother of some of his illegitimate children. 

1. This is the foundation charter. The only fixed limits of date are the death of the donor’s father on 
11 May 1138 and the donor’s departure in 1147 on the crusade on which he died. The foundation is 
usually said to have taken place shortly before the earl’s departure on crusade, but the fact that the charter 
mentions his mother and two brothers while remaining silent as to his wife, the Countess Ela, and his 
daughter Isabel suggests very strongly that the true date is earlier and before his marriage. 

2. The Countess Isabel of this charter was the daughter and heiress of the founder, the third earl. She 
married as her first husband, William, the second son of King Stephen, who died without issue in Oct. 
1159; thereafter she married the grantor of this charter, Hamelin, a natural son of Geoffrey, count of 
Anjou. The mention of King Richard shows the charter to be not earlier than 1189, while Roger de Cailli, 
a witness, died before 1199 (HKF iii. 383). The statement that Richard I had held the land in question 
seems to be an unintelligent following by the draftsman of a similar statement regarding Stephen in the 
previous charter. A feast of the Holy Sepulchre is found on 15 July in Egerton MS. 2902, a sacramentary 
of about the year 1200 apparently executed for a monastery connected with Jerusalem, and it has been 
noted on the same date at Fontevrault, Tours, Beaulieu-lés-Loches, and Nantes.® 


1 hominum BS. 3 Information supplied by Mr, Francis Wormald. 
2 est pro nobis omitted BS. 


nN 


288 SIR SIMONDS D’EWES 


3. The grantor’s father, Earl Hamelin, died in Apr. 1202, while the witness Ralf de Pleiz had been 
succeeded by his son Hugh by 1212 (Farrer, op. cit. iii. 335). An earlier Ralf de Pleiz witnesses charters 
of William the third earl, but the style of the present charter shows it to be one of the sixth earl. 

4. Henry II is spoken of as dead; the limits of date are therefore 1189 and the grantor’s death in 1202. 

5. The countess’s name shows this to be a charter of the sixth earl. The limits of date are therefore 
1202 and 1232, when the witness Nicholas de Kenet had been succeeded by his son Peter (HKF iii. 343). 

6. The address to Reginald de Warenne shows this to be a charter of the third earl.

Edmund de Lacy was son and heir of John de Lacy, earl of Lincoln, by Margaret suo iure countess of 
Lincoln, daughter of Robert de Quincy, grandfather of the donor, by Hawise sister and coheir of Rannulf 
earl of Chester and Lincoln. His mother Margaret outlived him and he seems never to have been invested 
with the earldom, though occasionally styled earl and receiving the third penny (CP, 2nd ed. vii. 680). 
This instrument seems to have been a step in an exchange between Roger and Edmund, for in Roger’s 
inquisition it is stated that he held the manor of Elmsall in South Kirkby, Yorks., W.R.., for life in exchange 
for the manors of Kippax and Scholes (Cal. Ing. p.m. i, No. 587). Kippax, however, belonged to the 
Lacys from early times; before 1123 Hugh de Laval, when temporarily in possession of the Lacy lands, 
gave or more probably confirmed the church to Pontefract priory (EYC iii, No. 1486), and the gift was 
confirmed by Thurstan and Roger, archbishops of York (ibid., Nos. 1469, 1479) and by Theobald arch- 
bishop of Canterbury (ibid., No. 1475). In 1233 a notification by Walter archbishop of York states that 
the priory had recovered the advowson against Roger de Quincy in an assize of darrein presentment 
(Chartulary of St. John of Pontefract, Yorks. Arch. Soc., Rec. Ser. xxv. 74), and in the same year John 
de Lacy, Edmund’s father, in a letter to the archbishop acknowledged the priory’s right to the advowson 
(ibid. 39). In these circumstances it is difficult to see on what ground Roger here purports to convey the 
advowson to Edmund. The limits of date are fixed by Philip Lovel’s appointment to the treasurership 
in 1252 and the death of the witness Robert de Quincy in 1257 (Matthew Paris, Chron. Mai., RS v. 609).

This charter, the foundation charter of Furness abbey, is in facsimile throughout and appears to have 
been a very beautiful document. It is curious that in the coucher an additional witness, ‘Roberto de 
Saccavile’, appears between the last two names in the list. In view of the extreme care and accuracy of 
the man who made the facsimile in BS it is difficult to accept the conclusion that in this charter, done 
apparently with particular precision, a witness can have been omitted. The year of grace and the indiction 
agree but the epact is that of 1128. It seems an example of the epact being changed not on 1 Jan. but 
on the previous 1 Sept. (Giry, Manuel de Diplomatique, 151). It follows that this charter must be later 
than 31 Aug. 1127. For a commentary on the charter see Farrer, loc. cit.

SEAL placed transversely on tag: pointed oval, c. 3? x2 in.; brown; chipped on dexter side. The queen 
standing crowned in mantle and gown, a fleur-de-lis sceptre in her right hand and a bird on her left; 
MATIUDIS DEI GRATIA.............. Slit only for seal tag now visible on original charter. 


This charter is immediately preceded in the Holy Trinity register (Ducarel, loc. cit.) by one of King Stephen 
also dated at Hedingham, which confirms it and is witnessed by Eustace the king’s son, Henry of Essex, 
Richard de Lucy, and Warner de Lisors. Queen Maud, the foundress of St. Katherine’s hospital, died 
at Hedingham, Ess., the caput of the Vere honor, on 3 May 1152 (Robert de Torigny, 166); a passage 
from the Holy Trinity register printed by Hearne in his notes on William of Newburgh (ii. 705-6) says 
that three days before her death Ralf prior of Holy Trinity arrived at Hedingham specially commissioned 
by the archbishop to administer the last sacraments, ‘cujus consilio eadem regina multas fecit elemosinas’. 
In view of this and of the king’s presence at Hedingham it would seem that the charter may safely be 
ascribed to the queen’s death-bed. Robert de Gant, who succeeded Philip de Harcourt as chancellor in 
1140-1, was still chancellor at this time, since he witnesses, as such, a charter of the king which, being 
also witnessed by Hugh du Puiset as bishop of Durham, must be of the year 1154. The witness ‘A. cancel- 
larius’ was therefore the queen’s chancellor; he is otherwise unknown. A charter in the Holy Trinity 
register shows William of Ypres to have been the original donor of the rent in Queenhithe here confirmed.

The queen’s confirmation was necessary because both Braughing and Bendysh were held of the honor 
of Boulogne, of which she was the heiress (Fees, 237-8). Being attested by both William of Ypres and 
Richard de Lucy, this charter can hardly be earlier than 1140 (Round, Geoffrey de Mandeville, 45, 49); 
on the other hand, it seems to be covered by the terms of the confirmation of Eugenius III dated 26 Oct. 
1147 (Mon. vi. 154). For other charters of the queen and Hubert the chamberlain see Mon. vi. 152-3.

Fragments of SEAL on tag; green. Obv.: a lion passant. Rev.: a ship. See the note below. 


The transcripts of this charter and of No. 432 printed in Manx Soc. vii, as also the coloured engravings 
of their seals which form the frontispiece of vol. v, profess to have been taken from the original charters 
in the British Museum. The editor Mr. Oswald writes (v. 8) that Dr. Oliver ‘has been so fortunate as to 
discover two others’ (i.e. these two charters) ‘among the Cottonian Manuscripts in the British Museum, 
fast hastening to decay’. A comparison of the engravings of the seals in vol. v with the drawings of them 
in BS yields an illuminating result. The drawings in BS show the seals in a very fragmentary condition, 
large portions of the circumference being broken away; the engravings show the seals after the lapse of 
more than two centuries in exactly the same condition to a hair’s breadth. The matter, however, does 
not rest there; in the BS drawing of the seal to No. 428 two long ends of the parchment tag are shown 
protruding below the seal and these display an elaborate series of twists and curls; all this is reproduced 
with the most meticulous accuracy in the engraving. Even if the drawing faithfully represented the con- 
dition of the tag in 1641 it is incredible that it should be the same in 1860, the date of the engraving. 
When it is added that there is no trace of these charters in the British Museum at the present day the 
conclusion is irresistible that they were destroyed by the Cottonian fire and that the engravings, and there- 
fore also the printed transcripts, were taken from BS, which, therefore, was used shortly before 1860.2 

Sandscale where the charter passed lies on the coast a mile and a half north of Furness where the gift 
was made. Gift and execution clearly took place on the same day, but there is a discrepancy between 
the year of grace and the regnal year which raises a difficulty. According to the Chronica Regum Manniae 
et Insularum (ed. Munch, 20-3). Harald succeeded his father Olaf in 1237, being then fourteen years old. 
He refused to do homage to his overlord the king of Norway, who in 1238 expelled and deposed him. 
In 1239 he went to Norway, where he stayed two years and more, and ultimately finding favour with 
the king of Norway was restored to his kingdom in 1242. He died in May 1249, being drowned on his 
way back from Norway. The regnal year in this charter must be reckoned from his restoration which 
was no doubt the beginning of his effectual reign, but even so his third year reckoned from 1242 would 
have ended some time in 1245. In the absence, however, of any clear knowledge as to how Harald 
reckoned his regnal years it seems safe to adopt the date of the year of grace. It is tempting to identify 
the first witness with the ‘Yvarus miles’ who killed Reginald, Harald’s brother and successor, after a 
reign of but a few weeks (Chronica, 24). 

There is no copy of this charter in the Coucher Book of Furness abbey.

Nigel de Mowbray’s charter giving the church of Banstead to Southwark priory is printed Mon. vi. 171; 
as it is there preceded by a charter of Tirel de Maneriis also giving the church to Southwark, it was, no 
doubt, really a confirmation. Nigel obtained Banstead with his wife Mabel whose parentage is unknown 
(CP, 2nd ed. ix. 372). He was the son of Roger de Mowbray by Alice de Gant, widow of Ilbert de Lacy 
who died in 1141; he could not therefore have been born before 1142. He was present at the Council 
at Clarendon in Jan. 1164, but his marriage, and consequently the confirmation to Southwark, can hardly 
have been much earlier. Henry de Blois, bishop of Winchester, to whom this notification is addressed 
died on 9 Aug. 1171.

The brothers whose agreement is here confirmed were members of the family afterwards known as Bohun 
of Midhurst. Humphrey de Bohun, contemporary with the Conqueror, had among his children two sons, 
Richard and Humphrey, who both left issue. Humphrey was the ancestor in the male line of the Bohun 
earls of Hereford. Richard, known as Richard de Meri, in 1092 gave his little son Humphrey to be a monk 
at Marmoutier, of which the priory of Bohon was a cell (CDF, No. 1213); to this notification is added 
a later clause containing a confirmation by Lucy, Richard’s wife, and his sons Robert, Henry, and 
Humphrey and their daughter Hawise. Richard must therefore have married twice, Lucy being his 
second wife. Humphrey was the monk and the two elder sons must have died without issue, for in the 
middle of the 12th century Enjuger de Bohun, another son of Richard, in a charter in favour of the family 
priory of St. George at Bohon, mentions his father Richard de Meri (ibid., No. 1215). Enjuger married 
Adelise, also mentioned in his charter to Bohon priory. She was a daughter of Stephen count of Aumale 
(ibid. 971). In 1172 Enjuger was holding 7 fees in the Cotentin (RB 627), and continuous entries in the 
Pipe Rolls show that he held Bloxham, Oxon., from 1158 to 1175 when he appears to have died. His 
brother Alexander (ibid. 669) predeceased him. It seems probable that they were sons of the second 
marriage. On Enjuger’s death the male issue of Richard de Meri became extinct. 

The lands of Enjuger passed through a sister, daughter of Richard de Meri, to a different family. In 
a charter which cannot be later than 1108 (CDF, No. 669) Savaric, son of Ralf de Beaumont vicomte 
of Le Mans and his wife Cana, together with his wife Muriel granted the church of Easebourne, Suss., 
to the abbey of St. Martin at Séez; it is witnessed by their sons Ralf and Savaric. By a charter which 
cannot be earlier than 1141 Savaric fitzCana, as he is usually called, and Muriel his wife gave the churches 
of Marden and Racton, Suss., to Lewes priory (Suss. Rec. Soc. xl. 79). The charter mentions their sons 
Ralf, Savaric, and Geldwin, whose identity with the brothers of the present charter is certain. A charter 
of Richard I of the year 1190 (Cal. Pat. Rolls, 1358-62, 534) shows that on Enjuger’s death Bohon and 
his Norman lands passed to Savaric son of Savaric fitzCana as his heir. His heirship can only have come 
through his mother Muriel, Enjuger’s sister. Savaric son of Savaric fitzCana in his turn died without 
issue and the Norman lands passed to his nephew Franco son of the Geldwin of the present charter, to 
whom they as well as the English lands were confirmed by Richard I’s charter mentioned above. The 
Norman lands were lost in 1205, but by the possession of Bohon Franco had become Franco de Bohun, 
and as the Bohuns of Midhurst his descendants are known to history. 

All the places mentioned in the charter are in Sussex. Since Savaric was his brother Ralf’s heir, it was 
only necessary to deal in this confirmation with the lands which were being diverted from the ordinary 
course of devolution and were going to Geldwin. Savaric’s title of heir meant that he needed no confirma- 
tion for the lands he retained. There is no information about Savaric’s lands, but in 1166 he held 3 knights’ 
fees of the earl of Arundel (RB 201). Geldwin’s share was a large one, and the case may be compared 
with the agreement made a few years later in the court of the earl of Derby, by which the succession of 
two members of the Shirley family was reversed (Stenton, English Feudalism, 51). Geldwin married a lady, 
Estrangia, whose origin and kinship with the emperor are discussed by Mr. A. L. Poole (Essays... presented 
to R. Lane Poole, 264-8). Their son Savaric, archdeacon of Northampton and later bishop of Bath, 
played an important part in international diplomacy.

The date of the present charter can be narrowly fixed. Thomas Becket was chancellor from the begin- 
ning of the reign until 1162, but the king left England in Aug. 1158 and did not return until 1163. On the 
Pipe Roll of 3 Henry II (p. 80), ie. at Michaelmas 1157, Savaric and Geldwin each owe 100 marks pro 


terra sua. No such entry appears on the previous roll, so that it may be inferred that Ralf did not die 
before 1156.

Sawtry abbey was founded in 1146 or 1147 by Simon de Senlis IJ, earl of Huntingdon, who established 
there monks from Warden abbey, Beds. (de Sartis). Though in form a gift, the present charter is really 
a confirmation by which Malcolm ratified the foundation by the rival line of the Senlis earls. Malcolm 
obtained the earldom from Henry II in 1157 (CP, 2nd ed. vi. 644); the witness Waltheof abbot of Melrose 
died 3 Aug. 1159 (Chron. de Mailros, Bannatyne Club, 76).

Richard earl of Cornwall was elected king of the Romans on 13 Jan. 1257 and crowned at Aachen on 
17 May. When he went to Germany in 1257 he left Fulk Basset, bishop of London, and his brother 
Philip Basset in charge of his English affairs. Philip Basset inherited Wycombe, Bucks., when Fulk Basset 
died in 1259. This made him the most important of Richard’s tenants in the honor of Wallingford. 
Philip played a prominent part in the politics of his day, being justiciar 1261-3; for his life see DNB. 
The indiction date in this document is erroneous; the sixth indiction was 1263. The indiction was used 
in dating imperial documents, but an English clerk might easily fall into error.

The donor, who held Conington of his brother’s honor of Huntingdon, was an illegitimate son of Simon 
de Senlis II, earl of Northampton; see BH RS ix. 181. In the cartulary of St. Andrew’s priory, Northampton 
(Cott. MS. Vesp. E xvii, f. 9), is a charter of Earl Simon III giving to the priory the church of Whissen-

Huntingdon the death must have been after Earl Simon obtained the honor in 1174. The present charter 
must be earlier than the death in 1184 of Earl Simon, since he confirmed the gift (Won. v. 212).

Lilford was-a member of the honor of Huntingdon, and the date of this charter therefore falls between 
1174 when Earl Simon obtained the honor and his death in 1184, but since it is witnessed by Simon the 
earl’s son who predeceased him (see No. 438) it appears to be earlier than 1184. Both before and after 
the period 1174-84 the family of Olifard were holding Lilford (HKF ii. 354-5). Since they were adherents 
of the Scottish kings (Round, Feudal England, 223) the then Olifard tenant may have been disseised when 
William the Lion was deprived of the honor in 1174. The elaborate provisions for an exchange in case 
the donor should be unable to warrant the gift are probably due to the existence of a possible Olifard 
claimant.

The original charter of Ursel de Crasmesnil together with one of his son Luke confirming it are at Belvoir 
and are printed in full in Hist. MSS. Com., Rutland Report, iv. 98-9: the original of this charter is not 
mentioned in the report as now at Belvoir; it is, however, entered in the cartulary (ibid. 133) together 
with the two Crasmesnil charters, which are followed by charters of William, chamberlain of Tancarville, 
and his son Ralf confirming the gift as overlords. This tenure under Tancarville shows the family to 
have come from St-Vincent-Craménil about 44 miles west of Tancarville, Seine-Infér., an identification 
which is supported by the fact that in the reign of Henry I a Walter de Crasmesnil gave a rent in England 
to the Tancarville foundation of St. Georges de Boscherville (CDF, No. 197). The occurrence of Robert 
de Gant as chancellor fixes the date between his appointment, probably in 1140, and the death of the 
king; see notes to Nos. 110 and 424 above.

The original charter of Ralf d’Aubigny is at Belvoir and is printed in full in Rutland Report, iv. 100; its 
limits of date are 1174-82, since in a charter confirming it (ibid. 113) Richard archbishop of Canterbury 
states that the gift was made in his presence and the archbishop’s charter is witnessed by Waleran arch- 
deacon of Bayeux who became bishop of Rochester in 1182. Ralf the donor was a brother of William 
d’Aubigny II of Belvoir (ibid. 99), who died in 1166. The present charter is therefore more probably 
one of William d’Aubigny III than of William IV. It is impossible to determine its date with any precision, 
but on the whole the circumstances point to the late 12th century rather than the early 13th.

The grantor was son and heir of Hawise countess of Aumale by her second husband William de Forz: 
he succeeded his mother in 1214 and died 29 Mar. 1241. The hand suggests a date very early in the 
century and it seems safe to assume that the monks would obtain this confirmation soon after the grantor’s 
accession to the lands; it is significant that two earlier confirmations by Hawise and her first husband 
William de Mandeville are within two years of her succession and marriage. The formula of address 
to all the grantor’s men, French and English, comes oddly after the loss of Normandy. Used as it is in 
Hawise’s charter of 1212-14 also, it seems probable that the clerks who wrote these confirmations based 
them on the charter issued by William count of Aumale at Easter 1181 (Rutland Report, iv. 5). The 
formulas are almost identical.

Letter of William Malbys, Robert de Ros (Roos) of Ingmanthorpe, and William de Plumpton, knights, 
addressed generally and notifying that they have quitclaimed to Nicholas de Cantilupe (Cauntelow) and 
Joan his wife, Nicholas and William sons of William son of the aforesaid Nicholas de Cantilupe all right 
and claim in 300 marks of yearly rent which had been reserved to them by an indented charter of feoffment 
made by them to Nicholas, Joan, Nicholas, and William. Sealing clause. York: 27 Mar. 1354. 


Three SEALS on tags: (i) round, 1;; in.; red. Ona traceried background a couched shield of arms, a chevron

(ii) round, 1 in.; red, Within a circle surrounded by a cusped panel a shield of arms, three water-

(ili) round, 1; in.; red. Couched shield of arms, five fusils in fess; above a helmet with lambrequin

PUVMPTUR 


Nicholas de Cantilupe made complicated arrangements, of which this document is one stage, to disinherit 
his son William in favour of that son’s children, Nicholas and William. The writers of this letter were 
feoffees to uses. In the event the two grandchildren predeceased their father and left no heirs. Nicholas 
died at Avignon in 1370-1 and William was murdered in 1375. Their father at length inherited part of 
the family possessions. See CP iii. 113 et seq., and Some Sessions of the Peace in Lincolnshire, LRS, 30. 
Ixv et seq. The editor of the latter volume gives an interesting account of the murder.

SEAL! on plaited uncoloured cord: round, c. 23 in.; green. Oby.: a triple-towered castle, the wall diapered 
lozengy; *« SIGIULVM [CIV...... ] RIDELES : REGIS : Rey. (on the tag as drawn): St. Peter

Drake supposed the archbishop here addressed to have been Gerard, but Farrer rightly regards him as 
Geoffrey, illegitimate son of Henry II, archbishop 1191-1212. Geoffrey left England in 1207 as a protest 
against excessive taxation and never returned. Drake describes this document as ‘amongst the records 
of the city on Ouse-bridge’, and it is now in the BM. In 1641 it was in Sir William Savill’s possession, 
perhaps because he was on the Council of the North which sat at York. Farrer (loc. cit.) has collected 
what information can be found about Ralf Nuvel. He belonged to a York family, possibly the same 
family which in Henry I’s reign produced Ralf Nuvel bishop of the Orkneys.

SEAL on tag: pointed oval, 24 x 1? in. when perfect; fragmentary; uncoloured. The Virgin crowned, seated 
on a carved throne, holding the Child with nimbus on her left knee, a fleur-de-lis on her right hand; 
ROMA Rn tose S alghnaean s Cf. BM 4168 


In 1202 before the judges at Lincoln an inquest was held to find out whether the patronage of Thornholme 
priory belonged to the king or John Malherbe. The jurors recorded that King Stephen founded the priory 
and Henry II gave Appleby (of the honor of Peverel of Dover), in which the priory is, to William Long- 
sword his brother, who gave it to John Malherbe, ‘so that there were two priors there through John 
Malherbe’. The jurors recited William Longsword’s charter, which, they said, was confirmed by Henry II 
(Earliest Lincolnshire Assize Rolls, LRS xxii. 6). In 1202 and in 1208 the prior’s name was Walter (VCH 
Lincs. ti. 168). John Malherbe is returned as holding the soke of Appleby as late as 1212 (Fees, 190), 
but the hand of the document suggests a date in the late 12th century.

Memorandum of an agreement between John Neville, knight, of Wymeswold, Leics. (Wymondwold), and 
Amice his wife of the one part and William Doddingeseles and Agnes his wife of the other as to the partition 
of the inheritance of Amice and Agnes in the manor of Hinton Hall (Henketon) in Haddenham and lands 
and tenements in Elm, Cambs., by the decease of Simon de Lisle (Lile), father of Amice and grandfather 
of Agnes. William and Agnes recognize Amice as heir and parcener of the lands and tenements in Hinton 
and Elm, and grant that if John and Amice can recover Amice’s reasonable share in the manor of Hinton 
against William de Tuddenham, John Barbour, and Alice his wife, she shall retain it as befits a third 
parcener. If John and Amice cannot so recover, William and Agnes his wife for themselves and their heirs 
grant that John and Amice shall for their lives share in Agnes’s part of the manor of Hinton (Hinketon’) 
as a parcener should, as fully as if they had recovered it by judgment of the king’s court, so that after 
the decease of John and Amice that part shall revert to William and Agnes and their heirs. John and 
Amice and William and Agnes mutually agree that they will each faithfully help the other against any other 
parcener. John and Amice will deliver when required to William and Agnes the writings and muniments 
touching Simon de Lisle in their possession against the security of a bond. The parties have bound them- 
selves to observe this agreement by the pledging of faith. Sealing clause. ‘Hiis testibus domino Hugone 
perpetuo vicario de Elm . Willelmo de Schirebek’ . Willelmo de Makesely . Willelmo de Quere . Johanne 
de Dikeby Waltero filio Willelmi et aliis.”’ Elm: 1 Oct. 1275. 


Two SEALS on tags: (i) tag only; (ii) oval, c. 1 x $ in.; green. Beneath a female head with head-dress a 
shield of arms, two bars; no legend. 


In 1302-3 John Ode of Lynn held for the term of his life one-sixth of a knight’s fee in Elm of the heirs 
of Simon de Lisle, who held of the bishop of Ely (FA i. 141).

Letter patent of Robert son of Roger to his uncle Hugh de Baliol, lord of Hélicourt, asking him to pay

Robert son of Roger (1247-1310) was son of Roger son of John (d. 1249). John was son of Robert lord 
of Warkworth by Ada daughter of Hugh de Baliol, lord of Barnard castle. John de Baliol, king of Scot- 
land, and Hugh de Baliol, lord of Hélicourt, were Ada’s brothers, so that the recipient of this letter was 
the writer’s great-uncle, not his uncle (Northumberland County History, v. 26 and vi. 73).

the ancestor of the fitzWilliams; his mother was Aubreye de Lisours, daughter and heir of Robert 

de Lisours, by Aubreye daughter of Robert de Lacy; she had two previous husbands, Richard son of

of the family see EYC iii, No. 1690 n. and CP, 2nd ed. v. 518. The original grant of these mining rights 

to Byland was made by Godric (EYC iii, loc. cit.). For other confirmations see Yorkshire Deeds (Yorks.

‘Arch. Soc., Rec. Ser. lix, v. 37-8 and notes). See also Add. Chart. 7432 (BM Facsimiles, No. 64), a some-

_ a large number of charters dealing with this property are in the British Museum (Add. Chart. 7409-65 
and 7467-82). Henry II is mentioned as dead, and since the charter is addressed to an archbishop of

but she was then of great age and must have died soon after.

Notification by Alice de Rumilly, daughter of William son of Duncan, in her

tenants of Eaglesfield from the cornage they used to pay for the land they held there. 
(1209-15)

Omnibus has litteras visuris uel audituris Alicia de Bomell’! filia Willelmi filii Duncani 
salutem. Noueritis uniuersi me in libera potestate et viduitate mea . concessisse . et

Tag only for seal. 


Eaglesfield was part of the liberty of Cockermouth in Cumberland, inherited by Alice de Rumilly as part 
of her share in the lands divided between the three daughters of her mother, Alice de Rumilly, and William 
son of Duncan II, king of Scotland. The Alice de Rumilly of the present charter married first Gilbert 
Pipard, who died c. 1192, and secondly Robert de Curtenay, who died 1207-9. In her second widowhood 
she made gifts to tenants in her Cumberland possessions and it seems probable that the present charter 
was made at this time. She died in 1215. The handwriting supports this suggestion. For the grantor’s 
family see C. T. Clay in EYC vii. 10-19.

Henry of Blois was bishop of Winchester 1129-71 and legate 1 Mar. 1139-Sept. 1143. yy he is not styled 
legate it cannot have been made during his legation. Henry the bishop’s chancellor witnessed a charter 
for St. Denis, Southampton, dated 1151 (BM Facsimiles, No. 32). It seems probable that this charter 
was made about the middle of the century also. Michelmersh is near Mottisfont and was given to the 
priory by its founder, William Briwerre (Mon. vi. 481). Walkelin appears to be the predecessor in title 
of William Briwerre at Michelmersh. This charter therefore carries the recorded history of the Briwerre 
family in Hants to the middle of the 12th century; see note to No. 473 below. The witness William 
Briwerre was probably the grandfather of John’s minister.

Notification of Robert de Mandeville to King John that he has given all his land 
of ‘Hulle’ to William Briwerre. (1212-16) 


BS FACSIMILE. 


Reuerendo domino suo .J. dei gracia regi Anglie . domino Hibernie . duci Normannie . 
et Aquitannie . comiti Andegauie . suus deuotus Robertus de Mandeuilla . salutem .

SEAL on strip: round, 13 in.; green. A crescent with star above; ** SIGIUL’ ROBERTI DE MANOS 


Hulle is now lost, but may be represented by Hall Place in Michelmersh, since in No. 473 a fishpond 
in Hulle is said to be next Braishfield, which is about a mile from Hall Place. The donor is Robert 
de Mandeville, who recovered the honor of Marshwood, Dors., in 1206 (Rot. Lit. Pat. i. 61b). An 
account of the family is given in the fine recorded in the Pipe Roll of 10 John (p. 113, n. 8), by which 
Robert finally secured the honor. The Mandevilles of Marshwood and the Mandevilles of Erlstoke, Wilts., 
descended from brothers, Geoffrey and Roger, who came to England from the Cotentin with Richard 
de Reviers, ancestor of the earls of Devon. These Mandevilles have no connexion with the family of the 
earls of Essex. The present letter cannot be earlier than 1212, when Robert was holding 60 solidatae of 
land in Hulle (Fees, 75).

Margery was one of the daughters of William Briwerre the elder and coheir of William the younger. She

proffered £500 for livery of the lands which descended to him from his father and his grandmother 
Margery Briwerre (HKF, loc. cit.). For the family of La Ferté see EYC vi. 53-4.

Ralf Gernun was son of Osbert de Gladefen and brother of Roger Gernun and Oliver de Gladefen 
(Bracton’s Note Book, No. 564). In 1202 William Briwerre offered 500 marks for the marriage of Hugh 
de Morville’s daughter with her inheritance for his son Richard or, failing him, for his nephew Ralf Gernon 
(PR 4 John, 256). It seems that a sister of William’s must have married Osbert de Gladefen. William 
gave Lavington (c. 1215) to Roger Gernun in marriage (Note Book, No. 1687). William Briwerre, bishop 
of Exeter, must have belonged to the family; probably he was another nephew of William. In 1208 William 
Briwerre, clerk, nepos of William Briwerre, was presented to the church of Braunton in the Exeter diocese 
(Rot. Lit. Pat. i. 86 b). Hugh Wake was son of Baldwin Wake by Isabel daughter of William Briwerre 
the elder. She was ultimately coheir of her brother William the younger. William the elder cannot have 
been dead when this charter was made, for his soul’s health is not mentioned. He died in 1226. The 
bishop was consecrated on 21 Apr. 1224. Ralf Gernun is still so young that he has not acquired his 
full seal.

For William Briwerre see DNB and No. 466. According to a charter of King John (Rot. Chart. i. 39) 
his grandfather William held land in Hampshire and the forestership of the forest of Bere in the time 
of Henry I, and his great-grandfather in that of the Conqueror. He founded the priory of Mottisfont 
before 1204, when King John by charter confirmed the earlier benefactions (Mon. vi, pt. i. 483). William 
of Shorwell became deputy sheriff at Michaelmas 1217 and his successor occurs at Christmas 1223. 
Another charter of William Briwerre (Mon. vi, pt. i. 481, No. iii) is contemporaneous, having the same 
witnesses. He married Beatrix de Valle (Oliver, Monasticon Exoniense, 173) and died in 1226.

Hugh derived his name from Coulonces, dép. Calvados, near Vire. His ancestor Richard de Coulonces 
died in 1125 leaving a large family, of whom Hugh, the eldest, succeeded him (Orderic, ed. le Prévost, 
iii. 17). Thomas, probably Hugh’s son, witnesses charters of Henry II circa 1170 and 1172 (Delisle, 
Recueil des actes de Henri IT, i. 446, 580). Between 1185 and 1189 Henry II confirmed the grant of 
Thomas de Coulonces and Hugh his son of the church of St. Jean-des-Baisants, dép. Manche, near 
Torigny, to the abbey of St. Lé (ibid. ii. 366). Hugh the son must be the present grantor. He witnessed 
a charter of Richard I at Montrichard in 1190 and in 1197 was one of those who swore to observe the 
treaty between Richard and the count of Flanders (Landon, Itin. 35, 118). He adhered to Philip II in 
1205, and at Rouen on 13 Nov. was one of the Norman barons who certified the rights which the kings 
of England had against the Norman clergy (CDF, No. 1318). His land at Stebbing, Ess., was forfeited 
(Fees, 615). He figures in the registers of Philip II as holding 2 fees in the bailiwick of Vire, one of them 
at Vaudry dép. Calv. (Rec. des hist. de France, xxiii. 707). His younger brother Thomas held of him 
4 fees which owed service to the castle of Torigny (ibid. 61 1). Hugh’s gift of Cadbury was confirmed by 
John in a charter dated at Woodstock 23 Oct. 1204 (Mon. vi. 483).

earl of Shrewsbury (Salop’), has released and quitclaimed to John Fray, chief baron of the exchequer, all 

his right and claim in the manor of Great Munden (Munden Furnyvale) and in the advowsons of the church

the homage and service of one knight’s fee for the said manor to be performed by John Fray, his heirs 
1 Tilustrated in Jewitt and Hope, Corporation Plate, i. 290-1, with discussion of the legend on the counterseal.

and assigns, being tenants of the said manor to John Talbot and his heirs. Sealing clause. ‘Hiis testibus 
Radulfo domino de Cromwell Radulfo domino de Sudeley Johanne Fortescu milite capitali iustic’ de 
Banco domini Regis Ricardi Neweton’ milite . capitali iustic’? de communi Banco domini Regis et multis

No seal or tag shown. 


The grantor was the son of John Talbot, created earl of Shrewsbury in 1442, by Maud daughter of Thomas 
Neville by Joan daughter and heir of William de Furnival lord Furnival (CP, 2nd ed. v. 589-92). The 
grantee became a baron of the exchequer in 1425-6, second baron in 1435, and chief baron in 1436; he 
ceased to hold office in 1448 and died in 1461 (Foss, Judges of England). For Great Munden, otherwise 
Munden Furnival, see VCH Herts. iii. 125. In 1285 Gerard de Furnival enfeoffed John de Kirkeby, 
bishop of Ely, of the manor and advowson, from whom it ultimately came to Thomas Hayward; on his 
death in or shortly before 1447 it was sold to John Fray. The present transaction thus regulated the terms 
of an existing subtenancy from Furnival and since it did not create a new tenancy it did not infringe the 
provisions of the statute Quia Emptores. It is witnessed by both chief justices.

of the said manors, &c., and to be dowered in the third part of all his manors, &c., and besides her dower 
of the manor of Saltfleetby to have the other two-thirds of that manor for life. If he shall have male issue,

and in payment of the testator’s debts at the discretion of the feoffees. If he die without male issue and

his debts and performance of his will, he and the said Elizabeth to be enfeoffed in the said manors, &c.,

On 5 Dec. 1384 a commission of oyer et terminer was issued on the complaint of John duke of Lancaster 
that certain persons named, not the present feoffees, had ejected him from land in Fillingham, Lincs., 
belonging to him until the majority of William son and heir of William Fraunk, knight (Cal. Pat. Rolls, 
Ric. IT, ii. 507); William the father was living in 1381 (ibid. 88). This suggests that the present William 
had only lately come of age in 1383. In 1424 there is mention of a tenement in Louth belonging to William 
Fraunk, knight (Cal. Close Rolls, Hen. VI, i. 184). In 1431 Walter Tailboys and others held land in 
Somercotes, Saltfleetby, Louth, Ashby, and Clee of the feoffment of William Fraunk, knight (FA iii. 353, 
354, 361), which seems to identify the lands here in question. In line 6 above ‘Ma dame de Northfolk 
et le viscount de Nicole’ is interlined above ‘notre Seigneur le roi dengleterre et per John Philipot de 
Londres’, which is cancelled. Professor Plucknett has been so good as to look at this document. He 
points out that Fraunk had already made his will, doubtless dealing with chattels only.

Charter of John de Chilton giving to Robert, son of Robert, son of Robert de Clifford, lord of Ellingham 
(Elyngham), and to Elena his wife, John’s daughter, the manor of Murton beside Norham (Morton); to 
hold to the said Robert and Elena his wife of the chief lords of that fee by the services due and accustomed. 
If Elena die without heirs of her body begotten by Robert, then to the said Robert and the heirs of his 
body. If the said Robert die without heirs of his body, then to the aforesaid Robert lord of Ellingham 
for his life and after his decease to John, brother of Robert son of Robert, and the heirs of his body. If 
the said John die without heirs of his body, then to Thomas his brother. If Thomas brother of John die 
without heirs of his body, then to Andrew son of the aforesaid Robert, lord of Ellingham, and the heirs 
of his body. If Andrew die without heirs of his body, then to Roger his brother and the heirs of his body. 
If Roger die without heirs of his body, then to John his brother and the heirs of his body. If John die 
without heirs of his body, remainder to the right heirs of the aforesaid Robert lord of Ellingham. Warranty 
and sealing clauses. ‘Hiis testibus Roberto de Manerio tunc constabulario castri de Norham dominis 
Roberto Gray Thoma Gray Roberto de Hornecliff militibus Roberto de Hagarston’ Ricardo de Clifford 
Roberto de Tuggall’ Patricio de Gossewick et multis aliis.’ Murton: 16 Nov. 1328. 


Tag only for seal. 


It will be noted that this elaborate settlement is entirely for the benefit of the Clifford family; if Elena 
outlived Robert and had issue by a second husband she and her children would take nothing, although 
she had no issue by Robert. Robert de Clifford, the son of Robert lord of Ellingham, was already dead 
at the date of this charter, and his son Robert, the husband of Elena, died without issue in his grand- 
father’s lifetime. On the death of Robert in 1339, therefore, the remainder to John de Clifford took effect. 
He murdered John de Coupland, a warden of the Marches, whereupon his lands were confiscated and 
given in 1366 to Joan de Coupland, the widow of his victim: see Northumberland County History, ii. 243.

the right heirs of Robert Cumberworth took effect. It follows that Katherine wife of Marmaduke Con- 
stable or her issue became heirs or coheirs of her brother Robert Cumberworth.

Charter of John de Pelham, knight, giving to the church of the Holy Trinity of Hastings and the convent 
there a place called Tornorsland in the parish of Warbleton containing 60 acres of land and 40 acres of 
heath; to hold to them and their successors of the chief lords of that fee by the services due and accustomed, 
for the purpose of the construction there of a new priory, inasmuch as the house and church of the afore- 
said priory are destroyed and wasted ‘per tempestates et cretinam marinam’. Warranty and sealing clauses. 
‘Hiis testibus Rogero Fynelds milite . Vincentio Fynche . Ricardo Cralle . Adam Iwode . Johanne Penherst 
et multis aliis.’ Warbleton: 12 June 1417. In facsimile: Henrici quarti post conquestum xij’. 


By letters patent dated 23 Oct. 1412 the king recites the ruin of the original buildings at Hastings and the 
fact that Sir John Pelham had granted the priory with the king’s licence certain lands at Warbleton upon 
which they had begun to construct a new church and habitation; the king goes on to grant certain lands 
in Withyham in augmentation (Cal. Pat. Rolls, 1408-17, 451). The present charter must therefore be more 
a confirmation of a transaction already carried out at any rate in part than an original gift. The note 
in facsimile at the foot of the charter may possibly have to do with the time of the original gift.

The copy in BS is extremely defective, more than a third of the document being omitted, and in these 
circumstances it has been thought sufficient to print the original without noting the omissions and variants 
in BS. The will seems of sufficient interest to justify reproduction in extenso, the more so as it seems to 
throw some light on the provincial draftsmanship of this period. In this connexion attention may be drawn 
to the fact that the original draftsman used the colloquial term ‘heirs male’, a limitation strictly speaking 
unknown to English law; a subsequent corrector started to alter this to the proper term, ‘heirs male of 
his body lawfully begotten’, but he tired of the work and left the later occurrences of ‘heirs male’ un- 
corrected: the result is a very slipshod instrument. For a discussion of the limitation to ‘heirs male’ see 
CP, 2nd ed. vii, App. E. Professor Plucknett comments that ‘Pelham has made a “‘last will”. To make 
it in triplicate is not so usual as to make three separate wills in favour of the three beneficiaries. Each 
would need a copy as part of his title to the lands.’

Charter of John abbot of Combe, Warw., and the convent of the same granting and binding themselves 
to Guy le Breton and his heirs to make a daily chantry at the altar of St. Edmund the archbishop in the 
church of Combe for the souls of William le Breton, father of the said Guy, and of Avice his wife and their 
ancestors by one particular monk deputed thereto. The abbot and convent shall present two monks to 
Guy and his heirs of whom they shall accept one to serve the said chantry during his whole life; and when 
it shall happen that the monk so chosen is prevented from serving by ill health or other good cause, 
another monk of the house shall be assigned to serve the chantry until the first monk be recovered or 
shall cease to hold office. When the monk so chosen shall die the abbot and convent shall present two 
others of whom Guy and his heirs shall accept one, and so on in perpetuity. On each presentation there 
shall be made an indented schedule between the abbot and convent and Guy and his heirs with the names 
of those presented, the one accepted, and the form of presentation. For the performance of all this the 
abbot and convent submit (obligamus) themselves and their successors as also their grange under the wood 
called ‘Wodegrange’ and their grange of Binley, Warw. (Bilneye) to the distraint and coercion of Guy 
and his heirs until any defect there may be in the said chantry or in presentation be amended to the

was made between Agatha Lestrange and the abbot of Combe by which the latter recognized that the

charter was probably made soon after the fine. For the descent of Wolston from Richard de Freville

For the early history of the Arden family see note to No. 46. There were three generations, all named 
William, who in succession held land in Radbourn. The first of them was party to a final concord in 1194, 
entered in the Combe Cartulary (Cott. Vitellius A 1, 121 v.) with other charters of which this is one, all 
apparently issued by the same William. He may have been a younger son of Thomas of Arden, for a 
charter of the second William speaks of the ‘consent of Thomas of Arden my lord’ (ibid. 121). Robert 
Balraven was party to a final concord in 1206 (Feet of Fines, 247/7/16). John of Ladbrooke occurs between 
1 John and 25 Henry III (Dugdale, Warwickshire, 1765 ed. 232). In the eyre roll of 1221-2 (Rolls of 
Justices in Eyre . . ., Selden Soc. lix) several of the witnesses appear; John of Ladbrooke (cases 385, 528, 
&c.), Robert Balraven (case 922), Henry Boscher (case 445), and William of Southam (cases 356, 571). 
The hand of the charter suits a date early in the 13th century.

be the same as the mill of Pirte, since presumably the marriage portion of Agnes was derived from Wolston.

At some time before 1153 William Giffard the elder gave to Bordesley abbey the land of ‘Suhanger’ in 
Langley, Warw., now represented by Songar Grange; it had been held by William son of Hunger, who 


CLEMENT THROCKMORTON, ESQ. 349 


surrendered it to William for the purpose of this gift. Charters 507, 508, 510, 512, and 513 deal with this 
land, and it will be observed that except 510, which is the latest, they are entered in BS in their reverse 
chronological order, 513, the original gift, being the last. The donor was ‘a younger son of the family 
of Giffard of Fonthill, of which an account is given by General Wrottesley in Staffordshire Collections 
(W. Salt Soc.), N.s. v. 9-13. The following pedigree illustrates the charters here printed. 


Robert Giffard of Fonthill, living 1135 


| 
Gerard Giffard of Fonthill, William Giffard, grantor of 


occurs 1159 and 1166 No. 513; d. before 1159 s.p. 
| | | | | 
Gerard Giffard, d. s.p. Robert Giffard of Fonthill, William Giffard, grantor of 507; Andrew Giffard, heir to 
living 1202; d. 1209 s.p. living 1176 and c. 1200; d. s.p. Robert and William 


William Giffard is a frequent witness to charters of Ro ger earl of Warwick, but he must have held Songar 
of Geoffrey of Glympton, who confirms the gift to Bordesley (No. 508). Songar doubtless formed part 
of the 17 fees held of the earl of Warwick by Geoffrey (RB 325). Another charter of William Giffard the 
elder made in the time of Earl William of Warwick (1153-85) states that Songar had been given him by 
Earl Roger (Bromley Davenport Coll., Hist. MSS. Com., 10th Rep., App. vi. 98). The names of the 
witnesses suggest that the charter was made some years after William became earl of Warwick. By it 
William confirmed the gift stating that Songar had been given him by Earl Roger; he stated that his con- 
firmation was conditional on Richard of Dassett and Gilbert his son and William son of Hunger, who 
claim the land by hereditary right, releasing it to the Church for ever. By another charter of the same 
collection Andrew Giffard confirms the land to Bordesley for the souls of his uncle William, the donor, 
and of his own brother William (ibid. 101). Robert Giffard must have been the elder brother of William, 
for he was in possession of Fonthill in 1176 (PR 22 Hen. II, 176), while at the same time William appears 
to have been involved in litigation touching land in Dasset with Gilbert de Unestonescote (ibid. 183, 184). 
This Gilbert is doubtless the Gilbert son of Richard of Dassett of William Giffard the elder’s second 
charter mentioned above. William the elder’s rights in Songar appear to have passed to William, the 
younger brother. The youngest brother, Andrew, was the ultimate heir of both. The present charter is 
not earlier than 1153, when William Giffard the elder was still living and not later than 1159, when William 
Cumin of Snitterfield was dead (see No. 509). The Dassett which the Giffards held was Avon Dassett 
(Dugdale, Warwickshire, 1765 ed. 380). Presumably the William Giffard who witnesses No. 5O1 is 
William Giffard the younger.

The date of place, Apud Diuisas, is absent from BS facsimile. On the other hand, it occurs in Birch’s 
copy from the original. Moreover, Dodsworth (MSS., vol. xc, f. 158 v.) inserted it in his copy from BS, 
and it also figures in the Mon. copy which would have been supplied by Dodsworth. The evidence for 
its existence is therefore overwhelming. In the facsimile the writing completely fills the right-hand bottom 
corner of the charter and the top of the turn-up of the fold comes immediately below the last line. The 
probable explanation is that the date of place was at the beginning of the next line and was hidden by 
the fold. Dodsworth doubtless saw the original charter. The point is of substance since the date of 
time depends on that of place, and has been so calculated by Mr. White whose conclusions are here 
adopted.

The real founder was Waleran count of Meulan, who started the abbey and supplied the original endow- 
ment; he apparently transferred his founder’s right of patronage to the empress, but there is no reason 
to believe that she ever gave a penny piece. Curiously enough, a similar case occurs in Normandy where 
Waleran founded the abbey of La Valasse, for which there exists a charter of date 1154-9 of the empress 
as foundress which follows closely the present one and indeed must have been modelled upon it (Somménil, 
Chronicon Valassense, 94). The last witness, Robert de Formoville, was a tenant of Count Waleran in 
Normandy and witnessed many of his charters.

Nos. 515 and 517 appear to be contemporaneous, for the witness list is very nearly the same in each 
charter. In 1086 the constable of Chester was William fitzNigel, founder of Runcorn priory, which was. 
later moved to Norton. He probably died in or before 1130, since the king had made fine on behalf of his 
son and successor, another William, with the earl of Chester, and William the younger paid an instalment 
of the debt (PR 31 Hen. I, 88). William the younger died without issue leaving two sisters as coheirs, this 
Agnes and Maud wife of Albert Grelley. Agnes must have been the elder, since the office of constable 
passed through her. She married first Eustace fitzJohn as his second wife. He was killed in Wales in 1157 

1 Sic. 


SIR WILLIAM CONSTABLE 355 


(DNB). She married secondly Robert fitzCount, the grantor of No. 517. Both her husbands were suc- 
cessively constable of Chester iure uxoris. William the younger must have died or been succeeded as 
constable by Eustace not later than the beginning of 1139, for a charter of King Stephen witnessed by 
Roger bishop of Salisbury confirms to Bridlington priory the church of Flamborough given by William 
fitzNigel and confirmed by Eustace (EYC ii, No. 1144). Eustace left a son Richard fitzEustace, who, by 
Aubreye de Lisours, left a son John the constable, the grantor of No. 519. There is no evidence for the state- 
ment that Richard fitzEustace succeeded his father as constable of Chester.’ On the contrary, the wording 
of the present charter suggests that he was dead, in which case he did not survive his stepfather, Robert 
fitzCount, who when this charter was made was constable of Chester (No. 517). From Robert fitzCount 
the office passed to John, son of Richard fitzEustace. John occurs as constable on the Pipe Roll of 1166 
(PR 12 Hen. II, 51). By that date it may be presumed that Robert fitzCount was dead. The witness, Roger 
son of the constable, or of William the constable, as in No. 517, must be an illegitimate son, presumably 
of William the younger. 

The priory of Watton was founded by Eustace fitzJohn (Mon. vi. 955), whose gifts were confirmed by 
William de Vescy, his son and heir by his first wife (EYC ii. 1110). Watton was held of the Fossard fee 
and Hilderthorpe of the Gant fee. The tenure of Loddington is not clear; probably it was held of the 
earl of Chester de constabulatu (see No. 519); in 1242-3 it was held by Richard le Baud of the heir of 
John de Lacy, earl of Lincoln and constable (Fees, 935). These charters supply the date and occasion 
of the entrance of the Baud family into Northamptonshire. 

A most curious feature of these charters is the occurrence in both of an apparent reference to a ‘little 
council’. In the charter of Agnes to Hurley priory printed in Madox, Formulare (No. ccccxv) the phrase 
paruo consilio appears again, this time apparently attached adjectivally to the name of one of the witnesses. 
Collation with the original document at Westminster (W.A.M. 3565) shows that Madox’s reading is 
correct. Nevertheless, the phrase cannot be dismissed as a nickname. In the Hurley charter the words 
follow the name Robert. In the two charters here being considered the description follows the name of 
Richard of Chester. Moreover, in neither No. 515 nor in No. 517 can the words be adjectival. In each 
case they are preceded by et. It is also worth noting that in No. 515 the phrase et petit consilii comes at 
the end of the witness list and apparently is a contemporary addition. The et is the tironian sign, whereas 
throughout the charter the ampersand is employed. The words seem an afterthou ght, added half in French 
and half in Latin. The conclusion, in fact, seems unavoidable that a small council, probably of household 
officers, must lie behind the phrase. The reference to the lord’s secret discussion of his affairs with his 
council in the Byland abbey foundation document led the author of English Feudalism to the conclusion 
that in 1140 a baronial council existed in the Mowbray fee (p. 73 and n.). These charters suggest that 
twenty years later a similar institution existed in the fee of the constable of Chester.

The family of Constable of Flamborough and Holme to which this charter and Nos. 522-5 relate was 
an offshoot of the constables of Chester (see note to No. 515). Two charters of Gilbert de Gant, earl of 
Lincoln, for Bridlington priory, of which the limits of date are 1147-56, are witnessed by a Robert son 
of the constable (EYC ii, Nos. 1157, 1219), and his identity is disclosed by Earl Gilbert’s foundation 
charter for Rufford abbey, c. 1148, witnessed by ‘Roberto filio Willelmi constabularii Cestrie’ (on. 
v. 518). As William fitzNigel, constable of Chester, had given the church of Flamborough to Bridlington 
priory (EYC ii. 440) and the arms of Constable of Flamborough appear to have been a variant of those 
of the constables of Chester! (Trans. East Riding Ant. Soc. xii, 8), it seems permissible to identify this 
Robert as the ancestor of Constable of Flamborough. Chronologically he is hardly likely to have been son 
of William fitzNigel, a Domesday tenant, but more probably of his son William; if so, he was illegitimate, 
since the heirs of William son of William were his sisters. There is no trace of a constableship of Flam- 
borough, and the name seems to be a surname inherited from the constables of Chester. The early pedigree 
of the family is obscure, and it is not clear that the Robert of the present charter is identical with the Robert 
of 1148; if, as is probable, the grantor of No. 522, whose sister was married after their father’s death, was 
his son, there were probably two Roberts, father and son. In a charter which appears to be rather later 
than the present grant Robert and his son William demised common of pasture in Holme upon Spalding 
Moor to Ormsby abbey (Gilbertine Charters, LRS, xviii. 65). The first occurrence of the witness Roger 
Arundel is in 1180-1 (PR 27 Hen. IT, 50). Farrer (EYC, loc. cit.) explains fligheres as flechers, bowed or 
bent timbers for the framework or covering of the bows of a ship.

Bridlington cartulary show them to have been in the possession of that house. Robert the present

and Ralf left issue and that the cross-remainders in these two charters did not take effect.. A charter of 
Robert Constable the nephew (ibid. 201) confirms to the priory all the gifts of Thomas de Alost his patruus; 
Gilbert de Alost must therefore have married the mother of Robert Constable the grantor, and Thomas 
and Ralf must have been his brothers of the half-blood. The witness William of Ottringham was dapifer of 
the count of Aumale; he died before 1194 (EYC iii. 81). By a fine at Westminster on 16 Oct. 1182 Thomas 
de Alost quitclaimed to Bridlington priory a carucate in Fraisthorpe (ibid. ii, No. 1220); since the present 
charter seems to be a restoration consequent on Gilbert’s death of the Alost holding in Fraisthorpe it 
is presumably earlier than this fine. Both charters are very closely written; the witness list in particular 
is crowded. The clerk has contrived to include the names but only by violent contractions. Stephen 
de Merfi’ is extended as ‘Merston’ by Farrer, but it is impossible to read the facsimile in BS in any way 
but Merfl’, a good form for Marfleet.

Nos. 526 and 527 cannot as they stand be accepted as genuine. Each is open to serious objections. No. 526 
purports to be a charter of Earl William of Warwick (1153-84). A set of detailed boundaries is common 
in the middle of the 13th century but highly unusual in the 12th century. The long clause beginning ‘in 
feedings and pastures’, too, is of very dubious validity; a 12th-century clerk could hardly have envisaged 
the unfortunate phrases ‘in fields and hedges, in ways, in paths, in boundaries and in moors, in hedges 
and in ditches, in waters, in pools, in marshes, in courts, in villeinages’. A 12th-century clerk would 
have found no difficulty in spelling ‘infangenetheof’, but he would have been surprised had his employer 
insisted on warranty and sealing clauses couched in the stereotyped phrases of the next century. No. 527 
professes to be a charter of Earl William’s successor, Earl Waleran (1185-1204). It makes the grantor 
*quitclaim’ the office to his cook, a very curious phrase. Even in Earl Waleran’s day warranty and sealing 
clauses were by no means of the common form of charters. The man who drafted No. 527 endeavoured 
to give it a genuine appearance by cutting not merely the usual one strip, but two strips at the bottom of 
the document and putting the seal on them. It would be more natural for a charter of Earl Waleran to 
have used a tag for the seal. Nevertheless, behind these two highly suspicious documents there probably 
lies a genuine grant. The opening phrases of each document have a ring of authenticity about them. It 
is fortunate that a genuine charter of Rannulf II, earl of Chester (1 129-53), survives to set out the words 
by which a great magnate gave to his cook the office of his father and the land that went with it (Stenton, 
English Feudalism, 104). A charter of this sort probably lies behind the forgeries here printed. The reason 
for and the time of the forgeries can only be guessed. It may be conjectured that a double incentive 
moved the drafter, a need to define the common rights of the lord of Woodloes and a desire to enjoy the 
protection of warranty and sealing clauses. Woodloes is now part of Warwick; and even in the 13th century 
a growing borough, in which an important castle stood, may have threatened the lord’s privileges. With 
regard to the warranty and sealing clauses comparison may be made with plate xxxi in Facsimiles of Early 
Charters from Northamptonshire Collections (NRS iv). One of the charters there portrayed is a genuine 
grant of 1180-9 with no warranty clause. The other is apparently a version of the same charter ‘improved’ 
by the inclusion of a clause of warranty. Dugdale (Warwickshire, 1765 ed. 339) quotes this charter 
“ex ipso autog. penes R. B. gen.’, accepting it as genuine. He does not refer to No. 527.

The grantor of this charter was described as Peter son of William up to 1123, but on the Pipe Roll of 1130 
he is called Peter of Studley and thereafter is styled thus or as Peter Corbezun. For his family see note 
to No. 153, a much later charter issued by him. The donor’s father, William son of Corbucion, held 


1 Cf. BM 6263, probably the same. 2 Sic. 


SIR EDWARD PETO 367 


Wolverton in chief when Domesday Book was compiled. The description of the grantor as P. son of 
William, the primitive writing and spelling of the charter, and the simplicity of its phrases all suggest 
a very early date. The precise annual value put at this early date on a fraction of a knight’s service is 
remarkable. Noteworthy also is the precise statement that the land is to be held hereditarily ‘because 
he has become my man therefor’. The witness list with its precise gradation of precedence, the three 
priests, the two masters who are not priests and so are of lesser dignity, the clerk, and then the laymen 
confirms the early date of the document. Dugdale (Warwickshire, 1765 ed. 467) quotes this charter 
ex autog. penes .. . Stanton gen.

No seal or tag shown. 


The grantor was a trusted official of Henry II. Much information respecting him will be found in P. Meyer, 
LT’ Histoire de Guillaume le Maréchal, iii. 98 n. The latest limit of date is 1178, when Richard du Hommet, 
who was Bertram’s foster-father (Mon. v. 662), became a monk (Delisle, Robert de Torigni, ii. 93 n.). The 
earlier limit is suggested by Nicholas who does not occur as a royal chaplain before about 1166. A charter 
of Richard du Hommet dated 1170 is witnessed by Bertram de Verdun, Gerold de Normanville, and 
Walter the Breton (ibid. iv. 261). The wording of the charter suggests that Bertram surrendered the land 
to his overlord Henry of Arden who regranted it to Walter. The efficient draftsmanship bespeaks the 
royal clerk. The charter has very much the appearance of a contemporary royal charter.
